stories.name: Isaac Newton
stories.title: The Boy Who Asked Why the Apple Falls
stories.hook: A quiet farm boy watches an apple fall — and discovers the invisible force that moves the whole universe.
text: A long time ago, in 1643, a baby boy was born on a small farm in England. His name was Isaac Newton. His father died before he was born, and Isaac grew up quiet and small, but his head was full of questions. While other children played, Isaac built little windmills and water clocks with his own hands.

One day, sitting under a tree, Isaac watched an apple fall to the ground. Everyone had seen apples fall before. But Isaac asked, "Why does it fall down? Why not up, or sideways?" He thought and thought, and discovered a great secret: an invisible force called gravity pulls everything toward the Earth — the apple, the rain, even the Moon.

Isaac wrote laws that explain how everything moves, from a rolling ball to the planets in the sky. That is why, hundreds of years later, we could fly rockets to the Moon — because one quiet boy never stopped asking why.
textM: A long, long time ago — on Christmas Day in the year 1643 — a very small baby was born on a quiet farm in England. His name was Isaac Newton, and he was so tiny that his mother said he could fit inside a big cooking pot. Nobody in the village that night could have guessed that this little baby would one day explain how the whole universe moves.

Isaac's father died before he was born, and when Isaac was small his mother had to go away for a while, so he lived with his grandmother. He was a quiet boy who didn't say very much — but his eyes were always busy. He watched the rain slide down the window. He watched the shadows creep across the wall as the sun moved. And inside his head, questions piled up like autumn leaves.

While other children played ball in the village square, Isaac built things. He built a little windmill that really spun, copying the big one being built nearby — and when there was no wind, he put a mouse inside on a tiny wheel to make it turn! He built kites, and paper lanterns, and a water clock that dripped, drop by drop, to tell the time. The neighbors thought he was strange. Isaac didn't mind. Builders and wonderers often look strange to people who have stopped wondering.

When Isaac grew up, he went to the great University of Cambridge to study. But then something frightening happened: a terrible sickness spread through the cities, and the university had to close. Isaac packed his books and went home to the quiet farm. Most people would have rested. Isaac did the opposite — alone in the countryside, with nothing but time, his mind opened up like a window. He later called it his "year of wonders."

It was there, in the orchard, that the famous moment came. Isaac sat thinking under an apple tree, and an apple fell — thump — onto the grass. Everyone in the world had seen apples fall. But Isaac asked the question nobody thought to ask: "Why does it fall down? Why not sideways? Why not up? And how high would the apple have to be before it stopped falling?" He looked up past the branches, up at the pale daytime Moon, and a shiver of an idea ran through him: what if the same invisible pull that grabs the apple… reaches all the way up to the Moon?

That invisible pull is called gravity, and Isaac discovered its secret: everything pulls on everything else. The Earth pulls the apple, and the apple pulls the Earth — just a tiny, tiny bit. The Earth holds the Moon in its arms, the Sun holds the Earth, and that is why the planets glide around the sky in great smooth circles instead of drifting away like lost balloons.

Isaac also wrote three simple rules — his laws of motion — that explain how everything moves: why a rolling ball slows down, why a rocket pushes up when fire rushes down, why you slide forward when a bus stops suddenly. Hundreds of years later, when engineers wanted to fly people to the Moon, they didn't need new rules. They used Isaac's.

So tonight, when you see the Moon following you home, remember the quiet boy from the farm, who watched, and wondered, and never stopped asking why. The same gentle gravity that holds the Moon in the sky is holding you softly in your bed. Let it hold you now… all the way into sleep. Goodnight.
textL: Are you cozy? Then let me tell you the whole story of Isaac Newton — the quiet boy who discovered why things fall, and why the Moon never does.

A long, long time ago, on Christmas Day in the year 1643, on a small farm called Woolsthorpe in the English countryside, a baby boy was born much too early. He was so small and so weak that his mother, Hannah, said he could fit inside a big cooking pot, and the neighbors whispered that he might not live through the winter. But the tiny baby held on. He breathed, and slept, and grew — slowly, stubbornly — and that quiet stubbornness stayed with him his whole life. His name was Isaac Newton.

Isaac's father had died before Isaac was born, and when Isaac was three, his mother married again and went to live in another village, leaving him with his grandmother. The farmhouse was quiet. The fields were quiet. And Isaac became a quiet boy — the kind who sits by the window during a storm, not because he is sad, but because he is watching. He watched raindrops race down the glass and wondered why some ran faster than others. He watched the sun throw shadows across the wall, and he began marking where the shadows fell at different hours, until the whole wall became a giant clock that only he could read.

At school in the nearby town, Isaac was not the best student at first. But he had clever hands and a head full of ideas. While other boys played, he built. He built a little windmill, copying the big one the workers were building near the village — except his really turned, and when the wind stopped, he put a little mouse inside on a wheel, and the mouse-power kept it spinning! He built kites and flew them at dusk with paper lanterns tied to their tails, so that they floated over the village like small warm stars. He built a water clock that told time drop by drop, and sundials so good the family used them. The neighbors shook their heads: "What a strange boy." But strange, sometimes, is just what wonderful looks like at the beginning.

Isaac's mother wanted him to become a farmer, like his father. So one year, she took him out of school to tend the sheep and sell vegetables at the market. It went terribly. Isaac would let the sheep wander off while he sat under a hedge reading a book, or he'd build a little water wheel in the stream while the cows walked into the neighbor's field. His uncle and his old schoolmaster saw the truth: this boy's mind was not made for farming. They persuaded his mother to send him back to school — and then onward, to the great University of Cambridge.

At Cambridge, Isaac read everything he could reach. He filled notebooks with questions — page after page, question after question, like: What is light? Why does the Moon follow the Earth? What makes things fall? He wrote in one notebook, in Latin: "Plato is my friend, Aristotle is my friend — but my best friend is truth."

Then, when Isaac was twenty-two, something frightening happened. A terrible sickness — the plague — spread through the cities of England, and the university closed its doors. Everyone was sent home. Isaac packed his books and rode back to the quiet farm at Woolsthorpe, where the only sounds were the wind, the sheep, and the creak of the apple trees.

And there, far from teachers and lectures, alone with his thoughts, the most amazing eighteen months in the history of science quietly happened. Isaac later called it his year of wonders. He invented a whole new kind of mathematics. He took a beam of sunlight into a dark room, passed it through a glass prism, and discovered that plain white light secretly contains all the colors of the rainbow. And one golden afternoon, in the orchard, he sat thinking under an apple tree…

Thump. An apple fell onto the grass beside him. Now — everyone in the world had seen apples fall. Farmers saw it every autumn. Nobody thought it was interesting. But Isaac looked at that apple, and then he did the thing that made him Isaac: he asked, "Why? Why does it fall straight down? Why not sideways? Why not upward? What is pulling it?" And then he asked the question that changed everything. He looked up, past the branches, where the pale daytime Moon was hanging in the blue sky, and he wondered: "Does the pull that grabs this apple reach higher than the treetops? Higher than the clouds? Does it reach… all the way to the Moon?"

It does. Isaac worked it out with his new mathematics, carefully, line by line. The same invisible pull — he called it gravity — holds the apple, the rain, you, me, and the Moon itself. But wait, you might ask: if the Earth pulls the Moon, why doesn't the Moon fall down like the apple? Here is Isaac's beautiful answer: the Moon is falling — it is falling around the Earth! The Moon rushes sideways so fast that as it falls, the Earth's surface curves away beneath it, and so it circles round and round, falling forever without ever landing, like a marble rolling round and round the inside of a great bowl. That is what an orbit is. The Moon is the apple that never hits the grass.

Isaac also wrote down three simple rules — his laws of motion — that explain every push and pull in the world: why a sled glides on and on across smooth ice, why you need to pedal harder to start a bicycle than to keep it rolling, why a rocket rises when its fire rushes down. Sailors used his rules to cross oceans. Engineers used them to build bridges and trains. And three hundred years later, when people finally flew to the Moon in a rocket, the scientists guiding them were still using Isaac's three rules, exactly as he wrote them by candlelight.

Isaac grew old and famous. He became the head of the Royal Society, where the wisest people of the land met, and he was made a knight — Sir Isaac Newton. But he never grew too grand to wonder. Near the end of his life, he said something lovely: "I seem to have been only like a boy playing on the seashore, finding a smoother pebble or a prettier shell than usual, while the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me." After all he had found — the rainbow hiding in light, the mathematics of the heavens, the secret of the falling apple — he still felt like a child at the edge of the sea, with everything left to explore.

And that, little dreamer, is the real secret of Isaac Newton. Not the apple. Not the equations. It is this: he kept the question "why?" alive in his heart his whole life, the way you keep it alive now. So tonight, when you lie still and feel your blanket resting softly on you — that gentle heaviness is Isaac's gravity, the same kindly pull that holds the Moon in the sky and the planets around the Sun. The whole universe is holding you in place, very gently, like a hand on a sleeping bird.

Close your eyes now. Somewhere high above the rooftops, the Moon is falling around the Earth, round and round, slow and faithful, just as it did over Isaac's orchard long ago. It will keep circling all night while you sleep. Everything is moving just as it should. Goodnight, my love. Sleep well… and dream big dreams.

stories.name: Albert Einstein
stories.title: The Boy Who Dreamed of Riding on Light
stories.hook: He was so slow to speak that his family worried — then his daydreams changed how we see time and space.
text: In 1879, in a town in Germany, a boy named Albert Einstein was born. He was slow to speak — so slow that his family worried. But when Albert was five and sick in bed, his father gave him a compass. Albert watched the needle always point north, moved by something invisible, and he was filled with wonder.

At school, some teachers thought he daydreamed too much. But Albert's daydreams were special. As a young man he asked himself, "What would I see if I could ride on a beam of light?" No one had ever asked such a question.

While working a simple job in an office, Albert did his thinking in the evenings. His ideas became the theory of relativity — it showed that time and space can stretch and bend, like rubber. His famous little equation, E = mc², revealed the enormous energy hidden inside tiny things.
Albert taught the world that imagination is more important than knowledge — and that a slow-speaking boy can change how humanity sees the whole universe.
textM: In 1879, in a town in Germany called Ulm, a boy named Albert Einstein was born. Soon afterwards his family moved to the city of Munich. Albert was slow to speak. He seemed to think each sentence all the way through before he let it out of his mouth, and his family worried about him. But there was nothing wrong. He was simply busy inside his own head.

When Albert was about five, he was ill in bed, and his father brought him a compass to cheer him up. Albert turned it this way and that. However he moved it, the little needle swung back and pointed north. Something he could not see was pushing it. He never forgot that feeling. All his life he believed that something deeply hidden lay behind ordinary things.

His mother gave him a violin, and he grumbled about practising until he discovered Mozart — and after that he played all his life, especially when a problem would not come loose. His uncle Jakob had a workshop full of wires and magnets, and he taught Albert algebra like a game: it is a merry hunt, he said, for a little animal whose name you do not know, so you call it x until you catch it.

When Albert was twelve, someone gave him a small book of geometry. He loved it so much that he called it his holy little book, and he worked through every proof. A young medical student named Max came for dinner each week and brought him science books, and the two of them talked about stars and atoms while the soup went cold. Albert did not want to be told the answers. He wanted to work them out for himself.

At school, some teachers thought he daydreamed far too much, and they did not like being questioned by a boy. But Albert's daydreams were doing serious work. When he was about sixteen, he asked himself something nobody had ever thought to ask: what would I see if I could ride along beside a beam of light?

Being a dreamer did not pay the rent. Albert took a quiet job in Switzerland, at an office where inventions were checked, and he did his real thinking in the evenings and on the walk home. In 1905, in one astonishing year, this young clerk published papers that changed physics forever. One of them held his idea of relativity: that time and space are not fixed, but can stretch and bend, like rubber.

From the same thinking came a tiny equation, E = mc², which showed the enormous energy hidden inside the smallest things. Years later, during an eclipse of the sun, astronomers measured starlight bending exactly as Albert had said it would. Overnight, the daydreaming boy became the most famous scientist in the world, with his wild hair and his crooked, friendly smile.

Later he moved to America and lived in a town called Princeton, where he walked to work, played his violin, and answered letters from children who wrote to ask him questions. He always answered them seriously. Albert taught the world that imagination matters even more than knowledge — and that a slow-speaking boy with a compass can change how all of us see the universe.

stories.name: Marie Curie
stories.title: The Girl Who Studied in Secret
stories.hook: Girls were not allowed at university — so she studied at night, in secret, and won two Nobel Prizes.
text: In 1867, in Warsaw, Poland, a girl named Maria was born. Her family was poor, and in her country, girls were not allowed to go to university. But Maria loved learning so much that she studied in secret, at night, sharing books with other brave young women.

She saved every coin she earned, and one day she took a train to Paris, France, to finally study science. She was often cold and hungry, but she was the best student in her class. There she became Marie Curie.

Working in an old shed with her husband Pierre, Marie discovered two new elements no one had ever seen — she named one polonium, after her beloved Poland. She discovered that some rocks give off invisible rays of energy, and she called it radioactivity.

Marie became the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize — and then she won a second one! Her discoveries help doctors see inside our bodies and fight sickness today. She showed the world that no door stays closed to a girl who refuses to stop learning.
textM: A long time ago, in 1867, in the city of Warsaw in Poland, a little girl named Maria Skłodowska was born. She was the youngest of five children, and her family's apartment was full of books, chalk dust, and big ideas — her father was a science teacher, and her mother ran a school for girls. Little Maria learned to read when she was only four, so early that it surprised everyone.

But Maria's childhood was not easy. Her family had little money, and her country was ruled at that time by a faraway empire that did not even allow children to learn in their own Polish language at school. Hardest of all, in Maria's world there was a rule that seems unbelievable now: girls were not allowed to go to university. Not because they weren't clever. Simply because they were girls.

Maria refused to let her mind be closed like a door. At night, in secret, she joined other brave young women at what they called the "Flying University" — secret classes that moved from house to house so no one would catch them, where girls studied science and history by lamplight, listening for footsteps on the stairs.

Maria made a plan with her big sister Bronya. First, Maria worked for years as a governess, teaching children in the countryside, and sent her wages to Bronya, who was studying in Paris. Then Bronya sent for Maria in return. And so, one cold day, Maria climbed into a fourth-class train carriage with a wooden stool, a blanket, and her books, and rode across Europe to Paris — to the famous Sorbonne university, which welcomed women.

In Paris she was often cold and often hungry — some evenings she ate only bread and tea, and in winter she piled every piece of clothing she owned on her bed to keep warm. But she was finally, finally allowed to learn, and she was so happy that she finished first in her physics class. There she met a gentle, brilliant scientist named Pierre Curie, and they married. Maria became Marie Curie.

Together, in a leaky old shed that other scientists laughed at, Marie and Pierre studied a mysterious rock called pitchblende that gave off invisible rays of energy. Marie boiled it, stirred it, and sifted it — tons of it, day after day, her arms aching — until she discovered not one but two brand-new elements hiding inside. One she named polonium, after her beloved Poland. The other, which glowed pale blue-green in the dark like a tiny captive star, she named radium. She called the strange energy radioactivity.

The world was amazed. Marie became the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize — and then, years later, she won a second one, in a different science, something no person had ever done. Her discoveries helped doctors see inside our bodies and fight sickness, and they still do today.

So remember tonight, little one: once there was a girl who was told 'no' — no school, no university, no science — and she answered with patience, courage, and a train ticket. No closed door stays closed forever to someone who refuses to stop learning. Now close your eyes, and glow softly, like radium in the dark. Goodnight.
textL: Snuggle in close, little one. Tonight's story is about a girl who was told she could not — and who quietly, patiently, became one of the greatest scientists who ever lived. Her name was Maria.

Maria Skłodowska was born in 1867 in Warsaw, the capital of Poland, the youngest of five children in a family that was rich in exactly one thing: learning. Her father taught physics and mathematics; her mother ran a school for girls. Their apartment was full of books, and on her father's shelf stood a cabinet of scientific instruments — glass tubes, scales, minerals — which little Maria admired the way other children admire sweets in a shop window.

Maria taught herself to read at four years old, peeking over her big sister's shoulder. Her memory was astonishing: she could recite poems after hearing them twice, and her family sometimes tested her just to laugh in amazement. But those bright early years grew hard. When Maria was small, her mother became very ill and died, and money grew short. And over the whole country lay a heavier shadow: Poland was ruled then by a faraway empire, which forbade schools from teaching in Polish. Even the children's own language had to be whispered.

In Maria's world there was one more unfairness, and it was aimed straight at her: universities did not accept girls. Maria finished school at fifteen with a gold medal — the best student in her class — and then stood before a closed door. Her brothers could study. She could not. Not because she lacked talent. Simply because she was a girl.

Did Maria give up? She did not. In the evenings she slipped through the streets of Warsaw to secret gatherings that the students called the Flying University — flying, because the classes flew from apartment to apartment so the authorities wouldn't find them. In dim rooms with curtains drawn, young women studied biology, chemistry, and history, sharing books hand to hand, listening for footsteps on the stairs. Learning, for them, was an act of courage.

Then Maria and her big sister Bronya made a pact — one of the loveliest pacts two sisters ever made. In Paris, far away in France, the great Sorbonne university accepted women. But the sisters were poor. So they agreed: Maria would work and send money so Bronya could study medicine first; then Bronya, once a doctor, would help Maria in return. And that is what they did. For six long years, Maria worked as a governess in the countryside, teaching other people's children, studying alone at night from borrowed books — physics, algebra, chemistry — waiting for her turn.

At last, the letter came: Come to Paris. Maria, now twenty-four, climbed into the cheapest railway carriage with a folding stool to sit on, a blanket, and a trunk of books, and rode for days across Europe. When she enrolled at the Sorbonne, she signed her name the French way: Marie.

Her student years were hungry and cold and completely happy. She rented a tiny attic room under the roof, where the water froze in the basin on winter mornings; some evenings she dined on bread, butter and tea; once she fainted from hunger beside her books. But no one could stop her from learning now. She studied as though making up for every closed door of her childhood, and she finished first in her physics degree — the top of the whole class.

Around that time she met a quiet, gentle scientist named Pierre Curie, who loved magnets, crystals, and long walks. Pierre saw at once that Marie's mind was extraordinary. He wrote her letters about science the way other men wrote poems. They married — Marie in a plain navy-blue dress she could wear in the laboratory afterwards — and became partners in everything: in life, and in the great mystery they were about to chase.

The mystery was this: a scientist named Becquerel had noticed that a rock containing uranium gave off strange, invisible rays, all by itself, without sunlight, without fire, without anything. Nobody knew why. Marie chose this puzzle for her research — and soon made a thrilling discovery: one crumbly black ore, called pitchblende, poured out far more rays than its uranium could explain. Something unknown was hiding inside it. Something new to the whole world.

To find it, Marie and Pierre were given only a leaky wooden shed with a cracked glass roof — too hot in summer, freezing in winter. Other scientists chuckled at it. In that shed, Marie boiled and stirred great cauldrons of pitchblende with an iron rod nearly as tall as herself, tons of it, sack after sack, month after month, her arms aching, her notebooks filling with careful numbers. And slowly, like someone panning a river for a single fleck of gold, she closed in on her invisible treasure. In 1898 the Curies announced not one but two new elements: polonium, named for Marie's beloved Poland, and radium, whose salts glowed in the dark with a soft blue-green light. At night, Marie and Pierre sometimes tiptoed back to the shed just to stand among the shelves and watch their little glass dishes glowing like captive stars. "Look," Pierre would whisper. "Look…"

Marie named the strange energy radioactivity, and the world took notice. In 1903 she became the first woman in history to win a Nobel Prize, sharing it with Pierre and Becquerel. And after great sorrow — for she lost her dear Pierre in an accident — she carried their work on alone, became the Sorbonne's first woman professor, and in 1911 won a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry. No one — man or woman — had ever done that before.

And here is the part of the story that glows brightest. Marie's discoveries became a gift to everyone. Doctors learned to use rays to see inside the body and to fight illness. When a great war broke out, Marie built little X-ray cars — the soldiers called them petites Curies, "little Curies" — and drove to the front herself, with her teenage daughter Irène, to help wounded soldiers. She could have become rich by keeping radium's secrets for herself. She refused. "Radium belongs to the people," she said. Years later, her daughter Irène won a Nobel Prize too — the wonder, it seems, ran in the family.

So, my little dreamer, remember Maria from Warsaw: the girl who studied in secret while listening for footsteps, who rode across Europe on a wooden stool, who stirred a cauldron for years to find a teaspoon of glowing treasure. "Nothing in life is to be feared," she said. "It is only to be understood." Whatever door ever seems closed to you, remember that patience and curiosity are the gentlest, strongest keys ever made.

Close your eyes now. Somewhere in the dark, atoms are quietly glowing, just as they did in Marie's little shed — tiny lights that never stop shining, like questions waiting for morning. Sleep well, my love. Goodnight.

stories.name: Wangari Maathai
stories.title: The Woman Who Planted a Forest
stories.hook: A girl from the hills of Nyeri planted fifty million trees — and won the Nobel Peace Prize.
text: In 1940, in the green hills of Nyeri, Kenya, a girl named Wangari Maathai was born. As a child she fetched water from a clear stream and played under a great fig tree her mother told her never to harm, because it was a tree of life.

Wangari loved school and worked so hard that she won a chance to study in America. She became a scientist of living things — a biologist — and the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate degree.

When she came home, Wangari saw that the streams were drying and the trees were disappearing. So she did something simple and powerful: she began planting trees, and she taught thousands of village women to plant them too. Her Green Belt Movement planted more than fifty million trees across Kenya.

Some powerful people tried to stop her, but Wangari stood as strong as her fig tree. In 2004 she became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. She showed the world that one person, planting one seed at a time, can heal a whole land.
textM: In 1940, in the green hills of Nyeri in Kenya, a girl was born and named Wangari Maathai. Her home was a small farm where the soil was red and rich, and mist sat along the ridges in the early morning. There were sweet potatoes and beans in the ground, woodsmoke drifting from her mother's kitchen, and above everything else, trees.

One tree mattered most of all. A great fig tree grew near a stream, and Wangari's mother told her something she never forgot: we do not cut that tree, and we do not gather its firewood. It is a tree of God. In her language such a tree was called a mugumo, and people would gather near it to pray. Wangari did not understand yet that the fig tree's deep roots were holding the water inside the hillside. She only knew that it was to be loved.

She loved the stream too. She would kneel at the edge with a gourd and try to scoop up the little glassy beads of frogs' eggs, hoping to wear them as a necklace. They always slipped away between her fingers. But she came back day after day to watch the tadpoles wriggle in the clear water, and to listen to the frogs after dark.

Her brother asked their parents why Wangari was not in school, and so she was sent — and once she was there, nothing could stop her. She studied so well that in 1960 she flew to America to study, together with hundreds of other young Kenyans, on aeroplanes that people at home talked about for years afterwards. She became a scientist of living things, and in 1971 she became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate degree.

But when she looked around her country, her heart hurt. The great forests were being cut down. The stream where she once hunted for tadpoles had dried up completely. The soil was washing away in the rain, and women had to walk further and further to find firewood and clean water for their children.

So Wangari did something simple and enormously powerful. She began to plant trees. She showed village women how to gather seeds, how to fill little bags with soil, how to water the seedlings and wait — most of them grown in gardens right behind their own houses. She paid them a few coins for every tree that lived. They called it the Green Belt Movement, and over the years those women planted more than fifty million trees.

It was not easy. Some powerful people did not want the forests saved, and they tried hard to stop her. Once she stood in front of a great park in the middle of Nairobi and refused to let it be built over — and that park is still green today. Wangari stood as steady as her old fig tree and did not give up. In 2004 she was given the Nobel Peace Prize, the first African woman ever to receive it, because caring for the earth, the world agreed at last, is one of the ways we make peace.

Wangari died in 2011, but her forests are still growing and the Green Belt Movement still plants. She left us the simplest instruction in the world. When a problem is too big to solve, she said, start with the part you can hold in your hand. Plant one seed. Then plant another.

stories.name: George Washington Carver
stories.title: The Plant Doctor
stories.hook: Born into slavery, he became the scientist whose peanuts and sweet potatoes saved poor farmers' land.
text: Around 1864, in Missouri, America, a baby named George was born into slavery. When slavery ended, George was free — but life was still very hard. He was a small, sickly boy who could not do heavy farm work, so he spent his days in the woods and gardens, talking to plants. Neighbors called him "the plant doctor," because their sick plants got well in his hands.
George walked many miles to find schools that would accept a Black child. He never gave up, and he became the first Black student at his university, and then a great scientist of farming.

George saw that poor farmers' soil was tired and worn out from growing only cotton. He taught them to plant peanuts and sweet potatoes to make the soil strong again. Then, so farmers could sell their crops, he invented over three hundred things to make from peanuts — milk, soap, paper, and more!
George became famous, but he stayed humble and gave his knowledge away for free. He showed that a person born with nothing can grow wisdom that feeds millions.
textM: Around 1864, on a small farm in Missouri, in America, a baby boy named George was born into slavery. He was tiny, and he was often sick. A bad cough when he was little left his voice soft and whispery for the rest of his life. When slavery ended, George was free — but freedom did not make life easy. He was too small and too frail for the heavy work of the fields.

So while others swung hoes and carried sacks, George slipped away to the woods. There, among the oak trees, he made himself a secret garden. He brought home plants that were droopy and spotted and yellow, and he tucked them into the soft dark soil. He gave one more shade. He gave another more sun. He moved a third away from the wet ground. Slowly, they grew strong again.
Soon neighbors were knocking at the door holding wilting roses and sad little seedlings. "Take it to the plant doctor," they said. The plant doctor was a boy who could not yet read.

George wanted to read more than anything in the world. But there was no school nearby that would accept a Black child, so George walked. He walked miles to the town of Neosho and slept in a barn, cooking and washing clothes to pay his way. He walked on to other towns and other schools. One college said yes to his letters and then turned him away at the door when they saw his face. George did not stop walking.

He studied painting first, because he loved flowers so much that he wanted to paint them. His art teacher watched him draw every single vein on every single leaf, and said gently, "George, I think you should study plants." So he did. At Iowa State he became the first Black student there, and later the first Black teacher. He woke before sunrise to walk in the fields, because he said the quiet early morning was when plants told him their secrets.

Then a letter came, inviting him to teach farmers in Alabama. What George found there made his heart ache. Year after year the farmers had planted only cotton, and the soil had grown thin and pale and tired. The plants came up small. The families went hungry.

But George knew a secret hidden in roots. Peanuts and sweet potatoes put goodness back into the ground, like a good meal for the soil. Plant those between the cotton, he told the farmers, and the land will wake up. It worked. But then the farmers had wagonloads of peanuts and nobody to buy them. So George went back to his laboratory and got busy, and found over three hundred things to make from peanuts: milk, soap, ink, paper, dye, and much more.

He filled a wagon with seeds and soil and drove it from farm to farm — a school on wheels for people who could not come to school. Rich men offered him fortunes to work for them, and he said no thank you. He gave his discoveries away for free, so they could reach everyone. Today, whenever a farmer rests a field by changing the crop, that is George's idea still at work. He showed that a small, sickly boy born owning nothing at all can grow a wisdom that feeds millions.

stories.name: Katherine Johnson
stories.title: The Girl Who Counted the Stars
stories.hook: She counted everything as a little girl — then her numbers carried astronauts to the Moon and safely home.
text: In 1918, in a small town in West Virginia, America, a girl named Katherine was born. She loved to count everything — the steps to church, the dishes she washed, the stars in the sky. She was so clever that she skipped grades and started high school at only ten years old.

In those days, many schools and jobs were closed to Black people, and especially to Black women. But Katherine's father worked extra jobs and moved the family so his children could keep studying. Katherine never forgot that.

She became a mathematician at NASA, where people called her a "human computer" because she solved enormous sums with just a pencil. When America sent its first astronauts into space, it was Katherine who calculated their paths. The astronaut John Glenn would not fly until he said, "Get the girl to check the numbers." Her numbers helped carry astronauts all the way to the Moon and safely home again.
Katherine showed the world that the path to the stars can begin with a little girl who loves to count.
textM: In 1918, in a small town called White Sulphur Springs, in West Virginia, America, a girl named Katherine was born. Almost as soon as she could talk, she began to count. She counted the steps from her front door to the road. She counted the steps up to the church. She counted the dishes as she washed them, and the forks as she dried them. At night she looked up and tried to count the stars.

Numbers were not schoolwork to Katherine. They were more like a game she could not stop playing. Anything that could be counted, she counted, and anything that could be measured, she measured. She learned so fast that her teachers moved her up a year, and then up again. By the time she was ten years old, she was ready for high school — a small girl among big teenagers, carrying books almost as heavy as she was.

But in her county there was no high school that Black children were allowed to attend. So Katherine's father, Joshua, made a plan. He worked extra jobs, and he moved the whole family more than a hundred miles away to a town with a school that would take them. Each year he drove them there and went back to his work. Katherine never, ever forgot what that cost him.

At college, a professor noticed how her mind reached for shapes and angles. He created brand-new geometry classes just for her, because the ones that already existed were not enough to keep her busy. "You would make a fine research mathematician," he told her, and then he set about teaching her how. She finished college at eighteen, at the very top of her year.

Years later she joined a place that would become NASA, in a big room full of women doing arithmetic by hand. People called them "human computers." They filled page after page with pencil, checking and re-checking, because a single wrong number could send a rocket the wrong way. Katherine was fast, and she was almost never wrong.

She was also curious, and curiosity made her brave. The engineers held meetings she was not invited to. "Is there a rule that says I can't come?" she asked. There wasn't. So she went — and she asked questions until she understood everything in the room.

When America sent its first astronauts up, it was Katherine who worked out their paths: where the capsule must go up, where it must turn, where it must come down in the sea. By then the office had a new electronic computer, but the astronaut John Glenn did not quite trust it. Before he would fly, he said, "Get the girl to check the numbers." She checked them, by hand, for a day and a half. Then he flew, and came home safe.

Her calculations helped carry astronauts all the way to the Moon and back again. Katherine lived to be a hundred and one years old, and she liked to say she was only doing the thing she had always loved. She showed the world that a journey to the stars can begin with one small girl who loves to count.

stories.name: Louis Pasteur
stories.title: The Man Who Fought Invisible Enemies
stories.hook: A patient painter's eye found a hidden world of germs — and gave us vaccines and safe milk.
text: In 1822, in a small town in France, a boy named Louis Pasteur was born. His father made leather for a living, and the family was not rich. At school, Louis was not the fastest student — but he was the most patient. He loved to paint, and he looked at everything slowly and carefully.

That careful eye made him a great scientist. Looking through his microscope, Louis discovered a hidden world: tiny living things called germs, too small to see, that make milk go sour and make people sick. Many scientists laughed at him. Invisible creatures? Impossible!

But Louis proved it. He showed that gently heating milk kills the germs — we still call this pasteurization. Then he made vaccines, tiny gentle doses that teach our bodies to fight sickness. One day, a mother brought him a boy who had been bitten by a rabid dog. Louis's new vaccine saved the boy's life.
Because of Louis Pasteur, doctors wash their hands, our milk is safe, and vaccines protect children everywhere. He proved that patience can defeat even enemies we cannot see.
textM: In 1822, in a small town in eastern France, a boy named Louis Pasteur was born. His family lived above his father's workshop, where hides were soaked and scraped and turned into leather. It was hard, smelly work, and it did not make them rich. But Louis's father had one great hope: that his son would learn things he himself never could.

At school, Louis was not the quickest boy in the room. He did not shoot his hand up first. He was, however, the most patient person anyone had ever met. What he truly loved was drawing. He made portraits of his mother and father and the neighbors, in soft chalky pastels, and they were so good that people thought he might become an artist. Instead, that painter's eye became his science.

As a young man he studied crystals — specks so small you needed a magnifying glass to see them. Louis noticed something nobody else had: some of the tiny crystals leaned one way, and some leaned the other. For days he sat sorting them into two little piles with a fine pair of tweezers. Other scientists thought it was madness. It turned out to be an important discovery.

Then a man who made drinks from beetroot came to him with a problem: sometimes his vats went bad, and nobody knew why. Louis put a drop under his microscope — and there, wriggling, were tiny living things. He looked at spoiled milk, and found them there too. Tiny creatures, too small to see, that make food go sour and people fall ill. He called them germs.

Many clever people laughed. Invisible creatures floating in the air? Impossible! So Louis built a very simple, very beautiful proof. He boiled broth in flasks with long necks bent like a swan's, so that dust could not fall in. The broth stayed clean and clear for months. Then he tipped one flask so the dust could reach the liquid — and it spoiled at once. The germs were coming from the air, and Louis had shown it.

If germs were the trouble, then getting rid of germs was the cure. Louis found that gently heating a liquid — not boiling it, just warming it for a while — kills them without spoiling the taste. He tried it first on wine, to stop it turning sour on long journeys. Then on milk. We still call it pasteurization, and it is the reason the milk in your fridge is safe to drink tonight.

Next came his greatest gift. By accident, Louis found that germs made weak and tired could be given to an animal safely, and afterwards that animal never caught the illness at all. It was as if the body had been shown a picture of the enemy and had learned its face. He called these gentle little doses vaccines. One day, a worried mother brought him a boy who had been bitten by a dog with a sickness called rabies. Louis's new vaccine saved the boy's life.

Because of Louis Pasteur, doctors wash their hands and sterilize their tools, our milk and juice are safe to drink, and vaccines protect children in every country on Earth. He never stopped saying that his secret was not cleverness but stubbornness. He proved that patience can defeat even the enemies we cannot see.

stories.name: Ada Lovelace
stories.title: The Girl Who Dreamed of Thinking Machines
stories.hook: A hundred years before computers existed, she wrote the first program — and imagined machines making music.
text: In 1815, in London, England, a girl named Ada was born. Her father was a famous poet who left when she was a baby, so her mother decided Ada would study numbers instead of poems. Ada loved both! As a little girl she drew plans for a flying machine with wings, and she called her way of thinking "poetical science."

When Ada was seventeen, she met an inventor named Charles Babbage. He was building a giant metal machine that could do sums — a machine the size of a room, full of wheels and gears. Most people saw only a big calculator. Ada saw something more.

Ada wrote instructions to make the machine solve a hard problem all by itself — today we call that a computer program, and Ada wrote the very first one. She even predicted that one day such machines could make music and pictures, not just numbers.

Ada dreamed all this a hundred years before the first real computer was built. Every phone, laptop, and game today follows her big idea — that a machine can follow a recipe of instructions. The first programmer in the world was a girl who mixed poetry with mathematics.
textM: In 1815, in a tall house in London, England, a girl named Ada was born. Her father was a very famous poet, but he went away when Ada was only a baby, and she never met him. Her mother loved mathematics, and she decided that Ada would fill her days with numbers rather than poems — with sums and shapes and careful thinking.

It was a quiet childhood, full of lessons. Ada studied for hours at a wide wooden desk, with a tutor sitting beside her and a clock ticking on the wall. There were sums before breakfast and sums after tea. But her imagination would not stay still. She loved numbers and she loved dreaming, and she could never see why anyone should have to choose between them.

When she was twelve, Ada decided she would fly. She studied birds. She sketched wings and worked out how big they must be to lift a girl. She thought about steam engines, and about a flying horse with a machine inside it. She wrote it all up in a little book she called Flyology. She did not build it — but she never stopped thinking that way. She called it her "poetical science."

One evening when Ada was seventeen, she went to a party where an inventor named Charles Babbage was showing off part of a strange machine. It was made of gleaming brass, full of numbered wheels, and when you turned the handle the wheels clicked round and worked out sums by themselves. Most guests thought it was a clever toy. Ada leaned in close and asked question after question. Mr Babbage had never met a young person like her.

He was already dreaming of something far bigger: a machine the size of a room, run by cards with holes punched in them — the same trick used by weavers to make patterned cloth. Ada understood at once. This machine, she wrote, weaves patterns of numbers the way a loom weaves flowers and leaves.

Years later, Ada translated an article about the machine from Italian into English. Then she added her own notes at the end — and her notes turned out to be three times longer than the article itself. In the last note she wrote out, step by careful step, exactly what the machine must do to work out a long and difficult sum all by itself. That set of steps is what we now call a computer program, and hers was the very first.

Ada also saw further than anyone else alive. If the machine could follow rules about numbers, she wrote, then it could follow rules about anything at all — notes, letters, shapes. One day, she said, machines like this might compose music and make pictures. Nobody else imagined such a thing. Nobody would, for another hundred years.

The great machine was never finished in Ada's lifetime. But every phone, every laptop, every game you have ever played runs on her big idea: that a machine can follow a recipe of instructions, written down in advance by a human mind. The first programmer in the world was a girl who refused to choose between poetry and mathematics.

stories.name: Ahmed Zewail
stories.title: The Boy by the Nile Who Photographed Atoms
stories.hook: A boy from a small Egyptian town built the fastest camera in the world — fast enough to watch atoms dance.
text: In 1946, in Egypt, a boy named Ahmed Zewail was born. He grew up in a small town near the great River Nile, in a house full of love for learning. On his bedroom door, his father hung a sign that said "Doctor Ahmed" — before Ahmed had even finished school! As a boy, Ahmed did little experiments in his room, watching how things burn and change.

Ahmed studied hard at Alexandria University, then crossed the ocean to America to learn more. He wondered about something nobody could see: when two chemicals meet and change into something new, the atoms move — but they move so unbelievably fast that no camera could ever catch them.

So Ahmed built a new kind of camera that used flashes of laser light — flashes lasting one femtosecond, which is to one second what one second is to thirty-two million years! With it, for the first time in history, humans could watch atoms move during a chemical reaction, like watching a dance in slow motion.

In 1999, Ahmed won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry — the first Egyptian, and the first Arab scientist, ever to win it. In Egypt they put his face on postage stamps. He showed every child by the Nile, and everywhere, that the fastest things in the universe can be caught by a patient mind.
textM: In 1946, in Egypt, a boy was born and named Ahmed Zewail. He grew up in a town called Disuq, beside the great River Nile, where boats drifted past with their tall white sails and the evening air smelled of river water and warm bread. Ahmed was the only boy in a house with three sisters, and the whole family expected wonderful things of him.

His home was full of love for learning. On the door of Ahmed's room, his father hung a small sign. It said "Doctor Ahmed" — and Ahmed had not even finished school yet. He slept in that room, did his homework in that room, and walked past those two words every single day. His family simply decided, very early, what he might one day become, and then they let him go on being curious.

And he was very curious. Ahmed wanted to know why things burn — why a piece of wood turns into flame and smoke and ash, and where the wood goes. So he made little experiments in his room, heating things and watching carefully to see what changed. One experiment made so much smoke that his mother came running, and she was not entirely pleased. He was doing chemistry, he later said, long before he knew the word.

Ahmed studied at Alexandria University, and he loved science so much that when it was time to sleep he sometimes stayed up with his books instead. He finished near the very top of his class, and his teachers asked him to stay and help teach the younger students. Then he crossed the ocean to America to learn more, and there he began to think about a question nobody had ever answered.

When two chemicals meet and become something new — when a match lights, or a leaf turns sunlight into food — the atoms inside them move and swap places. But they move unimaginably fast. Nobody had ever seen it happen. Chemists had been guessing about that tiny moment for a hundred years, because every camera in the world was far, far too slow. A whole story was happening inside a blink, and nobody could see a single frame of it.

So Ahmed built a camera made of light. It used flashes from a laser, and each flash lasted one femtosecond. A femtosecond is so short that one second beside it is like thirty-two million years beside one second. It was a flash so fast that a hummingbird's beating wing would look completely still. With flashes that quick, he could freeze the atoms in place, picture after picture after picture.

And there they were at last: atoms moving, breaking apart and joining together, like a dance filmed in slow motion. Chemists no longer had to guess — they could simply look. A whole new science was born, and people called it femtochemistry. In 1999 Ahmed won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, the first Egyptian and the first Arab scientist ever to win it.

Egypt was so proud that his face was printed on postage stamps, so letters travelled the whole country carrying the boy from the Nile. Young people wrote to him from everywhere, and he answered them, and he spent the rest of his life encouraging students to become scientists. He proved something lovely: the fastest things in the entire universe can still be caught by a patient mind.

stories.name: Thomas Odhiambo
stories.title: The Man Who Listened to Insects
stories.hook: A Kenyan boy fascinated by tiny creatures built a world-famous insect science centre in Nairobi — to protect Africa's crops.
text: In 1931, in Mombasa, Kenya, a boy named Thomas Odhiambo was born. While other people chased away insects, Thomas knelt down to watch them. Ants, crickets, butterflies — he wanted to know how such tiny creatures lived such busy, clever lives. Insects were everywhere in Africa, he noticed, yet almost nobody studied them.

Thomas worked hard in school and won a place at Cambridge University in England, where he became a doctor of insect science — an entomologist. Many people expected him to stay in Europe. But Thomas believed African problems needed African scientists, so he came home.

Insects were eating farmers' crops and spreading sickness, but Thomas knew that spraying poison everywhere hurt the land too. So in 1970 he founded ICIPE, a great centre of insect science in Nairobi, where African scientists learned to outsmart harmful insects using nature's own tricks — and to protect the helpful ones, like bees and silkworms, that give people honey, silk, and food.

Scientists from all over the world came to learn in Nairobi, and Thomas helped start an academy for Africa's best scientists. He showed that world-class science can grow on African soil — and that even the smallest creatures deserve a curious mind to listen to them.
textM: In 1931, in the coastal city of Mombasa in Kenya, a boy was born and named Thomas Odhiambo. His family came from beside Lake Victoria, far inland, but Thomas began his life where Kenya meets the sea. Mombasa was hot and salty and full of noise — sailing boats in the harbour, coconut palms overhead, and everywhere, if you looked down, tiny creatures going about their business.

Most people shooed insects away. Thomas knelt down to watch them. He followed lines of ants to see where they were going. He listened to crickets singing in the dark. He watched a butterfly unfold from a little case that had looked like nothing at all. He asked questions that grown-ups could not answer, and then went off to find the answers himself, keeping everything he saw in his head like a collection. How, he wondered, could something so small live a life so busy and so clever?

As he grew, he noticed something odd. Africa had more insects than almost anywhere else on earth — insects that ate the crops, insects that carried sickness, insects that made honey and silk — and yet hardly anybody was studying them properly. A swarm of locusts could strip a family's whole field in an afternoon, and there was nothing to do but watch.

Thomas worked hard at school, then at university in Uganda, and then he was invited to Cambridge University in England, where the winters were grey and the laboratories smelled of paper and dust. There he became a doctor of insect science — an entomologist. Many people assumed he would stay in Europe, where the fine laboratories were. But Thomas thought about the farmers back home. African questions, he believed, needed African scientists. So he went home.

In 1970 he founded a centre in Nairobi and called it ICIPE. It began small: a few rooms, a few researchers, hardly any money and very few instruments. But Thomas had a big idea and a question worth answering. Instead of spraying poison over everything, which harms the soil and the birds and the helpful insects too, why not use nature's own clever tricks?

So the scientists at ICIPE learned the secret languages of insects. They found plants that pests hate and planted them between the rows of maize, to push the pests away. They found plants that pests love and planted them around the edges, to pull the pests out of the field. Tricked by the plants themselves, the pests mostly left the maize alone. Farmers called it push-pull, and their harvests grew bigger without any poison at all.

The centre also protected the helpful insects — the bees that make honey and the silkworms that spin thread — so that families could earn a living from them. Scientists came from all over the world to learn in Nairobi, which meant young African researchers could do great work without ever leaving home. Some of them stayed on to teach the next group. Thomas also helped start an academy for Africa's finest scientists, so that good ideas would keep growing after him.

Thomas Odhiambo died in 2003, but ICIPE is still there and still working, and farmers still use what his centre discovered. He showed the world that world-class science can grow in African soil — and he showed every child that even the smallest creature on earth deserves a curious mind kneeling down to listen.

stories.name: Charles Drew
stories.title: The Doctor Who Taught Blood to Travel
stories.hook: He found a way to store and ship life-saving blood — and his blood banks still save lives every single day.
text: In 1904, in Washington, D.C., America, a boy named Charles Drew was born. He was a star athlete — fast in track, strong in football — and everyone thought sports would be his life. But when sickness took his sister, Charles decided to become a doctor instead.

In those days, many medical schools would not take Black students, so Charles went north to Canada to study. He became fascinated by a puzzle: blood could save a dying patient, but fresh blood spoiled in just a few days. What if blood could be stored, like food in a pantry, ready whenever someone needed it?

Charles discovered that plasma — the golden liquid part of blood — could be dried and kept for a long time, then used to save almost anyone. When a great war broke out, Charles led a rescue mission called Blood for Britain, shipping life-saving plasma across the ocean, and then set up the first big blood banks in America.

When officials wanted to separate blood by the donor's skin color, Charles spoke out bravely: blood is blood — it is all the same inside. Today, every time a hospital gives a patient blood, it works the way Charles Drew taught the world. The boy who lost his sister grew up to save millions of brothers and sisters everywhere.
textM: In 1904, in a busy neighborhood of Washington, D.C., in America, a boy named Charles Drew was born. His family lived by the river, and Charles was the eldest of five children. From the moment he could run, he ran fast. At school he won medals in track, played football and basketball and baseball, and everyone who watched him agreed on one thing: this boy's life would be all about sport.

Then something quiet and sad happened at home. Charles's younger sister fell ill, and the doctors could not save her. Charles was a young man by then, and afterwards he made a decision. He would not spend his life on a running track. He would become a doctor, and he would fight the thing that had taken her.

That turned out to be very hard. In those days most medical schools in America would not accept Black students, however good their marks were. So Charles waited, and saved every coin he could. He taught science and coached sports teams for years to pay the fees. Then he travelled north to Canada, to a great university in Montreal, where he was welcome. He studied through long, cold, snowy winters and finished near the very top of his class.

In Canada, one problem caught hold of him and would not let go. Doctors knew that giving a patient blood could pull them back from the very edge of death. But fresh blood spoiled in only a few days. So blood had to be given right there, right then, from one person straight into another. If you were far from a hospital, there was no blood at all.

Charles began to ask: what if blood could be kept? Stored, like food in a pantry, and carried to wherever it was needed? He went to New York to study the question properly, and he worked at it night after night, filling notebooks. His long report was called Banked Blood, and it was so good that it changed how the world thought about the problem.

His answer was plasma — the pale golden liquid part of blood, once the red cells are taken out. Plasma keeps far longer. It can even be dried into a powder, then mixed with clean water when it is needed. And plasma can be given to almost anybody. Suddenly, blood could travel.

Then a great war broke out across the ocean, and cities in Britain badly needed blood. Charles was asked to lead a rescue project called Blood for Britain. He organized donors, laboratories, careful testing, and ships — thousands of bottles of plasma crossing the sea. It worked. Afterwards he set up the first big blood banks in America, and drew up the rules for how they must be run.

But when officials ordered that blood be labelled and kept apart according to the donor's skin color, Charles refused to stay silent. There is no scientific reason for it, he said plainly. Blood is blood — it is all the same inside. He gave up his post rather than agree. Today, in every hospital in the world, blood is stored, tested, carried and given the way Charles Drew showed us. The boy who lost his sister grew up to save millions of other people's brothers and sisters.

stories.name: Tu Youyou
stories.title: The Woman Who Found Medicine in an Old Book
stories.hook: In a 1,600-year-old book she found the clue to a malaria medicine that has saved millions of children — many of them in Africa.
text: In 1930, in the city of Ningbo, China, a girl named Tu Youyou was born. Her name comes from an old poem about the gentle call of deer eating sweet herbs — as if her name already knew her future. When Youyou was sixteen, she caught a terrible sickness and had to stop school for two years. Lying in bed, she decided: when I am well, I will study medicine, so I can heal people like me.

Youyou studied both modern medicine and the old healing wisdom of China. Years later, a deadly problem needed her: malaria, carried by mosquitoes, was killing many people — and the old medicines had stopped working. Youyou and her team tested hundreds and hundreds of plants. Nothing worked.

Then Youyou searched through ancient books, and in one written 1,600 years ago she found a recipe using a plant called sweet wormwood. The book said to soak it in cool water — not to boil it! That was the secret: heat had been destroying the medicine all along. Her new medicine, artemisinin, worked wonderfully, and she bravely tested it on herself first to make sure it was safe.

In 2015, Tu Youyou won the Nobel Prize in Medicine. Her discovery has saved millions of lives — especially children in Africa, where malaria strikes hardest. She showed the world that sometimes the newest cure is hiding in the oldest book, waiting for a patient reader.
textM: In the winter of 1930, in the busy port city of Ningbo, in China, a baby girl was born. Her father opened an old book of poems and chose her name from a line about deer calling softly to one another — youyou — while they nibbled sweet wild herbs in a meadow. He could not have known it, but the herb in that little poem was a kind of wormwood. The very plant hidden inside her name would one day make her known all over the world.

Youyou loved school. Then, when she was sixteen, she became very ill with a sickness in her lungs, and had to stay at home for two whole years. The days were long and quiet. Doctors came and went. Slowly, medicine made her well again. Lying in bed, she made herself a promise: when I am better, I will study medicine. Then I can help people who are sick, the way people helped me.

She kept that promise. She went to university in Beijing and studied pharmacology — the science of how medicines are made from plants and chemicals. Later she spent more than two years learning the old healing knowledge of China as well, walking through markets of dried roots and leaves, learning to read brittle books written with a brush hundreds of years before. Most scientists chose one path or the other. Youyou chose both.

In 1969 she was given a very hard job. Malaria was making people terribly sick — a fever that arrives with shivering chills, carried from person to person by mosquitoes. Children caught it most easily. Worst of all, the medicines that used to cure it had stopped working. Youyou was asked to lead a team to find a new one. It meant travelling far from home, and leaving her little daughter with her parents for a long time. That was hard on her heart. She went anyway.

Her team began not with test tubes but with reading. They gathered more than 2,000 old recipes and remedies — from books, from village healers, from letters people sent them. From these they made hundreds of plant extracts, and tested every single one. Most did nothing at all. One plant, sweet wormwood, which the Chinese call qinghao, helped a little one time, and then did not help at all the next. Two years went by. Nothing worked.

So Youyou went back to the books. One night she was reading a small handbook of emergency cures written about 1,600 years ago by a healer named Ge Hong. His advice for fever was very simple: take a handful of qinghao, soak it in water, wring out the juice, and drink it. Soak. Not boil. Youyou sat very still. All this time they had been cooking the leaves in hot liquid — and the heat had been destroying the medicine before it ever reached a single patient.

They tried again, gently now, keeping everything cool. In October 1971, sample number 191 cleared the malaria out of every mouse and every monkey they tested. Youyou could hardly believe her eyes. Before giving it to any patient, she and two colleagues swallowed the new medicine themselves, to be sure it was safe. It was. Down in the south of China, people burning with malaria began to get better — and they got better fast.

That medicine is called artemisinin, and it is still the best malaria medicine in the world. In 2015, when she was eighty-four, Tu Youyou won the Nobel Prize in Medicine. She had no fancy title and no famous laboratory; she still lived in her ordinary flat in Beijing, quiet as ever. Her discovery has saved millions of lives, many of them children in Africa, where malaria strikes hardest. She showed the world that the newest cure can be hiding inside the oldest book, waiting patiently for someone patient enough to read it.

stories.name: Archimedes
stories.title: The Man Who Shouted Eureka
stories.hook: Long, long ago in Greece, a curious boy grew up to find the secret of why things float.
text: A very long time ago, in a sunny city by the sea called Syracuse, a boy named Archimedes was born in the land of Greece. He loved to draw shapes in the sand and ask big questions about the world.

As he grew, Archimedes became one of the cleverest thinkers of all. He loved numbers, circles, and machines. One day the king gave him a tricky puzzle, and Archimedes thought about it and thought about it.

Then, while climbing into his bath, he watched the water rise up and spill over the sides. Suddenly he understood! He was so happy he jumped up and shouted Eureka, which means 'I found it!' He had discovered how floating works.

Archimedes also learned about the lever, a simple bar that can lift very heavy things. 'Give me a place to stand and a long enough lever,' he said, 'and I can move the whole world.' His clever ideas still help builders and scientists today.
textM: A very long time ago, on a warm island in the middle of the sea, there was a city called Syracuse. It belonged to the land of Greece. The streets smelled of salt and warm bread. Fishing boats knocked gently against the harbour wall, and the sun made the white stone houses glow. In that city a baby boy was born, and his family named him Archimedes.

Archimedes' father studied the stars, so big questions were always floating around the house like dust in the sunlight. Little Archimedes loved to sit in the courtyard and draw with a stick in the dust. He drew circles. He drew triangles. He drew squares inside circles, and circles inside squares. 'Why does a wheel roll so smoothly?' he wondered. Nobody grew tired of his questions. They only smiled and let him think.

As he grew up, Archimedes became one of the cleverest thinkers who ever lived. He learned from wise teachers far across the sea, in a city full of books, and then he came home to Syracuse and carried on wondering. He loved numbers best of all. He worked out how to measure a circle. He even tried to count how many grains of sand it would take to fill the whole sky. Sometimes he forgot to eat his dinner because he was thinking so hard.

One day the king of Syracuse sent for him. 'I have a golden crown,' said the king. 'But is it truly all gold? I must know for certain — and you must not break it.' Archimedes bowed and went away to think. He thought while he walked. He thought while he ate. He thought for days and days, and still the answer would not come.

Then one evening he went to take a bath. As he lowered himself slowly into the water, he watched it climb up the sides of the tub and spill softly onto the floor. And all at once he understood! His own body was pushing the water out of the way. The bigger the thing, the more water it moves. He could test the crown like that, without harming it at all. Archimedes was so happy he leapt up and shouted Eureka, which means 'I have found it!'

That splashing bath had taught him the secret of floating. Water always pushes up on anything you put into it. That is why an enormous ship made of heavy metal can sit on the sea as lightly as a duck, and why your legs feel wonderfully bouncy in a swimming pool.

Archimedes loved simple machines too. He showed people the lever — only a strong bar and something to rest it on, yet with it a small child can lift something enormous. 'Give me a place to stand and a long enough lever,' he said, 'and I could move the whole world.' The story goes that one day he used ropes and pulleys to pull a great ship out of the water almost by himself, slowly and gently, while a crowd watched with their mouths open.

He also made a spiral inside a tube, called a screw, that carries water uphill so that farmers can water their fields. Farmers still use it today. Builders still use levers. Ships still float exactly the way Archimedes said they would. That is what happens when someone is brave enough to keep asking why: their answers go on helping people for more than two thousand years.

stories.name: Galileo Galilei
stories.title: The Man Who Looked at the Stars
stories.hook: In Italy, a boy who loved to wonder built a tube that let him peek at the moons of the sky.
text: In the beautiful city of Pisa, in Italy, a baby named Galileo was born. As a child he loved music and math, and he always asked 'why?' and 'how?' about everything around him.
When Galileo grew up, he heard of a special tube that made faraway things look close. So he built his own better one, called a telescope, and pointed it up at the night sky.
What he saw filled him with wonder! He found tiny moons dancing around the giant planet Jupiter. He learned that the Earth is not still at all — it travels around the Sun, spinning through space.

Some people did not believe him at first, but Galileo kept looking and kept asking questions. Today we call him the father of modern science, because he taught the world to look closely and find out what is true.
textM: In the city of Pisa, in Italy, where a famous tower leans a little to one side, a baby boy was born. His parents called him Galileo. Their house was full of music, because his father played the lute. In the evenings the soft notes drifted out of the window and down into the narrow street, and the whole family sang together.

Galileo learned to play the lute too, and he played it well all his life. But he was even better at noticing things. One day in the big cool cathedral, he watched a hanging lamp swing slowly to and fro on its long chain. He counted with his own heartbeat: thump, thump, thump. Long swing or short swing, each one seemed to take the same time. Nobody had taught him that. He had found it out simply by watching.

His father hoped he would become a doctor. But numbers kept calling him. Galileo filled his notebooks with shapes and sums until at last his father let him study mathematics instead. He wanted to know how things move. He rolled balls down long polished wooden slopes, over and over, timing them carefully. He learned that a heavy ball and a light ball fall together, side by side. Everybody had thought the heavy one would win.

Then, when Galileo was a grown man, news arrived from Holland. Someone had made a tube with glass at each end that made faraway things look close. Galileo had never even seen one. He simply went home, thought hard about the shapes the glass would need, and ground his own lenses by hand. His tube was better than the first. He called it a telescope.

On a cold, clear night he carried it outside and pointed it up at the sky. What he saw made his heart beat fast. The Moon was not a smooth silver coin at all. It had mountains and valleys and long soft shadows, like a country waiting to be visited. And the pale milky smudge that crosses the sky broke apart into thousands and thousands of tiny stars. 'There are more stars than anyone ever dreamed,' he wrote.

A few nights later he looked at Jupiter, the giant planet, and saw four little points of light beside it. He looked again the next night, and the next. They had moved. They were moons, dancing round Jupiter the way our Moon dances round us. So not everything in the sky circles the Earth. The Earth is not standing still either — it travels round the Sun, turning as it goes.

Not everyone was ready to believe him. Some people said the little tube must be playing tricks. That made Galileo sad. But he did not stop looking, and he did not stop asking questions. 'Come and look for yourself,' he would say, and he would hand his telescope to anyone willing to try. Slowly, one by one, people looked — and they saw the moons of Jupiter too.

He went on writing and teaching until he was a very old man, even when his eyes grew tired and dim. Today we call Galileo the father of modern science, because he taught the world a wonderful habit. Do not only guess. Do not only believe what you are told. Go and look. Measure it. Try it again. Every scientist since then — and every curious child with a question at bedtime — is walking along the path he opened.

stories.name: Johannes Gutenberg
stories.title: The Man Who Made Books for Everyone
stories.hook: In Germany, a clever boy dreamed of a machine that could make books fast enough for the whole world.
text: Long ago in the town of Mainz, in Germany, a boy named Johannes Gutenberg was born. Back then, every book had to be copied by hand, one word at a time, so books were very rare and only a few people had them.
Johannes grew up loving to work with metal and tools. He had a wonderful idea: what if he could make little metal letters, dip them in ink, and press them onto paper again and again?
So he built a machine called the printing press. Now a whole page could be printed in a flash, and then another, and another. Books could be made quickly, and many more people could own them.

Because of Gutenberg, stories and ideas and knowledge could travel far and wide. Suddenly, children and grown-ups everywhere could learn to read. His invention helped bring learning to the whole world.
textM: About six hundred years ago, in the German town of Mainz, beside the wide grey river Rhine, a boy was born and named Johannes Gutenberg. Church bells rang over the rooftops. Barges floated slowly past with wool and wine. His father worked with the men who made the city's coins, so from the time he was very small Johannes knew the smell of hot metal and the tap-tap-tap of little hammers.

In those days, a book was a treasure. Every single one had to be copied out by hand. A patient monk would sit at a high desk with a quill pen, forming one letter at a time, month after month after month. One book could take a whole year. Books were so precious that some were kept on chains so nobody could carry them away. Most children never held one in their lives.

Johannes trained as a goldsmith. His hands learned tiny, careful, beautiful work. And somewhere in all that quiet tapping, a wonderful idea came to him. What if every letter were its own small metal stamp? Then you could line the stamps up to make words, print a whole page, take them apart again — and use the very same letters for the next page, and the next, forever.

It sounds simple. It was not. He had to invent many things at once. He mixed a special metal, soft enough to pour into moulds but hard enough to press thousands of times. He made a thick, sticky ink, more like paint, because ordinary writing ink just slid off the metal. And he built a strong printing press, rather like the presses that squeeze grapes, so a big flat plate could push the paper down evenly. It took him years of trying, and failing, and trying again.

Imagine his workshop. Little metal letters sleeping in wooden trays. The apprentice picking them out one by one and setting them backwards, so they would come out the right way round. The smell of oily black ink. Then the great wooden handle pulled hard, a squeak, a pause — and the paper lifted away with neat rows of perfect words upon it. Then again. And again. And again.

One of the first big books he printed was a Bible, and it was so beautiful that people could hardly believe no hand had written it. Soon printers were setting up their workshops in other towns, and other countries, and other languages. Within one lifetime there were millions of books in the world, where before there had been only a few thousand.

That changed everything. A clever idea thought up in one town could now travel to a thousand towns. Sailors printed maps. Doctors printed what they had learned. Teachers printed lessons, and children began learning to read, not just kings and priests. Stories that had only ever been spoken aloud were caught on paper and kept safe.

Johannes Gutenberg never became rich, and he did not live to see how far his letters would travel. But think of your bookshelf tonight. Think of your school library, your comics, the words on a cereal box, the pages of this very story. All of it began with a patient man in Mainz who believed that books should not belong to a few people — they should belong to everyone.

stories.name: Anton van Leeuwenhoek
stories.title: The Man Who Saw the Tiny World
stories.hook: A cloth seller in Holland made tiny glasses and found a hidden world living in a single drop of water.
text: In the town of Delft, in the Netherlands, a boy named Anton van Leeuwenhoek was born. When he grew up he sold cloth, and he used little glass lenses to check that the threads were fine and neat.
Anton became very good at making his own tiny lenses — so good that they could make small things look huge. He grew curious: what would he see if he looked at ordinary things very, very closely?

So he put a single drop of pond water under his lens. And there they were — tiny living creatures wriggling and swimming about! No one had ever seen them before. He called them his little 'animalcules.'
Anton had discovered microbes, the tiny living things that are all around us but too small to see. People call him the father of microbiology, and his curiosity helps doctors keep us healthy today.
textM: In the little town of Delft, in the Netherlands, a boy named Anton van Leeuwenhoek was born. Delft was a town of quiet canals and red-tiled roofs, of windmills turning slowly against a big grey sky, and of painters who loved the way light fell through a window. Ducks paddled under the bridges. Boats carried cheese and cloth to market.
