Anton did not go to a great university. He never learned Latin, the language that clever books were written in. He grew up and opened a shop selling cloth. Every day he ran his fingers over linen and wool, checking that the weave was even. To count the threads properly, shopkeepers used a small lens on a little stand. Anton looked through his lens, and something inside him woke up.

He did not just want to count threads. He wanted to see more. So he taught himself, patiently, secretly, to make lenses of his own. He learned to melt glass until a drop rolled into a perfect tiny bead, no bigger than a seed. He fixed each bead into a small brass plate with a pin to hold whatever he wanted to look at. He had to hold it right up to his eye, close to the light, and squint. But oh, what it showed him!

Anton looked at everything. He looked at a bee's sting and the fuzzy hairs on a leaf. He looked at the eye of a fly, which was made of hundreds of little eyes. He looked at his own hair, and the point of a needle, which turned out not to be sharp at all but bumpy like a rock.

Then one day he did something no one had thought of. He fetched a single drop of green water from a pond and held it up to his lens. And there they were. Tiny creatures, wriggling and spinning and darting about, alive, in one drop of water. Anton could hardly breathe. He wrote that there were more of them in that little drop than there were people in his whole country. He called them his little 'animalcules'.

He grew bolder. He scraped a bit of white stuff from between his own teeth, mixed it with water, and looked — and there they were again, swimming happily about. So he tried rinsing his mouth with vinegar to see what would happen. Anton was curious about absolutely everything, even himself.

He wrote long, friendly letters about it all to the learned men in London. At first they did not believe a cloth seller from Delft. So they sent people to Delft to look through his lenses themselves. They looked, and they gasped, and they believed. They made Anton a member of their great scientific society, and he kept sending letters for fifty years. He never told anyone his secret for making lenses.

Anton van Leeuwenhoek had discovered microbes — the tiny living things that are on our hands, in our water, in the soil and all around us, far too small to see. That is why we wash our hands, why doctors can find what is making someone poorly, and why every school has a microscope. People call him the father of microbiology. He proved that you do not need to be famous or grand to change the world. You only need to look very, very closely, and to really want to know.

stories.name: Anders Celsius
stories.title: The Man Who Measured Hot and Cold
stories.hook: In snowy Sweden, a star-gazing scientist found a simple way to tell exactly how hot or cold things are.
text: In the cold, snowy country of Sweden, a boy named Anders Celsius was born. His family loved learning, and Anders grew up gazing at the stars and dreaming about the sky.
Anders became an astronomer, a scientist who studies the stars and planets. But he also wondered about something closer to home: how could people know exactly how hot or cold something was?
So he made a clever number line called a temperature scale. He decided that water turning to ice would be 0, and water bubbling and boiling would be 100, with all the numbers in between.
Today, when you check if it is a warm day or a cold one, you might use degrees Celsius, named after him. His simple idea helps people all over the world know just how warm or chilly it is.
textM: In the cold, snowy country of Sweden, in a town called Uppsala, a baby boy was born and named Anders Celsius. Uppsala winters are long and dark. The lake freezes hard enough to walk on. Snow sits on the rooftops like thick white icing, and candles burn in the windows all afternoon because the sun goes to bed so early.

Anders was born into a family that loved learning. His father was a professor, and so were both of his grandfathers. There were books and instruments and star charts all over the house, and grown-ups arguing happily about the sky. Numbers came easily to Anders, the way songs come easily to some children.

When he was a young man he became an astronomer, a scientist who studies the stars and planets. But the thing he loved most on those freezing Swedish nights was the northern lights — great green ribbons of light that ripple across the winter sky. Anders wrote down every time he saw them, more than three hundred times. He noticed something strange: when the lights danced, a compass needle nearby would tremble too. Nobody had spotted that before.

He was brave as well as clever. He travelled far, far north into Lapland, in the deep of winter, with reindeer and frozen rivers and nights that lasted nearly all day. He and his friends went there to measure the shape of our planet. And they discovered that the Earth is not a perfect ball — it is a little squashed at the top and bottom, like an orange.

Back home, something small kept bothering him. Thermometers already existed, but every maker used different numbers. One man's '20' was another man's '60'. If a scientist in Sweden wrote about the weather, a scientist in France could not tell what he meant. It was as if everybody were using a different ruler.

So Anders had a beautifully simple idea for a temperature scale. Choose two things that happen exactly the same way anywhere in the world. Water freezing into ice. Water bubbling into steam. Mark them both, then divide the space between them into one hundred equal steps. Now everyone, everywhere, could mean the same thing.

He was very careful about it. He tested and tested, and he even noticed that water boils a little differently high up on a mountain than down beside the sea, so he wrote down exactly how to do the test properly. On the scale we all use today, freezing water is 0 degrees and boiling water is 100 degrees, and every number in between has its place.

That is why, when you ask if you need a coat tomorrow, someone might say 'it will be twelve degrees'. It is why a nurse can check a fever, why bakers know how hot the oven is, and why scientists in every country understand one another. Anders Celsius took something everybody could feel but nobody could share, and turned it into numbers the whole world agrees on. His name is still spoken every single day, in every language, whenever anyone wonders how warm it is outside.

stories.name: Carl Linnaeus
stories.title: The Boy Who Named the Flowers
stories.hook: A flower-loving boy in Sweden gave every plant and animal its very own special name.
text: In a green corner of Sweden, a boy named Carl Linnaeus was born. His father kept a lovely garden, and little Carl loved flowers so much that people called him 'the little botanist' before he could even read well.

Carl spent his days wandering through fields and forests, gathering plants and looking closely at their leaves and petals. He noticed that all the world's living things came in wonderful families, some alike and some different.

But there was a problem: the same plant had many different names in different places, and it was very confusing. So Carl invented a tidy way to give each one two names, like a first name and a family name.

This clever idea is called naming with two words, and scientists still use it today. Thanks to Carl Linnaeus, every plant and animal on Earth has its own special name, so people everywhere can understand each other.
textM: In a green corner of Sweden, in a small house wrapped all around by a garden, a boy named Carl Linnaeus was born. The year was 1707. His father was a village pastor who loved growing things, and he had filled that garden with flowers gathered from all over the countryside. Carl's very first world was that garden: bees humming, warm earth, and petals opening in the short, bright summer of the north.

People used to say that when baby Carl cried, his father would place a flower in his hand, and the crying stopped at once. By the time Carl was eight, he had his own little patch of ground to plant whatever he liked. The grown-ups already had a nickname for him. They called him 'the little botanist'.

At school, though, Carl was not the star pupil. He preferred meadows to Latin lessons, and his teachers shook their heads and sighed. But a doctor in the town, named Johan Rothman, noticed what everyone else had missed. 'This boy is not lazy,' he said. 'He is simply in love with plants.' He took Carl into his own home and taught him about medicine and flowers, and Carl's whole life turned around.

When Carl was twenty-five, he set off on an enormous journey north into Lapland, where the summer sun never quite goes down. For months he walked and rode with a notebook, a small bag and a stubborn heart, writing down every plant, bird and stone he met, and learning from the Sami people how they lived with their reindeer in that cold, shining land.

Everywhere he went, Carl kept meeting the same problem. One single plant might have four different names in four different villages. Its proper name could be a whole long sentence of Latin, difficult to say and easy to forget. Scientists in different countries could not tell whether they were talking about the same thing at all. It was a beautiful, tangled muddle. But Carl loved order the way other people love music. He once planted a flower clock: a round bed of flowers chosen because each kind opened its petals at a different hour, so you could almost tell the time by looking at the garden. If flowers could be that neat, he thought, then their names could be neat too.

So Carl tidied it up. He gave every living thing just two names: one for the family group it belonged to, and one for itself — rather like a family name and your own first name. Then he sorted plants and animals into groups inside bigger groups, and wrote it all down in a book called Systema Naturae. He even gave our own kind a name: Homo sapiens, which means 'the wise human'.

Later Carl became a teacher at Uppsala, and his students sailed away to every corner of the world to collect plants for him. They sent back seeds, dried leaves, drawings and treasures from Africa, Asia and the Americas. Carl stayed in his garden, naming them one by one, patient and delighted, like a man opening parcels that had travelled across the sea.

Today every plant, animal and creature on Earth still carries two names, exactly as Carl decided. A scientist in Kenya and a scientist in Sweden can say one short name and know they mean the very same flower. Carl Linnaeus taught the world to look closely, and then to agree. So when you learn the name of a tree or a bird, you are using a gift from a Swedish boy who loved his father's garden.

stories.name: Benjamin Franklin
stories.title: The Boy Who Caught Lightning
stories.hook: He wondered if the light in the sky was the same little spark he made rubbing his hands.
text: Benjamin Franklin was born long ago in Boston, in the United States. He was one of many children in a small, busy home. He loved books more than anything, and he read every one he could find, even by candlelight.

As he grew up, Ben was always curious and full of questions. Why did the sky flash in a storm? He wondered if lightning was really electricity, the same little spark you feel sometimes. So one stormy day he flew a kite to find out. (Please never try this yourself, little one — storms are dangerous, and Ben was being very, very careful.)

He was right! The sky's light was electricity. To keep houses safe, he invented the lightning rod, a metal stick that gently carries lightning down into the ground. He also made glasses that help you see both near and far.
Benjamin helped build his young country and always tried to help others. He showed the world that a curious mind, and a kind heart, can light up the darkness.
textM: Benjamin Franklin was born long ago in Boston, a busy harbour town in America, where ships creaked at the docks and gulls cried overhead. He was one of seventeen children — the fifteenth, and the youngest boy of them all. His father made candles and soap, so their small, crowded house always smelled of warm wax.

Ben went to school for only two years. His family could not afford any more. But he loved books more than anything, so he found his own ways. He would borrow a book in the evening, stay up reading it by candlelight, and give it back spotless first thing in the morning. To teach himself to write well, he copied out sentences he admired, waited a few days, then tried to build them again from memory.

He was curious about everything, and he liked to try things out rather than only wonder about them. He loved swimming, so as a boy he made himself wooden paddles to hold in his hands, to see whether they would push him along faster. They did — a little. He was about eleven years old when he made them, and he tried wooden fins for his feet as well.

When he was twelve, Ben went to work in his big brother's printing shop. It smelled of ink and hot metal. He longed to write for the newspaper, but his brother only laughed at the idea. So Ben invented a pretend old lady called Silence Dogood, wrote funny, clever letters as her, and slid them under the shop door at night. The paper printed every single one. Everyone in Boston loved them — and nobody guessed who she really was.

Later, in Philadelphia, Ben kept on asking questions. Why does the sky flash in a storm? He wondered whether lightning was really electricity — the very same little spark you sometimes feel on a door handle. So one stormy day he flew a kite to find out, with a key tied to the string. (Please never try this, little one. Storms are dangerous, and Ben was being very, very careful, standing dry under a shelter.) When the key crackled with a tiny spark, he had his answer.

He was right. The light in the sky was electricity. To keep houses safe, he invented the lightning rod: a metal stick on the roof that quietly carries the lightning down into the ground, where it can do no harm at all. It was the first invention anywhere that could truly protect a home from a storm, and thousands of houses still wear one today.

He also made bifocal glasses, so you can see near and far without swapping spectacles, and a better stove that warmed a whole room using less wood. He drew charts of the warm ocean river that helps ships cross the sea. And he never took money for any of it. Since we all enjoy other people's good ideas, he said, we should share our own gladly and freely.

Ben started the first lending library in America, so that people without much money could still read. He started the first volunteer fire brigade in his city. And he helped build his young country. He showed the world that a curious mind and a kind heart, together, can light up the darkness.

stories.name: James Watt
stories.title: The Boy and the Steaming Kettle
stories.hook: He watched a kettle puff and puff — and imagined a whole world it could move.
text: James Watt was born in a small town in Scotland, near the cold, gray sea. He was a quiet, thoughtful boy who was often unwell, so he stayed home and used his hands to build and fix little things.

One day James sat by the fire and watched a kettle boil. The steam pushed the lid up and down, up and down. He thought, if steam can lift a lid, maybe it can push much bigger things! That little question stayed with him for years.

When he grew up, James made the steam engine far stronger and better. His engines powered trains that raced across the land, and machines in great factories. He helped begin a whole new age of the world.
James worked hard and never gave up on his ideas. Today, when we measure the power of a light or a machine, we say the word 'watt' — named just for him.
textM: James Watt was born in 1736 in Greenock, a small town in Scotland, right beside the cold, gray sea. Ships came and went from the harbour, ropes creaked, and gulls cried over the water. His father built ships and made instruments for sailors, and his workshop smelled of sawdust, tar and warm metal.

James was often unwell as a child, with headaches that kept him home from school, so he learned much of what he knew at his mother's side and at his father's bench. His father gave him his own small set of tools and a corner to work in. There James built little cranes, little pulleys and tiny models of ships, taking things apart just to see how they were made, and putting them back together better than before. On clear nights he lay outside and counted the stars.

People have told a story about him ever since. One evening, so it goes, James sat by the fire watching a kettle boil. The steam lifted the lid, puff, puff, up and down. His aunt scolded him for idling — but James was not idle at all. He was wondering: if steam can push a lid, what else could steam push?

When he was older, James travelled all the way to London to learn how to make fine instruments. He worked so hard there, and ate so little, that he came home thin and tired — but he came home knowing his craft. At the University of Glasgow he was given a small workshop, and there he mended compasses, quadrants and telescopes with beautiful, careful hands. Professors dropped in to warm themselves and talk, and James asked them question after question after question.

One day someone brought him a little model steam engine to repair. It huffed a few times and stopped. It gulped down coal and gave back hardly any work. James studied it for weeks and found the trouble: the same big cylinder had to be made hot, then cold, then hot again, over and over. All that heat was simply thrown away.

He thought about it while he ate, and while he walked, and probably while he was meant to be sleeping. Then, on a quiet Sunday stroll across Glasgow Green in 1765, the answer arrived in his head like sunlight through cloud. Let the steam rush out into a separate chamber to cool down there. Keep the hot part always hot, and the cold part always cold. It was such a simple idea, and it changed everything.

Making it real took years, though — years of tinkering, cracked parts, leaking joints and empty pockets, and James was not a man who found waiting easy. At last a warm-hearted partner named Matthew Boulton believed in him and helped him build the engines properly. Watt's engines pumped water out of deep mines, turned the wheels of great mills, and later helped move trains across the land. A whole new age of machines had begun, and James had helped push open the door.

James Watt worked hard, thought slowly and carefully, and never gave up on a good question. Today, when we measure the power of a lamp, a kettle or a motor, we use a word made from his name: the watt. Every light bulb in the world carries a small reminder of a quiet Scottish boy who watched a kettle and wondered.

stories.name: Charles Darwin
stories.title: The Beetle Collector Who Sailed the World
stories.hook: He loved beetles so much that one island of giant tortoises changed how we see all of life.
text: Charles Darwin was born in England, in a big house near a river. As a boy he was not the best at his school lessons, but oh, how he loved nature! He collected beetles, watched birds, and explored every field and wood he could find.

When he grew up, Charles sailed away on a ship called the Beagle. It carried him far across the sea to faraway islands called the Galápagos. There he saw giant tortoises, funny birds, and creatures he had never seen before.

Charles noticed something wonderful. Over long, long time, living things slowly change to fit the places they live. He called this idea evolution. A bird's beak, a tortoise's shell — each one fits its home just right.
Charles was gentle, patient, and always full of wonder. He taught the world that all living things are connected, like one great big family growing and changing together.
textM: Charles Darwin was born in England in 1809, in a tall red-brick house on a hill above the River Severn. There were gardens to dig in, a greenhouse full of warm air, and at the bottom of the slope a river where herons stood very, very still. From the moment he could walk, Charles wanted to be outside.

At school he was, to be honest, rather a disappointment. The lessons were all Latin verbs, and Charles could not make himself care about them. But put him in a field and he was a different boy altogether. He collected pebbles, coins, birds' eggs and, most of all, beetles. His father once sighed at him, 'You care for nothing but shooting, dogs and rat-catching.'

The beetles were serious business. One day Charles peeled the bark off an old tree and found two rare beetles at once. He grabbed one in each hand — and then spotted a third. So he popped one beetle into his mouth to keep it safe. The beetle did not think much of this and squirted something horrid, and Charles lost all three. He told that story, laughing, for the rest of his life.

When he was twenty-two, an invitation arrived. A small navy ship called the Beagle needed someone to study the rocks and animals of faraway coasts. Charles said yes. He was seasick almost the whole time, and the voyage lasted five years instead of two. He walked in rainforests, dug up giant fossil bones, felt an earthquake shake a whole coastline, and packed thousands of specimens into barrels to send home.

In 1835 the Beagle reached the Galápagos, black rocky islands sitting right on the equator. Charles met tortoises so huge that he tried, laughing, to ride on one. He met birds so unafraid of people that he could nudge them off a branch with his hat. And a man who lived there told him something odd: look carefully at a tortoise's shell, he said, and you can tell exactly which island it came from.

That small remark rolled around in his head for years. Back home, in a quiet house in the countryside, Charles studied barnacles, earthworms, orchids and pigeons. He wrote letters to gardeners and farmers all over the world, asking small, patient questions and waiting months for the answers. And every single day he walked the same gravel path around his garden — his thinking path — turning the puzzle over and over. He was in no hurry at all. He worked on that one question for more than twenty years.

Slowly the answer came. Living things have young that are all slightly different from one another. The ones that fit their home best survive a little better, and pass those differences on. Do that for millions of years, and a beak grows longer, a shell grows taller, and a new kind of creature appears. That was why the tortoises of one island did not look quite like the tortoises of the next one. Each island had been shaping its own tortoises, slowly, for a very long time. In 1859 he published his book, and he called the idea evolution by natural selection.

Charles was gentle, careful, and rather worried about upsetting anybody. Ten children clattered in and out of his study while he worked. One of them, visiting a friend's house, asked politely, 'And where does your father do his barnacles?' — he thought all fathers did. Charles's great idea became the beginning of modern biology. It is how we understand animals, plants, medicine and ourselves. All living things, he showed us, belong to one enormous family.

stories.name: Gregor Mendel
stories.title: The Monk Who Counted Peas
stories.hook: In a quiet garden, thousands of pea plants whispered the biggest secret of families.
text: Gregor Mendel was born in a small village in Austria, on a family farm. He grew up among gardens and fields, and he loved watching things grow. He was a bright, gentle boy who later became a monk in a quiet stone monastery.

In the monastery garden, Gregor grew pea plants — thousands and thousands of them. Some were tall and some were short. Some had purple flowers and some had white. Patiently, he counted and wrote down everything he saw.

Gregor discovered something amazing. Parent plants pass little hidden messages to their baby plants — messages for being tall, or short, or a certain color. Today we call these messages genes, and this was the very beginning of genetics.

Gregor was humble and worked alone for years. Long afterward, the world understood how special his peas were. Because of one kind, patient monk, we now know how children come to look a little like their parents.
textM: Gregor Mendel was born in a small village in Austria, in a farmhouse with an orchard beside it. His family had worked that same soil for a very long time. His father Anton taught him how to graft fruit trees — how to tie a young branch onto an old trunk so that one day it would grow sweeter apples. There were beehives too, humming all through the warm months. Little Gregor learned early that a garden is a place where patient people wait for answers.

He was a bright boy, and his teachers said he should keep studying. But the school was far away and the family had very little money. Some years he went hungry, and he was often unwell. Then his younger sister Theresia gave him part of the money that had been saved for her own future, so that he could stay at school. Gregor never forgot that kindness. Many years later, he quietly paid for her three sons to study too.

When he was twenty-one he joined a monastery in the city of Brno, and there he took the name Gregor. It was a calm place of stone corridors and a big library and — best of all — a garden. The monks sent him to Vienna to learn science, and he loved every minute of it. But to become a fully qualified teacher he had to pass a hard examination, and twice he did not pass it. He taught anyway, and the boys in his class thought he was wonderful.

Back at the monastery, Gregor began the work of his life. On a narrow strip of ground beside the garden wall he planted pea plants. Not ten. Not a hundred. Over eight years, close to twenty-eight thousand of them. He chose peas because they grow easily, and because they come in tidy opposites: tall or short, round seeds or wrinkled ones, yellow seeds or green, purple flowers or white.

He worked like the gentlest of gardeners. With a fine brush he carried pollen from one flower to another, choosing exactly which plant should be the parent of which. Then he tied a tiny paper bag over each blossom, so that no wandering bee could come along and muddle his experiment. When the pods were ripe he split them open and counted every single pea, writing the numbers in neat columns in his notebook.

And slowly the numbers began to sing. When he crossed a tall plant with a short one, all their children were tall — the shortness seemed to vanish completely. But in the next generation it came back, in almost exactly one plant out of every four. Three tall, one short. Again and again and again. Gregor realised that each plant carries two hidden messages, one from each parent, and passes only one of them on. Today we call those messages genes.

In 1865 he read his discovery aloud to a small science club in Brno. The room was polite. Nobody understood. His paper sat quietly on library shelves for thirty-four years while Gregor became the abbot of his monastery, looked after his bees, measured the weather every single day, and grew old. 'My time will come,' he is said to have told a friend.

And it did. In 1900, long after he was gone, three scientists working in three different countries each stumbled upon his forgotten pages — and gasped. Everything they were trying to prove, a quiet monk had already counted out, pea by pea, in a monastery garden. Because of Gregor we understand why you might have your grandmother's eyes, how farmers grow stronger crops, and how doctors help families stay well. Patience, it turns out, is a kind of superpower.

stories.name: Alfred Nobel
stories.title: The Inventor Who Chose Peace
stories.hook: He wanted to be remembered not for a loud invention, but for a kind gift to the whole world.
text: Alfred Nobel was born in Sweden, in a family that loved to build and invent. As a boy he was often unwell, so he stayed inside and read many books. He grew up loving both chemistry and poetry, mixing things in the lab and writing in his notebook.

When he grew up, Alfred invented dynamite. It could break through solid rock, so workers could build tunnels, roads, and railways more safely and easily. It helped people reach places they never could before.
But Alfred felt sad, because his invention was sometimes used to harm instead of to help. He thought hard about how he wished to be remembered, and he decided to do something good and lasting.

So Alfred gave his whole fortune to create the Nobel Prizes. Every year they honor people who help humanity — in science, in stories, and in kindness. The Peace Prize rewards those who help the world get along. Alfred is remembered, just as he wished, for hope.
textM: Alfred Nobel was born in Sweden, in a family that loved to build and invent. His father was always drawing machines and bridges, and the house was full of plans and half-finished ideas. When Alfred was small the family moved far away to a cold city in Russia, where the river froze in winter and the workshops rang with hammers. As a boy Alfred was often unwell, so while other children ran outside, he stayed in and read.

Because he could not go to school like his brothers, tutors came to the house instead. Alfred turned out to be remarkable. By the time he was seventeen he could speak five languages — Swedish, Russian, French, English and German. He loved chemistry, mixing careful drops in the laboratory. But he loved poetry just as much, and he filled notebooks with verses. All his life he was two people at once: a scientist and a dreamer.

His father sent him abroad to study, and in Paris young Alfred met a chemist who had made a strange oily liquid called nitroglycerine. A single drop could burst with astonishing force. It was so unreliable that even the man who made it said it should never be used. Alfred could not stop thinking about it. If a thing that strong could be made safe, he thought, workers would never again have to break mountains by hand.

So he set to work, and he worked for years. First he invented a small cap that would set the liquid off only when you chose. Then came the real answer, and it was beautifully simple: he mixed the oil into a soft chalky powder made of the shells of tiny sea creatures. The result was a paste you could knead like bread dough and cut into sticks, carry in a bag, and even drop without worry. He called it dynamite, from an old Greek word meaning power.

Dynamite changed the world's map. Tunnels went through the Alps. Canals joined seas. Harbours were deepened and railways crossed whole countries. Alfred built factories in many lands and became very rich, with more than three hundred inventions to his name. Yet he lived out of suitcases, moving from city to city, and he often felt lonely.

Then his invention began to be used to harm as well as to help, and that made Alfred deeply sad. People tell a story that one morning a newspaper printed, by mistake, an article about Alfred himself, saying he would be remembered only for making terrible things. Whether or not it truly happened, we know he thought long and hard about the same question: when I am gone, what will my name mean? A friend of his, a writer named Bertha, wrote to him for years about peace, and Alfred listened carefully.

In 1895, in Paris, he sat down and wrote his will by hand on a single page. He gave nearly his entire fortune away — not to a family or a country, but to the whole world. The money was to be invested, and every year the interest was to be shared among the people who had done the most good for humanity.

So the Nobel Prizes began. Every year, on the tenth of December, they honour discoveries in science, healing in medicine, beauty in stories, and above all the work of peace. Alfred's friend Bertha won that Peace Prize herself. Today, children everywhere learn the names of Nobel winners — scientists, doctors, poets and peacemakers. Alfred Nobel is remembered, exactly as he wished, not for a loud invention but for hope.

stories.name: Dmitri Mendeleev
stories.title: The Man Who Made a Map of Everything
stories.hook: He sorted all the building blocks of the world into a tidy table — and left empty spaces on purpose.
text: Dmitri Mendeleev was born far away in Siberia, in Russia, where the winters are long and snowy. He was the youngest of a very big family with many brothers and sisters. His mother believed in him and traveled a long, long way so he could go to school.
Dmitri loved to know how everything was made. All around us are tiny building blocks called elements — like the oxygen we breathe and the iron in a nail. But no one had put them in order yet.

So Dmitri sorted the elements into a neat chart called the Periodic Table. He even left some boxes empty, saying, 'There are elements here we haven't found yet.' Years later, people found them — exactly as he had guessed!
Dmitri worked with patience and a clever, curious mind. His table hangs in classrooms all over the world today, helping every child learn what everything is made of.
textM: Dmitri Mendeleev was born far away in Siberia, in Russia, where the winters are long and snowy and the great river freezes so hard that sledges cross it. He was the youngest of a very big family with many brothers and sisters — so many that his mother must have known every one of their footsteps by sound. The house was noisy, warm, and full of books, because his father was the headmaster of the town school.

Then his father's eyes grew weak and he could no longer teach. Money became very short. So Dmitri's mother did something brave: she reopened the family's old glass factory and ran it herself. Little Dmitri was allowed to stand and watch the glassblowers at work, turning glowing sand into bottles right in front of him. He never forgot it. That was his first chemistry lesson, and nobody had to teach it to him.

His mother saw that this last child of hers had an unusual mind. When he was a teenager she packed up their things and travelled with him thousands of miles across Russia — by cart, by sledge, by whatever they could find — knocking on the doors of one college and then another, until at last, in Saint Petersburg, a teachers' college said yes. Dmitri never forgot what she had done for him, and years later he dedicated one of his books to her.

He grew up to become a professor, with a wild mane of hair and a long beard he only trimmed once a year. He needed a chemistry textbook for his students, and none of the ones he found were good enough — so he decided to write his own. And straight away he met a puzzle. All around us are tiny building blocks called elements — like the oxygen we breathe and the iron in a nail. Sixty-three of them were known. But nobody had put them in a sensible order.

So Dmitri made himself a set of cards. On each one he wrote an element's name, how heavy it was, and what it was like. Then he spread them out on his desk and moved them around, like a long game of patience, swapping and sorting, day after day. He worked so long without sleeping that one afternoon he dozed off at his desk — and afterwards he said the whole arrangement had appeared to him, complete, in a dream. He woke up and wrote it down.

The answer was to lay the elements in rows, so that the ones that behave alike stand in the same column, like families lining up for a photograph. This was the Periodic Table. And then Dmitri did the boldest thing of all. Where the pattern needed an element that nobody had ever seen, he left the box empty — and described what would one day be found there: how heavy it would be, what colour, how it would melt.

People laughed a little. Then, six years later, a scientist in France found a soft silvery metal that melts in the warmth of your hand. It fitted one of the empty boxes perfectly. Another was found in Sweden, and another in Germany. Dmitri had been right every time. He was so sure of his table that when the French scientist measured his new metal, Dmitri wrote and told him to measure again — and Dmitri was right about that too.

He stayed curious to the very end. He made his own suitcases as a hobby, and once he climbed alone into a hot-air balloon and rose above the clouds to watch an eclipse of the sun. His table hangs in classrooms all over the world today, helping every child learn what everything is made of. And far along the bottom row sits an element named mendelevium — a quiet thank-you, forever, to the boy from Siberia whose mother believed in him.

stories.name: Alexander Graham Bell
stories.title: The Man Who Sent Voices Down a Wire
stories.hook: What if your voice could travel all the way across a whole city?
text: Long ago in Scotland, a boy named Alexander was born into a family that loved sound and speaking. His mother could not hear well, so young Alexander learned to speak close and clear, and he wondered how words move through the air.

He grew up gentle and curious. He would press his lips near his mother's forehead so she could feel the humming of his voice. Later he married a kind woman who was deaf too, and helping people hear and be heard became the dream of his life.

Alexander studied how sound travels as tiny vibrations. After much patient trying, he built a machine that could carry a voice along a wire. One day he spoke into it, and his friend in another room heard every word. He had invented the telephone!

Because of Alexander, people far apart could hear each other's voices again. Grandparents could talk to grandchildren, and friends across the miles could say goodnight. His love for the people he cared about helped the whole world feel a little closer.
textM: Long ago, in the grey stone city of Edinburgh in Scotland, a boy named Alexander Graham Bell was born. His house was full of sound. His father taught people how to shape their mouths to make each letter. His mother, Eliza, played the piano beautifully, though she could not hear well. She held a little trumpet-shaped horn to her ear to catch people's words. Alexander learned early that a voice is a precious thing to carry to someone you love.

He found his own way to talk to her. He would lean close and press his lips gently against her forehead, and speak in a low, warm hum. She could feel the vibrations travelling through her skin. 'Say it again,' she would smile. And so, before he was ten years old, Alexander already knew a secret that most grown-ups had never thought about: sound is a shiver in the air, and a shiver can travel.

He was a tinkering sort of boy. He and his brother built a strange little machine out of wood and rubber that could puff out one word — 'Mama' — until the neighbours came to see who was crying. Once, at a friend's flour mill, he watched workers scrubbing the husks off wheat by hand. Alexander was twelve. He went home, thought about it, and built a brush-and-paddle machine that did the job for them. It was his very first invention.

When he grew up, he moved across the sea, and in Boston he became a teacher of deaf children. He loved that work best of all. He knelt beside his pupils, put their hands on his throat so they could feel the buzzing, and helped them find their own voices. One of his students was a bright young woman named Mabel, who had lost her hearing as a little girl. Years later, she became his wife.

At night, Alexander worked on a much bigger idea. If a voice makes the air shiver, he thought, perhaps it could make a thin sheet of metal shiver too — and perhaps that shiver could be carried along an electric wire and turned back into a voice at the other end. It sounded impossible. He had a patient helper, a young workshop man called Thomas Watson, and together they tried, and failed, and tried again.

Then came the tenth of March, 1876. Alexander was in one room, Thomas in another, with a wire strung between them. Alexander leaned toward his machine and said, 'Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you.' Down the hallway, Thomas heard every single word — and came running. The telephone was born. Alexander was twenty-nine years old.

At first, hardly anyone believed it. A talking wire? Impossible. So that summer Alexander carried his machine to a great exhibition in Philadelphia, where an emperor visiting from Brazil put the little cup to his ear, listened, and cried out in astonishment, 'It talks!' After that, everybody wanted one. Alexander kept teaching deaf children all his life. One family he helped was that of a small girl named Helen Keller, and years later she dedicated a book to him.

Soon wires stretched from house to house and city to city, carrying laughter and news and goodnight kisses. Funnily enough, Alexander refused to keep a telephone in his own study, because its ringing interrupted his thinking! Today your voice can fly to the other side of the world in less than a second. Every time someone far away says 'I miss you', there is a little echo of a boy who once spoke softly against his mother's forehead.

stories.name: Thomas Edison
stories.title: The Boy Who Never Stopped Asking Why
stories.hook: Can you imagine a world with no light at night?
text: In America long ago, a boy named Thomas was born full of questions. Why does the sky do this? How does that work? He asked so many questions that his teacher grew tired, but his mother believed in him and taught him at home.

Thomas loved to try things and build things. He set up a little laboratory and tinkered for hours. He learned that a mistake is not the end. 'I have not failed,' he liked to say. 'I have just found ways that do not work.'

He dreamed of making a light that people could use at home. He tried thousands of different threads inside a glass bulb before one finally glowed softly and stayed bright. At last, the light bulb worked! He also built a machine that could record and replay sound.

Because Thomas never gave up, homes and streets could shine at night, and voices could be saved and heard again. He taught the world that patience and curiosity can turn many small tries into one bright idea.
textM: In a small town in Ohio, in America, a boy named Thomas Edison was born, and he came into the world full of questions. Why is the sky blue? Where does the river go? What is inside this? He asked so many questions that his schoolteacher lost patience and said the boy's mind was muddled. Thomas was only seven. He came home with a note, and everything might have ended there.

But his mother, Nancy, had been a teacher herself, and she did not agree at all. 'I will teach him myself,' she said. So the kitchen table became his classroom. She gave him books about science, and he read them the way other children eat cake. Thomas never forgot it. 'My mother was the making of me,' he said when he was old. Someone believing in him was the first spark.

He turned the cellar into a little laboratory full of bottles and labels. At twelve he got a job selling newspapers and sweets on the train, and he even carried his experiments into the baggage car so he could keep working between stations. A kind station master taught him how to send messages by telegraph, tapping out words in dots and dashes. Thomas travelled from town to town, tapping, listening, thinking.

Grown up, he built something quite new: a workshop at Menlo Park, in New Jersey, where a whole team of clever people invented things together, day after day. Thomas did not hear very well, and he always said the quiet helped him concentrate. He would nap on a bench, wake up, and go straight back to work. One day in 1877 he wrapped tinfoil round a little cylinder, turned the handle, and called out, 'Mary had a little lamb!'

Then the machine said it back to him, in his own voice. Everyone in the room jumped. Thomas had invented the phonograph — the first machine that could keep a sound and give it back later. People began calling him the Wizard of Menlo Park, though he said there was no magic in it at all, only work.

His biggest dream was a light gentle enough to live inside a house. The trouble was the thin thread inside the glass bulb: every one he tried burned away in seconds. So he tried another, and another — cotton, paper, even bamboo — thousands of tries. 'I have not failed,' he liked to say. 'I have just found ways that do not work.' At last a carbon thread glowed all night long, and then longer still.

On the last evening of 1879, people rode the train out to Menlo Park to see the little lamps shining in the dark, and they gasped. Three years later Thomas laid wires beneath the streets of New York and switched on a whole neighbourhood at once. Shops could stay open later. Children could read after supper. Over his life he made more than a thousand inventions, and he kept working at them until he was very old.

Today, when you switch on a lamp to read one more page, or press play to hear a song again, you are holding the ending of a very patient story: many small tries, gathered up into one bright idea. Thomas would tell you that the secret is not being clever. The secret is trying once more, after the last try did not work.

stories.name: Robert Koch
stories.title: The Doctor Who Found the Tiniest Troublemakers
stories.hook: What if the thing that makes us sick is too small to see?
text: In Germany long ago, a boy named Robert was born who loved to look closely at everything. He collected little plants and stones and wondered what secrets they held. He grew up to become a careful, kind doctor.

Robert had a microscope, a tool that makes tiny things look big. Peering through it, he saw living things so small that no one could see them with their eyes alone. He called them germs, and he wanted to know if they made people sick.

Like a patient detective, he studied and tested and wrote down everything. He proved that certain germs cause certain illnesses. He even found the tiny germ behind a sickness called tuberculosis. For his careful work, he was given a great award called the Nobel Prize.

Because of Robert, doctors learned to keep things clean and to fight the right germ for each illness. His gentle, careful looking helped keep children and families all over the world healthy and safe.
textM: In Germany long ago, in a little town tucked into wooded mountains, a boy named Robert was born who loved to look closely at everything. He was one of thirteen children, so the house was never quiet. When he was five he surprised his mother and father completely: he announced that he had taught himself to read, all on his own, from the newspapers lying about the house.

Robert spent his childhood outdoors among the pine trees. He collected little plants and stones and mosses and beetles, laid them in boxes, wrote labels for them, and wondered what secrets they held. When he was older he studied medicine, and he grew up to become a careful, kind country doctor, riding out to farms in rain and snow to help whoever needed him.

On his twenty-eighth birthday his wife Emmy gave him a present that changed everything: a microscope, a tool that makes tiny things look big. Robert hung a curtain across one corner of the room where he saw his patients, and behind that curtain he built himself a laboratory. When the last patient had gone home, he sat down and looked.

In the fields nearby, a sickness was making the farmers' sheep and cows unwell. Robert put a single drop under his microscope, and there they were — living things so small that no one could see them with their eyes alone. Tiny rods, drifting. He called them germs. He watched them for hours, then days, and saw them change into tough little seeds that could rest quietly in the soil for years and wake up later. That was why the same field stayed unsafe season after season. Nobody had ever seen such a thing.

To study germs he first had to grow them, and that was a mess — in a bottle of broth they all swirled together. So Robert had a clever idea: give each germ its own solid ground. He tried a slice of boiled potato, and sure enough every germ grew its own separate little spot. Then he tried a jelly, but it melted in summer. The answer came from a friend's wife, Fanny, who used a firm jelly made from seaweed in her kitchen. It worked perfectly, and scientists still use it today. A young helper of Robert's, named Petri, made a small flat glass dish with a lid to hold it — and we still call it a Petri dish.

Then Robert turned to a coughing sickness called tuberculosis, which made a great many people ill. Its germ was almost impossible to see. Like a patient detective he tried dye after dye, week after week, staining and washing and waiting. At last, one morning, he looked down the microscope and there they were: tiny, slender blue rods, glowing against the pale background. He had found it.

In March 1882 he read out his discovery in a small room full of scientists. When he finished, nobody clapped and nobody asked a single question. They were simply too astonished to speak. Later he sailed to Egypt and to India and found the germ of another illness, one that travelled through dirty water — which showed the world just how much clean water matters. For all his careful work he was given a great award called the Nobel Prize.

Because of Robert, doctors learned to keep things clean, to wash their hands, to boil what needed boiling, and to fight the right germ for each illness. His rules for proving which germ causes which sickness are still taught to young doctors today. Every glass of safe water, every washed hand, every medicine that works, carries a little of his patience inside it. His gentle, careful looking helped keep children and families all over the world healthy and safe.

stories.name: Sigmund Freud
stories.title: The Doctor Who Listened to Dreams
stories.hook: Have you ever wondered why we dream at night?
text: In Austria long ago, a curious boy named Sigmund was born who loved to read and think. He always wanted to understand what was happening deep inside people, even the things they could not see.
He grew up to be a doctor, but he was most curious about feelings and dreams. He noticed that when people talked about their worries out loud, they often felt lighter and better inside.

Sigmund began the study of the mind, which we call psychology. He believed our dreams and hidden thoughts could tell us gentle secrets about how we feel. So he sat and listened carefully as people shared their hearts.

Because of Sigmund, the world learned to listen to feelings and to take dreams seriously. He taught us that it is kind and helpful to talk about how we feel, so that no one has to carry their worries alone.
textM: Long ago, a baby boy named Sigmund Freud was born into a large, busy family, and while he was still small they moved to the city of Vienna, in Austria. Vienna was a city of cafés and horse-drawn carriages, of music drifting out of open windows. Sigmund grew up there among seven brothers and sisters, in rooms that were always noisy — except in the one small corner that belonged to him.

That corner was where he read. He read and read: history, science, poetry, and books in six or seven languages. His family believed in him so completely that when his sister's piano practice disturbed his studying, the piano was carried right out of the flat. He was given an oil lamp when the others had candles. Sigmund never forgot how it felt to be taken seriously.

He grew up and became a doctor. But the puzzles that interested him most were not broken bones. They were the invisible ones: why a person can feel sad without knowing why, why a worry can make a body feel unwell, why we sometimes do things we cannot explain. Nobody had a map of that country. So Sigmund decided to start drawing one.

In his consulting room at Berggasse 19, he did something unusual for a doctor of his time. He asked people to lie down on a couch spread with a soft Persian rug, and simply to say whatever came into their heads — anything at all, in any order. And then came the hardest part. He sat quietly behind them, and he listened. One of his patients called it 'the talking cure', and the name stuck.

He listened to their dreams too, and wrote a whole book about them. He thought dreams were like little night-time letters from a hidden part of ourselves — muddled, strange, but worth reading. His desk was crowded with tiny ancient statues, and his chow dog, Jofi, curled up on the floor during the sessions. Sigmund used to joke that Jofi always knew exactly when the hour was over.

He had a picture in his head for how a mind might work, too. Imagine an iceberg, he said. The small shining part above the water is what we know we are thinking. The great quiet part underneath is everything else — old memories, wishes, worries we have half forgotten. And he believed that what happens to us when we are children stays with us, so a child's feelings should never be brushed away as silly.

Not everyone agreed with his ideas, then or now, and doctors who came after him have corrected quite a few of them. When Vienna was no longer safe for his family, kind friends helped him travel to London, where he set out his little statues on a new desk, beside a window looking onto a garden.

But one thing he gave us has never gone out of fashion: the idea that what happens inside a person matters, and that talking about it helps. Every counsellor, every therapist, every grown-up who says 'tell me how you feel, I have time' is walking a path he helped to open. And every night, when you close your eyes, your own mind begins telling you stories that nobody else will ever see.

stories.name: Frederick Banting
stories.title: The Doctor Who Gave His Gift to Everyone
stories.hook: What if you found a medicine that could save millions of lives?
text: In Canada long ago, a boy named Frederick was born on a family farm. He grew up hardworking and kind, helping with the animals and caring about people who were unwell.

He became a doctor and worried about people with an illness called diabetes, whose bodies could not use sugar the right way. Frederick had an idea, and with helpers he worked late into the night to test it.

At last they discovered insulin, a medicine that helps the body use sugar again. Suddenly children who had been very sick began to grow strong and well. It was one of the most wonderful discoveries in all of medicine.

Frederick had a big, generous heart. He sold his special right to the medicine for just one dollar, so that everyone, rich or poor, could have it. Today insulin saves millions of people, all because a farm boy chose to share.
textM: In Canada long ago, on a family farm near a small town called Alliston, a boy named Frederick was born. The farm smelled of hay and wet earth. There were horses to brush and cows to bring in before dark, and Frederick did his share before school and again after. He was a quiet boy, not the quickest in his class, but he never gave up on anything he started. When an animal was sick, he was the one who sat up with it.

Frederick loved people the way he loved those animals. When he grew up he went to the city of Toronto to learn to be a doctor. Later he opened a small office of his own, and at first hardly anyone came. To fill the long, empty hours he read medical books and taught a class at the university. That quiet, patient reading turned out to matter more than anyone could have guessed.

One illness worried him more than any other: diabetes. In those days, a child with diabetes could not use the sugar in food to make energy. Doctors had no medicine at all. All they could do was watch. Frederick could not stop thinking about it. One night, after reading very late, he fell asleep, woke at two in the morning with an idea glowing in his head, and wrote twenty-five words in his notebook by lamplight.

His idea was about a small organ called the pancreas, tucked in behind the stomach. Frederick believed it made something the body needed, and that this something could be taken out and given as a medicine. He asked a professor in Toronto for a room, and got one: a hot little laboratory up under the roof. A young student named Charles Best came to help him. All that summer of 1921 the room was stifling, the work was slow, and the experiments failed again and again.

Then, at last, something worked. They made a liquid from the pancreas, and when they gave it to a sick dog, the dog grew bright and lively again. Frederick could hardly speak. With help from a chemist named James Collip the liquid was made pure and safe, and they called it insulin. In January a boy of fourteen named Leonard, so ill that he could barely lift his head, was given the very first proper dose. Within days he sat up. Within weeks he was walking about, hungry and laughing.

Word spread from hospital to hospital. In wards where families had been sitting silently beside children who slept and slept, doctors went from bed to bed with insulin, and one by one the children opened their eyes. Parents wept in the corridors. Nothing quite like it had ever happened in medicine before.

Then Frederick did the thing people remember best of all. He and his friends could have kept the medicine for themselves and become very rich. Instead they signed away their rights to the university for one dollar each. 'Insulin does not belong to me,' Frederick said. 'It belongs to the world.' He was given a great prize for the discovery, and he shared his prize money with young Charles Best, who had sweated beside him all summer long.

Today, all over the world, millions of people take insulin every single day and live long, ordinary, happy lives — going to school, playing football, growing up. It all began with a farm boy who was not the cleverest in the room, who woke in the night with an idea, and who decided that a gift as big as this one was meant to be shared.

stories.name: Otto Hahn
stories.title: The Chemist Who Found the Secret Inside an Atom
stories.hook: What if the smallest things in the world held a hidden surprise?
text: In Germany long ago, a boy named Otto was born who loved mixing things and watching what happened. He grew up gentle and thoughtful, and he became a chemist who studied the tiny pieces that everything is made of.

Everything around us, this book, the air, even you, is made of teeny building blocks called atoms. Atoms are so small we cannot see them, and each one has a busy little center. Otto and his friends wanted to understand that center.

After careful work, Otto discovered something amazing. The tiny center of an atom can split into smaller pieces, and when it does, it lets out a bit of hidden energy. This discovery is called nuclear fission, and it filled scientists with wonder.

Otto knew that such a powerful discovery must be used with great care. He bravely spoke up for using science kindly and responsibly, to help people and to keep the world safe. He reminds us that a discovery is a gift, and gifts should be used to do good.
textM: In Germany, long ago, in the city of Frankfurt, a boy named Otto Hahn was born. His father made and fitted glass, so Otto grew up among panes and bottles and the bright ringing sound of glass being tapped. He was a cheerful, gentle boy who liked to mix things together in the laundry room at the back of the house, just to see what would happen. Sometimes there was a bang. Sometimes there was a smell that lasted for days.

His father hoped Otto would become an architect and build fine houses. But Otto had made up his mind. He wanted to spend his life finding out what things are made of. So he became a chemist, and he never stopped being that curious boy in the laundry room.

Everything around us — this book, the air, the sea, even you — is made of teeny building blocks called atoms. Atoms are so small that a single grain of sand holds more of them than you could ever count. And each atom has a busy little centre, right in the middle, holding it all together. Otto wanted to understand that centre more than anything.

In Berlin he found the best possible partner: a quiet, brilliant physicist named Lise Meitner. In those days a woman was not allowed into the main laboratory upstairs, so the two of them worked in a room in the basement that had once been a carpenter's workshop. It smelled faintly of sawdust. They worked side by side there for thirty years, and when the day's experiments were done they would sing together to cheer themselves up.

Then, one winter, Otto and his colleague Fritz Strassmann did an experiment and got an answer that could not possibly be right. They had been gently knocking on the centres of very heavy atoms — and afterwards they found a much lighter substance in the dish, one that should not have been there at all. Otto checked. He checked again. "This is impossible," he wrote, and he posted the puzzle in a letter to Lise, who by then was living far away in Sweden.

Lise read the letter on a snowy day, out walking in the woods with her nephew, who was a scientist too. They sat down on a fallen tree trunk in the snow and did the sums on a scrap of paper. And there, among the pine trees, they found the answer: the centre of the atom had split in two. Nobody had ever imagined such a thing.

And when it splits, it lets go of a little of the hidden energy that had been holding it together. The discovery was called nuclear fission, and it filled scientists everywhere with wonder — and a little fear, because so much energy from something so small is a very powerful thing indeed. Otto was given the Nobel Prize for it.

Otto knew that such a discovery must be handled with enormous care. For the rest of his long life he spoke up, again and again, asking the world to use this power only to help people and never to harm them. He reminds us of something worth remembering at the end of the day: a discovery is a gift, and gifts should be used to do good.

stories.name: Werner Heisenberg
stories.title: The Boy Who Found the Rules of the Tiny
stories.hook: At the smallest sizes, the world plays a game of hide-and-seek.
text: Long ago in Germany, a boy named Werner loved two things: music at the piano and climbing high in the mountains. He was quiet and thoughtful, and he liked to wonder about how the world was put together.
When he grew up, Werner became a physicist. He studied the very tiniest bits of everything — smaller than a speck of dust, smaller than we can ever see. These tiny pieces are called particles.

Werner made a surprising discovery. Down among the smallest things, you can never be perfectly sure exactly where a particle is and where it is going, both at the very same moment. He called this the uncertainty principle.

It sounds strange, but it is one of the great truths of nature. Werner taught the world that even a little bit of mystery can be beautiful, and that wondering is one of the finest things a person can do.
textM: Long ago in Germany, in a town called Würzburg, a boy named Werner was born. His father was a professor who loved old Greek books, and the house was full of reading. Werner loved two things above all: the piano, which he played so well that grown-ups stopped what they were doing to listen, and the mountains, where he walked for days with his friends and slept under the stars.

He was quiet and thoughtful. He liked puzzles, and he liked questions with no easy answer. Once he found an old book of mathematics and read it right through, just to see what was inside. Even on the mountain paths, while the others sang, Werner would be wondering to himself: what is everything actually made of?

When he grew up, Werner went to study with the finest teachers he could find, and became a physicist. He studied the tiniest bits of everything — smaller than a speck of dust, far too small for any eye or any microscope to see. These tiny pieces are called particles, and nobody could work out the rules they obeyed. Whatever the scientists tried, the answers came out wrong.

Then one spring Werner became terribly ill with hay fever. His face swelled up so much that his teacher hardly knew him, and he went away to a little rocky island in the North Sea called Helgoland, where almost nothing grows and the wind blows all the pollen away. There he swam, and walked along the cliffs, and learned poems by heart — and worked and worked at his numbers.

One night, at about three o'clock in the morning, the numbers finally came out right. Werner was so excited that he could not sleep at all. He said afterwards that he felt almost dizzy, as if he were looking through the surface of things at something beautiful underneath. As the sky grew light he went outside, climbed a rock at the tip of the island, and waited for the sun to come up out of the sea.

He had found a new kind of mathematics for the world of the very small. A little later, walking alone very late at night in a park in Copenhagen, turning a question over and over in his mind, he found something stranger still. Down among the smallest things, you can never be perfectly sure exactly where a particle is and exactly where it is going, both at the very same moment. Look closely at one, and the other slips away. He called this the uncertainty principle.

It was not that anyone's instruments were poor. That is simply how nature is. Werner talked it over for weeks with his friend Niels Bohr in Copenhagen, the two of them walking and arguing until they were worn out, and at last they agreed. When Werner was thirty-one, he was given the greatest prize in all of science for what he had found.

Today the strange rules Werner discovered are hidden inside almost everything: the phone in a pocket, the lasers that read music, the computers of tomorrow. And he left us something else besides. He taught the world that a little mystery is not a failure but a beautiful part of nature — and that wondering, quietly and honestly, is one of the finest things a person can do.

stories.name: J. Robert Oppenheimer
stories.title: The Dreamer Who Loved to Learn
stories.hook: Great power in the world needs great care and a kind heart.
text: In the United States, a boy named Robert grew up gazing at rocks and reading poems. He was dreamy and clever, and he loved to learn so much that he studied many languages, just for the joy of it.
Robert grew into a wonderful physicist and a beloved teacher. He could take the hardest ideas about atoms and make his students feel excited and curious. People traveled far just to learn from him.

During a war, Robert was asked to lead a big team of scientists working with tiny atoms to make something very, very powerful. He led them well, but afterward he felt the heavy weight of how strong it was.

For the rest of his life, Robert reminded the whole world of an important lesson: great power must always be used with great care, wisely and for peace. Cleverness is a gift, he taught, but kindness must guide it.
textM: In New York City, in a tall apartment high above the river, a boy named Robert was growing up. He was thin and dreamy and often unwell, and he read the way other children run. When his grandfather in Germany gave him a small box of minerals — crystals that caught the light in green and violet and gold — Robert was enchanted. In the summers his family went to the seashore, and there the dreamy, delicate boy learned to sail a small boat, steering it out into the wind and the salt spray, brave as anything.

He collected rocks everywhere he went, and wrote careful letters about them to grown-up scientists in the city. The letters were so clever that the New York Mineralogical Club invited the writer to come and give a talk. When the door opened, in walked a boy of twelve. They had to find a wooden box for him to stand on, so that everyone could see him above the top of the desk. He read out his paper. The old collectors clapped and clapped.

Robert loved learning the way some people love sweets. He studied physics in America, in England and in Germany. In the evenings he read poetry. He even learned Sanskrit, an ancient language of India, just for the joy of reading its old poems in the very words they were written in.

Then he came home and became a teacher, and this is where he truly shone. He could take the hardest ideas about atoms — the tiny building blocks that everything is made of — and make them feel like an adventure. His students loved him so much that they copied the way he walked and the way he held his hands. Some followed him from one university to another rather than miss a single lecture.

Robert also loved the desert of New Mexico, with its red flat-topped hills and its enormous sky. As a young man he had ridden horses there for whole summers at a time. He used to say that his two great loves were physics and that desert, and what a pity it was that they could not be brought together.

Then came a war, and Robert was asked to lead a great team of scientists working with atoms, to build something very, very powerful before anyone else could. He chose a lonely place high on a flat hill in his beloved desert, and thousands of people came there to live and work. Robert remembered everybody's name. He seemed to be in every room at once. It was the hardest task of his whole life, and he did it.

When it was over, Robert felt the heavy weight of how strong the thing they had made truly was. He did not hide from that feeling. He spent the rest of his life telling presidents and generals and ordinary people the same thing, quietly and stubbornly: that the nations of the world must talk to one another, share what they know, and use such power only for peace.

We remember Robert Oppenheimer as the dreamy boy who stood on a box to give his first talk, and grew up to lead the cleverest people in the world. But the lesson he left behind is simpler than any of his physics: cleverness is a wonderful gift, and it must always be guided by kindness and by very great care.

stories.name: Richard Feynman
stories.title: The Boy Who Kept Asking Why
stories.hook: Science is play, and curiosity is a gift you never lose.
text: In New York, a joyful boy named Richard loved to take things apart. He fixed broken radios for his neighbors, and best of all, he never stopped asking one little question: "Why?"

Richard grew up to be a famous physicist. But he was a very special kind of scientist. He could take a tricky idea and explain it so simply and so happily that everyone around him would smile and understand.
Richard loved fun as much as he loved science. He played the bongo drums, told funny stories, and giggled his way through the biggest puzzles about how the universe works.
He taught the whole world a wonderful truth: science is not boring at all — it is play, it is wonder, it is joy. And curiosity, that little urge to ask "why," is a gift we should keep forever.
textM: In 1918, in a corner of New York City where you could smell the sea, a boy named Richard Feynman was born. Before he arrived, his father Melville said something rather bold: if the baby is a boy, he will be a scientist. Melville was not a scientist himself — he sold uniforms — but he knew exactly how to grow one.

He did it with games. He would sit little Richard in a high chair with a pile of bathroom tiles and lay them out in patterns, blue, white, blue, white, so the boy could see the rhythm coming. On walks in the woods he said something Richard never forgot: "You can know the name of that bird in every language in the world, and still know nothing at all about the bird. Look at the bird. Watch what it is doing."

Richard turned his bedroom into a laboratory. There was an old wooden packing box, a battery, switches he wired himself, little lamps, and a microscope. Money was scarce in those years, and when neighbours' radios broke they could not buy new ones — so they brought them to the boy down the street. Once he paced up and down for a long while before touching a single wire, thinking hard, and the puzzled owner told everyone afterwards, "He fixes radios by thinking!"

Richard grew up to be a physicist, and he treated the whole universe as one enormous, delightful puzzle. The very smallest things — light and the tiny specks inside atoms — behave in ways that make grown-ups' heads spin. The mathematics filled page after page. So Richard did something wonderfully simple: he drew little pictures.

Straight lines for particles, wiggly lines for light, meeting and bouncing away. Anyone could follow them with a finger. Those small doodles are called Feynman diagrams, and physicists all over the world still draw them today, on blackboards and napkins and the backs of envelopes. For that work he was given the Nobel Prize. He nearly said no — all the fuss embarrassed him. The real reward, he said, was simply the pleasure of finding things out.

He was a marvellous teacher. At his university in California the students nicknamed him the Great Explainer. If he could not explain an idea to a class of first-year students, he said, that meant we did not really understand it yet. He would jump about at the blackboard, wave his arms, tell a joke, and suddenly the hardest thing in the world would seem easy.

And he never stopped playing. He learned to beat out rhythms on bongo drums. He taught himself to open locked filing cabinets, just to prove that he could, leaving cheeky notes inside for his colleagues. He learned Portuguese so he could teach in Brazil. He drew portraits. He once spent days following the ants in his kitchen with a pencil, marking their trails, until he had worked out how they tell each other where the sugar is.

Richard Feynman taught the whole world a lovely truth: science is not a dull list of facts to memorise. It is play, it is wonder, it is joy — and finding out how something works makes it more beautiful, never less. That little urge to ask "why" is called curiosity, and it is a gift you never have to grow out of.

stories.name: Francis Crick
stories.title: The Boy With a Thousand Questions
stories.hook: Inside every living thing hides a tiny twisted ladder.
text: In England, a boy named Francis asked so many questions that his parents finally bought him a big encyclopedia, so he could look up all the answers himself. But new questions kept popping up in his busy mind.

When Francis grew up, he wanted to solve one of life's greatest mysteries. Every plant, every animal, every person carries a secret code inside them. That code is called DNA, and it decides how living things grow.

Working with his friend James Watson, and using beautiful photographs taken by a clever scientist named Rosalind Franklin, Francis figured out the shape of DNA. It looked like a tiny twisted ladder, spiraling round and round.
This discovery helped us understand what makes each of us who we are. Because a curious boy never stopped asking questions, the whole world learned one of the deepest secrets of life.
textM: In 1916, in a green corner of England near the town of Northampton, a boy named Francis Crick was born. His family made shoes, and the workshops of that town smelled of leather and glue. Francis was a small boy with an enormous number of questions. Why is the sky blue? What is fire made of? How does a bird know the way home?

He asked so many questions that his parents finally bought him a big children's encyclopedia, so he could go and look up the answers himself. He read it from cover to cover. Then one evening a worry crept up on him. "What if everything has already been discovered by the time I grow up?" he asked his mother. She smiled. "Don't worry," she told him. "There will be plenty left for you."

As a boy he liked experiments almost as much as questions. He mixed things in bottles at home and made small, loud bangs, until his parents gently suggested he try electricity instead. So he did, and he wired up bells and lamps and anything else that would hold still long enough.

Francis grew up and studied physics, but for years he could not find the one big question that was his. He was already in his thirties, which felt terribly old to him. So he invented a little test. What do I chatter about when I am not working? Whatever that is, he decided, is what I truly care about. And the answer was clear: he chattered about how the brain thinks, and about the strange line between things that are alive and things that are not. So he chose biology.

He went to Cambridge, to a laboratory of cold corridors, blackboards and endless cups of tea. There he met a young American named James Watson, and the two of them talked so much, so loudly, and so happily that they were given a room of their own so the rest of the building could think in peace. They were chasing one thing: the shape of DNA, the secret code hidden inside every plant, every animal, every person.

Nobody had ever seen DNA. But in London, a brilliant scientist named Rosalind Franklin had learned to shine X-rays through damp threads of it and catch the shadows on film. One of her photographs showed a blurry, beautiful X. To someone who knew how to read it, that X whispered a secret: whatever this thing is, it is twisted like a spiral staircase.

So Francis and James started cutting shapes out of cardboard and bending bits of metal, and sliding them about on a bench like puzzle pieces. Wrong, wrong, wrong — and then, one morning in the spring of 1953, right. Two long strands, winding round each other, joined by rungs that always fitted in pairs. A twisted ladder that could unzip down the middle and copy itself. That is how living things pass their instructions on. Francis walked straight to the pub next door and announced to everybody there that they had found the secret of life.

He was not exaggerating by much. Because of that little twisted ladder, doctors can understand illnesses, farmers can grow better food, and we can explain why you have your grandmother's eyes. Francis never stopped questioning; he spent his later years asking how the brain works, right up to the end. His story is a promise to every curious child: the questions you cannot stop asking may one day open the world.

stories.name: Rosalind Franklin
stories.title: The Girl Who Took the Famous Photo
stories.hook: One careful photograph revealed the shape of life itself.
text: In England, a bright and determined girl named Rosalind loved facts and getting things exactly right. Even as a child, she liked to measure carefully and find true answers.

Rosalind became a scientist who used special cameras that could take pictures with X-rays. With great skill and patience, she photographed something no one had ever seen clearly before: the tiny shape of DNA.

Her most famous picture was called Photo 51. It gave the very first clear clue that DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder. Her careful work was the key that unlocked one of science's greatest discoveries.
For a long time, Rosalind did not get all the thanks she deserved. But today the whole world honors her. She reminds us that patience, care, and hard work can change what everyone knows about life.
textM: In London, in a house on a quiet street, a baby girl was born on a winter day in 1920. Her family named her Rosalind. Almost as soon as she could talk, she wanted to know why things were the way they were. She did sums for fun, and she got them right. She liked her drawings neat and her answers exact. If someone gave her half an answer, she would keep asking until she had the whole one.

At school, science was her favourite thing in the world. When she was fifteen, she told her family that she was going to be a scientist.
