In those days not many girls did that, and even her father was not sure at first. Rosalind did not shout about it. She simply kept studying, went to university in Cambridge, and learned chemistry until she knew it inside out.

Then she went to work in Paris. She loved it there — the bread, the French language, and long walks up mountains with a rucksack on her back in the holidays. In her laboratory she learned a kind of magic. If you shine X-rays at something far too small to see, the rays bounce off in a pattern. Read the pattern, and you can work out the shape of the thing itself. She was patient with machines that other people found difficult.

Back in London, Rosalind was given a very hard puzzle. Inside every living thing — every child, every cat, every blade of grass — there is a tiny thread called DNA. It holds the instructions for building a whole living creature. Nobody knew what it looked like. Rosalind pulled DNA out into fibres finer than spider silk, and kept the air around them damp, exactly damp enough, so that the fibres lay still and neat.

Then she waited. In a small dark room, her camera stared at that thread hour after hour after hour, catching the faintest scatter of rays. The picture took so long to make that a whole day and a whole night went by while the camera worked. Most people would have grown bored. Rosalind wrote careful notes in a careful hand. And when at last she lifted the film out of the developing tray, there it was: a soft, dark X made of spots. An X like that means only one thing. A spiral.

The picture was called Photo 51, and it was the clearest clue anyone had ever had. It showed that DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder, winding round and round and round. Other scientists used what her photograph revealed to build a model of that shape, and the world cheered. But for a long time hardly anyone said Rosalind's name out loud. She moved quietly on to another laboratory and made beautiful pictures of viruses instead. Her own life was short; she died young, still working, still curious.

Today the whole world knows what she did. Her photograph hangs in books and museums, and a robot explorer sent to search for life on Mars carries her name across the sky. Rosalind reminds us of something worth remembering at bedtime: being careful is a kind of courage. If you look closely enough, and patiently enough, you can be the very first person ever to see how something works.

stories.name: Carl Sagan
stories.title: The Boy Who Wondered About the Stars
stories.hook: We are all made of star-stuff, twinkling far, far away.
text: In Brooklyn, a boy named Carl loved to look up at the night sky and wonder. What were those tiny lights? How far away were they? His questions were as big as the whole universe.
Carl grew up to be an astronomer, a scientist who studies the stars and planets. He helped send spacecraft to explore faraway planets, sending back pictures no one had ever seen before.
But most of all, Carl loved to share his wonder. Through his books and his television shows, he helped millions of people all over the world fall in love with the sky.

Carl told everyone something amazing and true: the tiny bits inside our bodies were once made deep inside the stars. "We are made of star-stuff," he said — so when you look up at night, you are looking at family.
textM: In 1934, in Brooklyn, New York, a boy named Carl Sagan was born. His father cut cloth in a clothing factory, and his mother had a mind full of questions she had never been allowed to ask at school. Their apartment was small and the city was loud. But up on the roof, and out of the window at bedtime, there were the stars.

When Carl was five, he asked his mother what the stars were. She did not simply answer him. She gave him a library card and told him to go and find out. The library was cool and quiet and smelled of paper. Carl asked the librarian for a book about stars, and she brought him one about film stars in Hollywood. Very politely, Carl said that was not quite what he meant. When at last he opened the right book, he read something that made his heart thump: the stars are suns, just like ours, only unimaginably far away. He walked home feeling that the world had suddenly grown enormous.

Carl grew up to be an astronomer. He worked out why the planet Venus is so terribly hot — a thick blanket of cloud and gas that traps the heat and will not let it go. Then he helped plan the spacecraft that flew out to explore: little robot travellers that swung past Mars, Jupiter and Saturn and sent home photographs no human eye had ever seen. Carl would sit by the screen as the pictures arrived, line by slow line, like a present being unwrapped.

He did something else too, something only a dreamer would think of. When two spacecraft called Voyager were sent off toward the stars, Carl and his friends put a golden record on board — with music from many countries, the sound of rain, a whale singing, a kiss, a baby's laugh, and hellos in fifty-five languages. Those records are still travelling tonight, further from home than anything people have ever made.

Years later, Carl asked the engineers to turn Voyager around one last time and photograph the Earth from billions of miles away. In that picture, our whole planet is only a tiny pale blue dot, smaller than a speck of dust. Carl said: everyone you love, everyone you have ever heard of, lived right there, on that little dot. It made him think we should be very gentle with each other, and very careful with our home.

Most of all, Carl loved to share his wonder. He made a television programme called Cosmos, and hundreds of millions of people, in dozens of countries, watched it. He never talked down to anybody. He was a teacher, too, and his students said he made the whole universe feel like a place you had been invited into. He believed a child's question deserved a real answer, and that not knowing something is nothing to be ashamed of — it is the beginning of finding out.

Carl told us something amazing and true. The iron in your blood, the calcium in your bones, the oxygen you are breathing right now — all of it was made long, long ago, deep inside stars, and scattered across space when those stars grew old. "We are made of star-stuff," he said. So when you look up tonight, you are not looking at strangers. You are looking at family.

stories.name: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam
stories.title: The Newspaper Boy Who Reached the Sky
stories.hook: Dream big, work hard, and the sky becomes your friend.
text: In a small fishing town in India, a poor boy named Abdul woke up early each morning to sell newspapers and help his family. He loved to watch the birds soar over the sea and dreamed of flying.
Abdul worked incredibly hard at school and never gave up. He grew up to become a great rocket scientist, helping his country reach up into space. People proudly called him the "Missile Man."
Because he was so kind and wise, Abdul was later chosen to be the President of India. He was so loved that people called him the "People's President." Yet he still lived simply and gently.
More than anything, Abdul loved to talk with children. "Dream, dream, dream," he would say with a warm smile, "for dreams turn into ideas, and ideas change the world."
textM: On a small island town in southern India, where the sea lies on both sides and the air smells of salt and drying fishing nets, a boy named Abdul was born in 1931. The town was called Rameswaram. It had a great old temple, painted fishing boats pulled up on the sand, and coconut palms that rattled in the wind. Abdul was the youngest child of a big, warm family.

His father was a boat-builder who carried travellers across the water, and his mother fed anyone who came to the door hungry. They had very little money. So Abdul got up before the sun and went to collect the newspapers that came in on the early train, then ran through the sleeping streets to deliver them. After that he washed, went to his lessons, and did his schoolwork by lamplight.

One day his teacher took the whole class down to the seashore. He pointed at the seabirds turning above the waves. “Look,” he said. “Look how the wing bends. Look how the tail steers.” Abdul stood in the wet sand and watched, and something inside him lit up. That evening he told his family he wanted to fly. It sounded impossible for a newspaper boy. Nobody laughed at him.

Abdul worked incredibly hard at school, then studied physics, and then how to build aeroplanes. His dream was to become a fighter pilot. When the day came, he was one of many young men trying for eight places — and he came ninth. He walked away with his heart aching. He sat alone for a long while. Then he decided something important: the sky was still there, and there must be another way up to it.

There was. Abdul joined the people who were teaching his country to build rockets. It was slow, patient, difficult work in hot sheds with not much equipment. Once, when a rocket he was in charge of failed, he felt terrible. But his kind boss stood in front of everyone and took the blame himself, and told Abdul quietly to try again.

They tried again. In 1980 their rocket rose off the pad, up and up through the clouds, and placed India's own little satellite into orbit around the Earth. This time his boss made Abdul stand up and tell the world about it. India could reach space. People proudly called him the “Missile Man.”

Abdul stayed exactly the same person all the way through. He owned almost nothing. He read poetry and wrote it. He played an instrument called the veena in the evenings. He was so kind and so wise that in 2002 his country asked him to be its President. He opened the gardens of the great president's house to schoolchildren, and he was so loved that people called him the “People's President.” When his years were over, he packed his few things into a couple of suitcases and walked out as simply as he had walked in.

More than anything else, Abdul loved to talk with children. He answered thousands of letters from them. He went to school after school after school, and he was standing in front of a hall full of students on the very last day of his long life, doing the thing that made him happiest. “Dream, dream, dream,” he would say with a warm smile, “for dreams turn into thoughts, and thoughts turn into ideas, and ideas change the world.” Somewhere tonight, a child who has very little is reading his words — and deciding to try.

stories.name: Hypatia of Alexandria
stories.title: The Teacher Who Read the Stars
stories.hook: In the greatest library of the ancient world, a girl grew up among scrolls — and became the most famous teacher of stars and numbers.
text: Long, long ago, in the city of Alexandria in Egypt, there lived a girl named Hypatia. Her city had the most wonderful library in the whole ancient world, full of scrolls about stars, numbers, and faraway lands. Her father was a mathematician, and instead of keeping his books to himself, he shared everything he knew with his daughter.

Hypatia loved mathematics and the night sky. She studied how the planets wander among the stars, and she learned to use an astrolabe — a beautiful round instrument that helps sailors and stargazers find their way by the stars.

She became such a wise teacher that students traveled across the sea just to hear her speak. In a time when very few women were allowed to study at all, the wisest people of the city would say, "Go and ask Hypatia — she will know."

Hypatia lived more than one thousand six hundred years ago, yet we still remember her tonight. She reminds us that knowledge is a gift that grows when it is shared — like starlight, it can travel a very, very long way.
textM: In the city of Alexandria, in Egypt, the sea was blue and the streets were wide and straight, so straight that the sun poured all the way down them. Ships came from everywhere. And in the middle of it all stood the most wonderful library of the ancient world, with shelf after shelf of scrolls about stars, numbers, medicine and faraway lands. In that city, about sixteen hundred years ago, a girl named Hypatia was born.

Her father was Theon, a mathematician who worked among those scrolls. He copied out Euclid's old book of shapes, and he checked the great tables that told people where the planets would be. In those days many fathers taught only their sons. Theon did not. He shared every single thing he knew with his daughter, and she grew up with ink on her fingers and questions on her lips.

Hypatia loved mathematics. She loved the way a hard problem slowly opens, like a knot coming undone in your hands. And she did something very kind with what she knew: she wrote books that explained other people's books — the puzzling number riddles of Diophantus, the beautiful curves of Apollonius — so that students who had found them far too hard could understand them at last. Her explanations were so clear that copies were carried away to other cities, and some of those old books are still with us only because she helped keep them alive.

She loved the night sky even more. Up on the flat roof, with the sea breathing quietly below, she watched the planets wander slowly among the fixed stars. She knew how to use an astrolabe — a round instrument of metal with discs that turn, one over another. With it, a sailor or a stargazer can look up and say: here is where I am standing, and here is the hour of the night.

One of her students, a young man named Synesius, wrote her letters that we can still read today, all these centuries later. He asked her about an instrument for measuring how heavy water is. He told her his troubles when he was sad. He called her his teacher and his mother, and he said that whatever he knew, she had given it to him.

Students crossed the sea just to hear her speak. She wore the plain cloak of a philosopher, and she taught in her own home and out in the open street, and she welcomed young people of every religion who wanted to learn. In a time when very few women were allowed to study at all, the wisest people in the city would simply say, 'Go and ask Hypatia. She will know.'

She was famous for being calm, and fair, and for answering one question with another question, so that in the end you found the answer yourself and it belonged to you. That is the mark of a truly fine teacher: not to hand you the treasure, but to lend you the lamp and walk beside you while you look.

Hypatia lived more than sixteen hundred years ago, and here we are, remembering her tonight. There is even a crater on the Moon that carries her name, so that when you look up, part of the sky is called Hypatia. She reminds us that knowledge is a gift which only grows bigger when it is shared — like starlight, it can travel a very, very long way.

stories.name: Chien-Shiung Wu
stories.title: The First Lady of Physics
stories.hook: Her father opened a school just so girls could learn — and his daughter grew up to test the deepest rules of nature.
text: In 1912, in a small town near Shanghai, China, a girl named Chien-Shiung Wu was born. In those days, many people thought school was not for girls. But her father believed the opposite — he opened a school for girls himself, and Chien-Shiung was one of its very first pupils.

She loved physics, the science of how the world works, and she sailed far across the ocean to America to keep studying. She became famous for doing experiments so careful and so precise that other scientists said, "If Wu measured it, it must be true."

One day, two scientists had a wild idea: maybe one of nature's oldest rules — that the world works the same as its mirror image — was sometimes broken. Everyone said it was impossible. But Chien-Shiung built a brilliant experiment with atoms colder than the coldest ice, and proved the impossible was true.

People called her the First Lady of Physics. She showed the world that a careful mind and patient hands can uncover secrets hiding in the smallest corners of nature — and that every girl deserves a school that believes in her.
textM: In 1912, in a little town of canals and willow trees near Shanghai, in China, a girl was born. Her family gave her a name that meant Courageous Hero: Chien-Shiung. In those days, most girls in her town never went to school at all. They stayed home, and nobody thought that was strange.

But her father thought it was very strange indeed. So he did something about it: he opened a school for girls himself, right there in the town. Chien-Shiung was one of its very first pupils. "Ignore the obstacles," her father told her. "Just put your head down and keep walking forward." She remembered those words her whole life.

At eleven she packed a small bag and went away to a boarding school far from home. There she was training to be a teacher, not a scientist — so she borrowed physics and mathematics books from the girls in the science class and taught herself, quietly, after the lamps were meant to be out. Nobody made her do it. Nobody even knew. She simply wanted to know how the world worked, and the books would not tell her unless she went and fetched them.

In 1936 she boarded a ship and sailed across the whole Pacific Ocean to America. She meant to study in Michigan, but she stopped in San Francisco, visited a university in Berkeley with a big shining laboratory, and never left. The voyage had taken weeks, and it would be many, many years before she saw her home town again. She missed it, and she worked all the harder.

Chien-Shiung became famous for one thing above all: experiments so careful that nobody could argue with them. She checked, and rechecked, and checked once more. Other physicists used to say, "If Wu measured it, it must be true." She studied the quiet way certain atoms change all by themselves — one of the softest, shyest happenings in all of nature, far too small and too gentle for any eye to see.

Then, in 1956, two scientists came to her with a wild idea. Everyone believed that nature works exactly the same as its reflection in a mirror. What if, sometimes, it doesn't? People said the idea was silly. Chien-Shiung did not. She cancelled a long-planned trip, rolled up her sleeves, and built an experiment: atoms of cobalt chilled to almost the coldest temperature there can be, colder than the coldest ice, so cold that they lined up like tiny compass needles. She worked all through the winter.

And the answer came: the little particles flew out more in one direction than the other. Nature can tell its left hand from its right. Physicists all over the world gasped. A great prize was given for the discovery — to the two men who had had the idea, and not to the woman whose careful hands had proved it. Many people thought that was unfair, and said so. Chien-Shiung simply went back to her laboratory and kept working, and years later she was honoured with a great prize of her own.

People called her the First Lady of Physics. Today her ashes rest in the courtyard of the very school her father built for girls. Her life says two things, gently and clearly: a patient mind can uncover secrets hidden in the smallest corners of the universe — and every girl deserves a school that believes in her.

stories.name: Gladys West
stories.title: The Girl Whose Maths Guide the Whole World
stories.hook: She worked in the fields as a child and dreamed of more — today, every map on every phone follows her calculations.
text: In 1930, on a small farm in Virginia, in the United States, a girl named Gladys was born. Her family worked hard in the fields, and Gladys worked beside them. But she noticed something: the sun was hot, the work was endless, and she wanted a different life. Her teachers told her the way out was education.

So Gladys studied harder than anyone. She finished first in her whole school and won a place at university, where she fell in love with mathematics. She became one of only a few Black women hired to work as a mathematician for the American navy.

Gladys was given a wonderful puzzle: to use satellites circling high above us to measure the true shape of the Earth — every bump, every valley, every curve of the oceans. For years she calculated and checked, calculated and checked, until her numbers described our planet more perfectly than ever before.

Her work became the heart of GPS — the system that tells phones, cars, ships, and airplanes exactly where they are. So when someone's map says "turn left here," a little bit of Gladys's math is whispering the way. Not bad for a girl who started in a farm field, dreaming under the same sky her satellites now watch.
textM: In 1930, on a small farm in Virginia, in the United States, a girl named Gladys was born. Her family grew corn and cotton and tobacco. There were rows and rows of plants, stretching away to the trees, and a sky so wide you could watch the weather coming from far off. Everyone in the family worked, and Gladys worked beside them, even when she was quite small.

The days in the fields were long. The sun was hot on her back, her fingers grew sore from the cotton, and the rows never seemed to end. Gladys loved her family, but she looked at that long field and thought: there must be another way to live. Her mother worked in a tobacco factory. Her father worked on the railroad. And her teachers told her the door out was education.

So Gladys studied harder than anyone. She walked a long way to school and did her homework by lamplight when the farm work was done. In her school there was a wonderful rule: whoever came top of the class won a scholarship to college. Gladys finished first in her whole school, and off she went — the first in her family to go.

At college she looked around for the hardest subject she could find, and chose mathematics. There were very few girls in that classroom. Gladys did not mind. She loved the quiet, stubborn joy of a problem that finally comes out right. She taught school for a while, and then, in 1956, she was hired at a navy base at Dahlgren, beside a wide river, as a mathematician.

She was one of only a handful of Black people working there, and only the second Black woman ever hired. The rooms hummed with adding machines and enormous computers that filled whole walls. Gladys learned to talk to those machines using cards with little holes punched in them. And there she met a fellow mathematician called Ira, who became her husband.

Then Gladys was given a wonderful puzzle. The Earth, it turns out, is not a perfect ball. It bulges a little at the middle, it is slightly flat at the top and bottom, and it has mountains and deep valleys and oceans that pile up higher in some places than others. Her job was to use satellites circling high above us to measure that true shape, exactly, everywhere.

It took years. Numbers came down from space, and Gladys turned them into instructions for the computers, then checked the answers, then found the small mistakes, then began again. Calculate and check. Calculate and check. Slowly, her numbers began to describe our planet more perfectly than anyone ever had before — every bump, every hollow, every curve of the sea.

That model of the Earth became the heart of GPS, the system that tells phones and cars and ships and aeroplanes and tractors exactly where they are. For a long time hardly anyone knew her name. Then people found out, and in 2018 she was honoured in front of a great crowd — and, at eighty-eight, she finished a doctorate too, because she still liked to learn. So when a little voice on a map says “turn left here,” a bit of Gladys's maths is quietly whispering the way. Not bad for a girl who began in a cotton field, dreaming under the very same sky her satellites now watch.

stories.name: Jane Goodall
stories.title: The Girl Who Listened to the Chimpanzees
stories.hook: With no diploma and endless patience, she sat quietly in a forest in Tanzania — until the chimpanzees told her their secrets.
text: In 1934, in London, England, a girl named Jane was born. When she was little, her father gave her a toy chimpanzee named Jubilee, and she carried him everywhere. Jane loved animals so much that once she hid in a henhouse for hours, perfectly still, just to see how a hen lays an egg. Her mother didn't scold her — she saw a little scientist being born.

Jane dreamed of Africa. She saved her money working as a waitress, and when she finally arrived, a famous scientist saw how patient and sharp-eyed she was. He sent her to the forest of Gombe, in Tanzania, to watch wild chimpanzees — something no one had truly done before.

For months the chimpanzees ran away from her. But Jane came back every day, sitting quietly on the same hill, until they decided she was a friend. Then she saw something amazing: a chimpanzee stripping the leaves off a twig to fish termites out of a mound. Chimpanzees could make tools! Until then, people thought only humans could do that.

Jane spent her whole life learning from the chimpanzees and protecting the forests where they live. She showed the world that patience is a superpower — and that if you sit quietly enough with nature, it will begin to talk to you.
textM: In 1934, in London, England, a girl named Jane was born. When she was very small, her father gave her a toy chimpanzee with soft hair, and he was called Jubilee. Jane took him everywhere — to bed, into the garden, on the train. Some grown-ups said the toy was far too ugly and would frighten her. It did not frighten her at all. She kept him for years and years, worn thin with hugging.

Jane loved animals more than anything. One afternoon, when she was four, she wanted to know where eggs came from. So she crept into the henhouse, sat down in the straw, and stayed perfectly still for nearly four hours, hardly breathing, until a hen settled beside her and laid an egg right in front of her eyes. Meanwhile her family had searched the whole farm and called the police. But when Jane came running out, shining with her news, her mother did not scold her. She sat down and listened to the whole story. That is how you raise a scientist.

Jane dreamed of Africa. There was no money for university, so she learned to type, and worked as a waitress, saving every coin until she could buy a ticket on a boat. She was twenty-three when she sailed to Kenya. There she met a famous scientist named Louis Leakey, who noticed how patient she was, and how carefully she watched. He asked her a strange question: would she go and live in a forest and watch wild chimpanzees? Nobody had ever truly done it.

So Jane went to Gombe, on the shore of a long silver lake in Tanzania. The forest was steep and green and full of noises. Every morning, before sunrise, she climbed to the same hill with her binoculars and a notebook. And every morning the chimpanzees took one look at her and vanished into the trees. Weeks went by. Months went by. It would have been very easy to give up.

Jane did not give up. She wore the same dull-coloured clothes each day so they would learn her shape, and she never chased them, and slowly, very slowly, they let her come closer. She gave them names instead of numbers — Flo, Fifi, Goliath, and a calm old male with a silvery chin whom she called David Greybeard.

Then, one grey morning, she saw David Greybeard crouched beside a termite mound. He picked a twig, stripped off its leaves, and pushed it gently down a hole. When he pulled it out, it was covered in termites, and he ate them off it like a lollipop. Jane's heart raced. He had not found a tool. He had made one. Until that day, people had said that making tools was the one thing only humans could do. Her teacher sent word back: now we must think again about what it means to be human.

Jane spent the rest of her life learning from the chimpanzees and speaking up for the forests where they live. She travelled the world telling children that they, too, can look after the earth, and that every single day each of us chooses what kind of difference to make. She showed us that patience is a kind of superpower — and that if you sit still enough, and quietly enough, and long enough, the wild world will begin to talk to you.

stories.name: Stephen Hawking
stories.title: The Man Who Raced Through the Stars in His Chair
stories.hook: Doctors said he had only two years to live — instead, he spent fifty more unlocking the secrets of black holes.
text: In 1942, in Oxford, England, a boy named Stephen Hawking was born. At school his friends called him "Einstein," because he was always asking enormous questions: Where did the universe come from? How will it end? He wasn't always the best student — but no one wondered about things more deeply than Stephen.

When Stephen was only twenty-one, doctors gave him very sad news: he had an illness that would slowly stop his muscles from working, and they thought he had only a short time left. Stephen was frightened. But then he decided something brave: if his time was short, he would spend every bit of it thinking about the stars.

The illness put Stephen in a wheelchair, and later he could only speak through a computer with a robot voice. But his mind stayed free, racing through space faster than any rocket. He discovered astonishing things about black holes — places where gravity pulls so hard that not even light can escape — and he found that even black holes slowly glow and fade away.

Stephen lived not two years but more than fifty, becoming the most famous scientist of his time. He wrote a book that millions of families read together, and he loved to joke and laugh. "Remember to look up at the stars," he said, "and not down at your feet." Tonight, that is exactly what we will dream of doing.
textM: In 1942, in the old city of Oxford, England, a boy named Stephen Hawking was born. His family were a little unusual and terribly fond of books — at dinner, everyone might read at the table instead of talking. Their car was a worn-out old London taxi, and their house was rather cold and full of clutter. Stephen loved it.

At school his friends nicknamed him "Einstein". He was not top of the class — his handwriting was messy and his homework was often late — but nobody asked bigger questions. Where did the universe come from? How will it end? With a few friends he built a simple computer out of old clock parts and telephone bits, and he invented board games with rules so complicated that one game could last for days.

He went to university to study physics, and steered a rowing boat for his college, shouting at the rowers over the cold grey river. He was not a great worker at first — he reckoned he studied about an hour a day — but he could see straight to the heart of a problem, and his friends found that just a little bit frightening. Then he moved to Cambridge to think about the biggest thing there is: the whole universe. He was twenty-one, and he was very happy.

That was when the sad news came. Stephen kept dropping things and stumbling, and the doctors found that he had an illness which would slowly stop his muscles from working. They thought he had only a short time left. Stephen was frightened, and for a while he did not want to do anything at all. But then something inside him decided: if his time was short, he would spend every last bit of it thinking about the stars. His family and friends stayed close beside him, and a young woman named Jane, who loved him, told him they would face it together. They married, and in time there were three children in the house. Strangely, he said afterwards, he became happier than before, because at last he knew what mattered.

The illness put Stephen in a wheelchair, and years later he could speak only through a computer, choosing each word with a small twitch of his cheek, in a flat robot voice he grew rather fond of. He could not hold a pen. So he learned to do enormous mathematics entirely inside his head, turning shapes and numbers over in the dark. His body slowed right down. His mind travelled faster than any rocket.

And what he found was astonishing. Black holes are places where gravity pulls so hard that not even light can escape — everyone believed nothing could ever come out of one. Stephen showed that this is not quite true: black holes glow, very faintly, like a warm coal in the dark, and over unimaginable ages they slowly fade away. Scientists still call that glow by his name.

Stephen lived not two years but more than fifty. He became the most famous scientist in the world, wrote a book that millions of families kept on the shelf, popped up in cartoons, and once floated weightless inside an aeroplane, grinning like a boy. He loved a good joke. "Remember to look up at the stars," he said, "and not down at your feet." Tonight, that is exactly what we will dream of doing.

stories.name: Tim Berners-Lee
stories.title: The Man Who Gave the Web to Everyone
stories.hook: He invented the World Wide Web that connects the whole planet — then gave it away for free, to everyone, forever.
text: In 1955, in London, England, a boy named Tim Berners-Lee was born. His mother and father were both computer scientists, back when computers were as big as wardrobes. At the dinner table, his family played maths games for fun, and little Tim built a pretend computer out of cardboard boxes.

When Tim grew up, he went to work at a huge science laboratory in Switzerland where thousands of scientists worked together. But there was a problem: their computers could not easily share information with each other. Ideas were locked away like books in rooms without doors.

So in 1989, Tim had a world-changing idea. What if every document could link to every other document, anywhere on Earth, like an enormous spider's web of knowledge? He built it, and he called it the World Wide Web — the "www" you still see in web addresses today.

Then Tim did something wonderful. Instead of selling his invention to become rich, he gave it away — free, for everyone, forever. That is why today a child in Nairobi, a grandmother in Paris, and a scientist in Tokyo can all learn from the same web. The best gifts, Tim showed us, are the ones we share with the whole world.
textM: In 1955, in London, England, a boy named Tim Berners-Lee was born. His mother and his father were both computer scientists, in the days when a single computer filled a whole room and stood as tall as a wardrobe. Together they had helped to build one of the very first computers in the world.

At the dinner table, Tim's family played maths games for fun. His father talked about how a computer might one day work a little like a human brain, making connections between one idea and another. Tim listened. He built a pretend computer out of cardboard boxes, and later he made switches and gadgets from old bits of electronics to control his model railway.

Tim grew up and went to university to study physics. Then he went to work at an enormous science laboratory in Switzerland, near the mountains, where thousands of scientists from all over the world worked side by side. It was a busy, exciting place — and it had a problem.

The scientists all used different computers, and those computers could not easily share what they knew. To find one piece of information, you had to track down the right person, on the right machine, in the right building. Ideas were locked away like books in rooms without doors. And people were always leaving, taking everything they knew away with them.

So in 1989, Tim wrote a big idea down on paper. What if every document could link to every other document, anywhere on Earth, so that you could hop from one to the next with a single click, like an enormous spider's web of knowledge? He handed the paper to his boss. His boss wrote three words at the top: 'Vague, but exciting.' It was a yes.

Tim got to work on one computer in a quiet office. He wrote the very first web page, the first program for reading web pages, and set up the first machine that served them out to the world. He stuck a note on that computer so nobody would switch it off by accident. Then he gave his invention a name: the World Wide Web — the 'www' you still see in web addresses today.

Then Tim did the most wonderful thing of all. He could have sold the Web and become extremely rich. Instead, in 1993, he and the laboratory gave it away — free, for everyone, forever, with no permission to ask for and nothing at all to pay.

That single decision is why a child in Nairobi, a grandmother in Paris and a scientist in Tokyo can all learn from the same Web tonight. Tim still works to keep it open, safe and kind for everybody. The best gifts, he showed us, are the ones we share with the whole world.

stories.name: Katalin Karikó
stories.title: The Scientist Nobody Believed
stories.hook: For forty years people said her idea would never work — then it helped protect millions of people around the world.
text: In 1955, in a small town in Hungary, a girl named Katalin Karikó was born. Her family lived in a simple house with one room warmed by a stove, and her father was a butcher. Katalin loved watching nature work — and at school, she fell in love with the tiniest nature of all: the busy world inside our own cells.

Katalin became fascinated by something called mRNA — a tiny messenger inside every cell that carries recipes for making the things our bodies need. She had a bold idea: what if we could write our own messages, and teach our bodies to protect themselves from sickness?

For many, many years, almost nobody believed her. She lost jobs. She was told to give up. She sold her car and sewed money into her daughter's teddy bear when the family moved to America to keep trying. But every morning, Katalin went back to her laboratory. "Work hard," she told herself, "and one experiment at a time."

Then one day the world needed her idea urgently: a new sickness had spread everywhere. Thanks to Katalin's forty years of stubborn work, scientists made vaccines faster than ever before, and millions of people were protected. She won the Nobel Prize, and the world finally understood: an idea nobody believes in may simply be waiting for its moment.
textM: In 1955, in a small Hungarian town called Kisújszállás, a girl named Katalin Karikó was born. Her family's home was very simple: one room, warmed by a stove, with no running water and no refrigerator. Water came from a well in the yard. Reeds grew on the roof, and vegetables grew in the garden. Her father was a butcher, and her mother kept the accounts for a small company. It was not a rich house, but it was a house full of talking, and questions were always welcome.

Katalin was a curious child. She followed her father while he worked and noticed how carefully everything inside a body fits together. She watched the poplar trees, the storks on the chimneys, the beetles in the grass. At school a teacher told her about cells — the tiny living rooms that make up every plant, every animal, every child. Katalin thought this was the most exciting thing she had ever heard. When she was fourteen, she came third in the whole country in a biology competition.

She grew up and became a scientist in a laboratory in the city of Szeged. There she fell in love with something called mRNA. Think of it as a tiny messenger inside every one of your cells, carrying a recipe that says: please make this. Katalin had a bold idea. What if scientists could write their own gentle message, send it into the body, and teach the body to protect itself from sickness? It was, she thought, the most beautiful idea in the world.

Almost nobody agreed. Her laboratory ran out of money. So she and her husband and their little daughter Zsuzsanna packed their bags for America. They were not allowed to carry much money out of the country, so they sold the family car and sewed the money into the girl's teddy bear. The bear sat on Zsuzsanna's lap all the way across the ocean, keeping its quiet secret.

In America the years were hard. Her requests for research money were refused, again and again. She was told her idea would never work. She lost jobs. Once she was moved to a smaller position with a smaller desk. But every single morning Katalin went back to the laboratory anyway. "One experiment at a time," she told herself. She was not doing it to become famous. She simply wanted to know whether it could work.

Then one day in 1997, standing at the photocopier, she met a scientist named Drew Weissman, who was waiting for his copies too. They began to talk. He wanted to make vaccines; she had the messenger. Together they worked for years, and at last they found the missing piece: one small change to the message, so that the body would welcome it kindly instead of fighting it.

Years later a new sickness spread all around the world, and everybody needed a vaccine quickly. Because Katalin had never stopped, scientists already knew how to write that message. Vaccines were made faster than ever before in history, and millions of people were protected. In 2023 she was given the Nobel Prize, together with her friend from the photocopier.

Katalin still says the happiest part was not the prize. It was the quiet work: the long mornings, the many small steps, the joy of finding out. Her story matters tonight because it tells us something true. An idea nobody believes in may simply be waiting for its moment — and the person who keeps going, gently and stubbornly, may be the one who changes the world.

stories.name: Mae Jemison
stories.title: The Dancer Who Flew to the Stars
stories.hook: She loved dancing, science, and the stars — and became the first Black woman to travel into space.
text: In 1956, in Alabama, in the United States, a girl named Mae Jemison was born. Her family moved to the big city of Chicago, where little Mae spent hours in the library reading about the stars. When she looked up at the night sky, she didn't just wonder about space — she knew, deep in her heart, that one day she would go there.

Mae loved many things at once: science experiments, and also dancing — ballet, jazz, African dance. Some people told her to choose just one thing. But Mae believed curiosity doesn't have to pick favorites. She went to university at only sixteen, became an engineer, and then a doctor who cared for people in Sierra Leone and Liberia.

Then Mae chased her oldest dream. She applied to become an astronaut, and out of thousands of people, she was chosen. In 1992, aboard the space shuttle Endeavour, Mae became the first Black woman to fly into space. Floating above the Earth, she looked down at Chicago, the city where a little girl had once dreamed in a library.

"Never be limited by other people's limited imaginations," Mae tells children. Loving dance did not stop her from loving science — it made her braver. Tonight, remember: you are allowed to love many things, and all of them can lift you higher.
textM: In 1956, in Decatur, Alabama, in the United States, a girl named Mae Jemison was born, the youngest of three children. When she was three, her family moved north to the big, noisy city of Chicago. Of all the places in that city, Mae loved the library best. She would carry home a tall wobbly pile of books, and most of them were about the stars.

Mae was full of questions. When a splinter went into her thumb, she read about pus and infection until she understood exactly what her body was doing. Her uncle told her about science. Her parents let her know that wondering was a perfectly fine way to spend an afternoon. At night she looked up at the sky above Chicago, and she did not merely wish for space — she knew she would go.

Not everyone understood. In kindergarten her teacher asked what she wanted to be when she grew up. 'A scientist,' said Mae. 'Don't you mean a nurse?' asked the teacher. Mae put her hands on her hips and said no, she meant a scientist. She was five years old, and she never once changed her answer.

Mae also loved to dance. From about the age of nine she took lessons — ballet, jazz, modern, African dance. Some grown-ups told her to choose: dancer or scientist, not both. Mae disagreed. Curiosity, she thought, does not have to pick a favourite. On television she watched a story about a starship, and there among the stars sat a Black woman doing important work, and Mae's heart lifted.

She went to university at only sixteen. She studied engineering, and African and African-American history at the same time, because she wanted both. Then she went to medical school and became a doctor. For more than two years she looked after people in Sierra Leone and Liberia, in West Africa, often with very few supplies and a great deal of cleverness.

Then Mae wrote to NASA and asked to become an astronaut. She had to wait, and then apply all over again. Out of about two thousand people, fifteen were chosen — and Mae was one of them. She learned to fly, to float, to work inside a heavy suit, and to mend things while upside down.

On the 12th of September 1992, the space shuttle Endeavour lifted off with Mae on board: the first Black woman ever to travel into space. She carried with her a poster from an African-American dance company and a small statue from Sierra Leone, because she wanted space to hold something belonging to all the people of Earth. Each work shift she began with a line from her favourite starship story: 'Hailing frequencies open.' Floating high above the planet, she looked down and found Chicago.

"Never be limited by other people's limited imaginations," Mae tells children today. She runs science camps so that young people can spend a summer being scientists. Loving dance never stopped her loving science — it made her braver. So tonight, remember this: you are allowed to love many things, and every single one of them can lift you higher.

stories.name: Segenet Kelemu
stories.title: The Girl Who Made the Grass Strong
stories.hook: A farm girl from the Ethiopian mountains became one of the world's great plant scientists — and came home to help Africa's farmers.
text: In 1957, in a small village in the mountains of Ethiopia, a girl named Segenet Kelemu was born. Like the other village girls, she was expected to fetch water, cook, and one day marry young. But Segenet had other plans. She loved school fiercely, and she studied by firelight until she became the best student in the whole region.

Segenet became the first woman from her region to go to university, where she learned the science of plants — how they grow, how they get sick, and how to make them healthy again. She traveled far away to great laboratories in America and around the world, and became famous for her discoveries.

But Segenet never forgot the farmers back home. "African problems need African scientists," she said — just like the great Thomas Odhiambo before her. So she returned to lead ICIPE, the centre of insect science in Nairobi that Thomas had founded, becoming the first woman to guide it.

Segenet studies the tiny living helpers that live inside grasses and crops, making them stronger against drought and disease, so that farmers can feed their families even in hard years. The girl who was told to stay in the village now helps millions of farms grow — proof that a determined child can change what a whole continent grows for dinner.
textM: In 1957, in a small town in the mountains of Ethiopia, a girl named Segenet Kelemu was born. Her home stood among fields of teff and barley, with blue mountains all around and mist lying in the valleys each morning. Her family were farmers, and Segenet knew from very early on how much a whole family can depend on one small field.

Like the other village girls, she was expected to fetch water, cook, and one day marry young. But Segenet had other plans. She loved school fiercely. She walked a long way to get there, leaving before the sun was properly up, and at night, when all the chores were finished, she studied by firelight until she became the best student in the whole region.

Not everyone thought a girl should do that. Some people shook their heads at a girl with a schoolbook. Segenet kept going anyway, one exam at a time, with nobody ahead of her on that road to show her how, until she became the first woman from her region to go to university. There she learned the science of plants — how they grow, how they get sick, and how to make them healthy again.

Then she travelled far, far away, to study in great laboratories in America. The winters there were colder than anything she had ever felt, and home was very far away. She missed the blue mountains. She wrote letters. And she stayed. She became a plant doctor, a scientist who can look at a sick leaf and say what is wrong with it, and afterwards she worked for many years in Colombia, studying the tropical grasses that feed cattle.

That is where she found something wonderful. Inside the leaves and stems of a grass there live tiny living helpers, too small to see — friendly fungi and bacteria that make the plant stronger against drought and disease. A blade of grass, it turns out, is never really alone. It is more like a small village, full of neighbours doing quiet jobs. And if you understand those neighbours, you can help whole fields survive a year with too little rain.

But Segenet never forgot the farmers back home. 'African problems need African scientists,' she said — just like the great Thomas Odhiambo before her. So she came back to Africa, and in 2013 she was chosen to lead ICIPE, the centre of insect science in Nairobi that Thomas had founded, becoming the first woman ever to guide it.

At ICIPE, scientists find clever, gentle ways to help farms. They plant one kind of plant beside the maize to send hungry pests away, and another to invite them out of the field — no expensive sprays needed, just a good idea and good seeds. Farmers across Africa now grow more food this way, and Segenet has been given some of the world's biggest science prizes for the work.

The girl who was told to stay in the village now helps millions of farms grow. When she visits a school, girls crowd around her, and she says the same thing every time: study, ask questions, believe you are able — and then bring what you learn home. She is proof that one determined child can change what a whole continent grows for dinner.

stories.name: William Kamkwamba
stories.title: The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind
stories.hook: He couldn't pay for school — so he taught himself from library books and built a windmill from junk to light up his village.
text: In 1987, in a small farming village in Malawi, a boy named William Kamkwamba was born. His family grew maize, and William loved taking radios apart to see the little pieces inside. Then came a terrible year: the rains did not fall, the maize did not grow, and there was very little food. His family could no longer pay his school fees, and William had to leave school.

But William refused to stop learning. He walked to the little library near his village and borrowed books about science. One book had a picture that made his heart jump: a tall windmill, spinning in the wind, making electricity. William could not read all the English words — but he could read the diagrams.

So he began collecting treasures from the scrapyard: a broken bicycle, an old tractor fan, plastic pipes, a small dynamo. The neighbours laughed and called him crazy. But piece by piece, on a tower of blue-gum wood, fourteen-year-old William built his windmill. And when the wind blew, a little bulb flickered on — light, made from wind and junk and stubbornness.

Soon his windmill charged phones and pumped water for the crops, and news of the boy who harnessed the wind traveled around the world. William went back to school, then to university, and wrote a book that children everywhere now read. When the winds of trouble blow hard, William teaches us, some people build walls — and some people build windmills.
textM: In 1987, in a village of small farms in Malawi, a boy was born and named William Kamkwamba. His family grew maize, and their year turned like a wheel: plant when the rains come, weed under the hot sun, harvest, and hope. William had six sisters, a dog called Khamba, and a habit that drove people slightly mad — he took things apart. At night there were no street lights at all, so the sky above the village filled with more stars than anybody could count.

Old radios especially. He would open the back, look at the tiny copper coils and glass tubes inside, and wonder how a voice could travel invisibly through the air and land inside a box. He and his best friend even started a little business, repairing the neighbours' radios for a few coins, working by the light of the doorway because there was no electricity in the house.

Then came a terrible year. The rains did not fall properly, the maize did not grow, and there was very little to eat. The whole village grew thin and quiet. When the time came to pay school fees, there was simply no money. William, who loved school, had to stop going. He was thirteen, and he stood at the fence some mornings watching the other children walk past in their uniforms.

But he refused to stop learning. There was a small library near his village — one room, three shelves, books that had been given away for schoolchildren. William walked there again and again. One afternoon he pulled down a book about energy, turned a page, and there it was: a photograph of tall windmills, spinning, making electricity. His heart jumped. Electricity out of wind. Wind was free, and Malawi had plenty of it.

He could not read all the English words. So he read the diagrams instead, tracing the lines with his finger until he understood them. He worked out what he needed: blades to catch the wind, a shaft to spin, and something to turn spinning into power. Then he went to the scrapyard. He found a broken bicycle, an old tractor fan, a rusty piece of a car, plastic pipes that he melted and flattened into blades, and a small dynamo. He hammered. He tied. He burned his fingers. He tried again.

People walking past laughed at him. They called him crazy — the boy playing with rubbish. His mother worried, and his father said nothing but let him keep going. William built a tower out of blue-gum poles, and with his cousin and his friend he hauled the heavy machine to the top, one rung at a time. A crowd gathered below, half of them waiting to watch him fail.

The wind came. The blades turned. And the little bulb in William's hand flickered, glowed, and shone — light, made from wind and junk and stubbornness. He was fourteen years old. His mother and sisters came out to look. The whole village went quiet, and then it cheered. Soon four bulbs burned in his family's house, and later a bigger windmill pumped water for the crops and charged the neighbours' phones.

News of the boy who harnessed the wind travelled around the world. William went back to school, then to a school in South Africa for bright young Africans, then to university far away, and he wrote a book that children everywhere now read. He teaches us something worth remembering at bedtime: when the winds of trouble blow hard, some people build walls — and some people build windmills.

stories.name: George Washington
stories.title: The General Who Went Home
stories.hook: He could have ruled like a king forever — instead he did something almost no leader had ever done: he said goodbye.
text: In 1732, on a farm in Virginia, a boy named George Washington was born. As a young man he worked as a surveyor, walking through deep forests to measure the land, sleeping under the stars and learning to be patient, careful, and brave.

When the American colonies decided to become their own country, they asked George to lead their little army. The war was long and hard — his soldiers were cold and hungry at a place called Valley Forge — but George never gave up, and in the end, a brand-new country was born: the United States.

The people loved George so much that they made him their first president, and some wanted him to rule for life, like a king. But George believed the country belonged to its people, not to one man. After eight years he simply… went home to his farm.

That quiet goodbye became one of the most important gifts in history: the idea that leaders should hand over power peacefully. Every time one president leaves and another arrives calmly, the world can whisper, "Thank you, George."
textM: In 1732, on a farm in Virginia, a boy named George Washington was born. His home stood among tobacco fields, near a wide, slow river where herons stood still as statues. It was a world of horses, ploughs, woodsmoke and long summer evenings. George grew up tall and strong and rather quiet — the sort of boy who listened much more than he spoke.

When George was eleven, his father died. There was no money to send him far away to school, so he learned at home instead, and he discovered that he loved numbers and maps. He filled notebooks with careful figures and neat lines. He also copied out a long list of good manners, rules like 'when you speak, be brief' and 'be kind to those who are not your friends'.

At sixteen he took his measuring chains and rode west into the Blue Ridge mountains to work as a surveyor, drawing maps of land nobody had measured before. He waded rivers, slept on straw or under the stars, and once wrote in his diary about a night beside a smoky fire. Out there he learned patience, care, and how to keep calm when things went wrong.

Years later, the American colonies decided they wanted to be their own country, and they needed someone to lead their small, new army. They chose George, partly because everyone trusted him, and partly because he was the one man in the room who never seemed to want the job. He did not give a grand speech. He simply said he was not sure he was good enough, and that he would take no pay for it — and then he got on his horse and went.

The war was long and hard. One winter, at a place called Valley Forge, the soldiers had thin coats and worn-out boots, and the snow was deep. George stayed there with them, in a little hut, and wrote letter after letter asking for food and blankets for his men. He crossed an icy river on Christmas night to surprise the enemy, and slowly, year by year, his army held on until the fighting ended and a brand-new country was born: the United States.

Then George did the thing that astonished everybody. He gave back his sword, said thank you, and went home to his farm at Mount Vernon. It is said that when the king of Britain heard he meant to do this, he answered that if it were true, George would be the greatest man in the world. Almost no victorious general in history had ever handed power back.

A few years later the people asked him to come back as their first president, and he agreed. Some wanted him to stay for life, like a king. But George believed the country belonged to its people, not to one man. So after eight years he said goodbye once more, and rode home to his fields and his fig trees, a private citizen again.

That quiet goodbye became one of the most important gifts in history: the idea that a leader borrows power for a while and then hands it back gently, and steps aside. It is a hard thing to do, and it takes more courage than winning a battle. Every time one president leaves and another arrives calmly, in any country in the world, someone can whisper, 'Thank you, George.'

stories.name: Abraham Lincoln
stories.title: The Boy Who Read by Firelight
stories.hook: A poor boy from a log cabin taught himself with borrowed books — and grew up to free millions of people.
text: In 1809, in a tiny log cabin in Kentucky, a boy named Abraham Lincoln was born. His family was very poor, and Abraham could only go to school for about one year in his whole childhood. But he loved books so much that he walked miles to borrow them, and read at night by the light of the fire.

Abraham grew very tall and very strong — he could split logs with an axe all day — but his greatest strength was his honesty. People trusted him so much they called him "Honest Abe," and one day, the boy from the log cabin was elected President of the United States.

It was the hardest time in the country's history. Americans were quarrelling so badly that the country split in two, and worst of all, millions of people were held in slavery — bought and sold as if they were things, not people. Abraham knew this was deeply wrong. He kept the country together, and he signed the great order that declared enslaved people free.

Abraham showed the world that a gentle, honest heart can carry the heaviest burdens. "With malice toward none, with charity for all," he said — be angry with no one, be kind to everyone. That is a good thought to fall asleep on.
textM: In February 1809, in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky, a baby boy was born and named Abraham Lincoln. The cabin had a dirt floor, one small window, and a fire at one end. Outside stood forests so thick that the family had to cut their farm out of the trees. Abraham grew up with an axe in his hands almost as soon as he could hold one.

There was no school nearby, and there was always work to be done. Altogether, Abraham went to school for about one year in his whole childhood, in little scattered pieces. But a kind stepmother named Sarah came into the family, and she saw at once what this quiet boy needed: books. She made room for his reading, and she never once told him it was a waste of time.

Books were rare and precious out on the frontier. Abraham walked miles to borrow them and read them again and again, lying by the fire at night while the light flickered on the page. Once a borrowed book was soaked by rain that came through a gap in the cabin wall. Abraham walked straight to its owner and worked three days in the fields to pay for it. He kept the book, and he kept his good name.

He had no paper, so he practised writing with a piece of charcoal on the back of a wooden shovel, then scraped it clean and started again. He grew and grew until he stood six feet four inches tall — taller than almost anyone he met — and he could split logs all day long. But it was his honesty that people remembered. As a young shopkeeper he once walked miles after closing time to return a few pennies he had accidentally overcharged. People began calling him 'Honest Abe'.

He taught himself law from borrowed books, became a lawyer, and then a speaker people travelled far to hear. And in 1860 the boy from the log cabin was elected President of the United States. Just before the election, an eleven-year-old girl named Grace had written to tell him he would look better with a beard. He wrote back to her kindly — and then he grew one.

It was the hardest moment in the country's history. Americans were quarrelling so bitterly that the country split in two, and worst of all, millions of people were held in slavery — bought and sold as if they were things and not people. Abraham knew, all the way down inside, that this was wrong. Those were heavy years. Often he could not sleep, and he walked the quiet halls at night, thinking.

Then Abraham did the bravest thing of his life. On the first day of 1863 he signed a great order declaring that enslaved people should be free. His hand was shaking that morning — not from fear, he said, but because he had shaken hundreds of hands at a New Year's party. 'If my name ever goes into history,' he said, 'it will be for this act.' Then he signed it slowly and firmly.

Abraham showed the world that a gentle, honest heart can carry the heaviest load. Because of him the country stayed one country, and a law was passed to end slavery everywhere within it. 'With malice toward none, with charity for all,' he said — be angry with no one, be kind to everyone. Today a great stone statue of Abraham sits in Washington, looking out over the city, still thinking. That is a good thought to fall asleep on.

stories.name: Woodrow Wilson
stories.title: The Professor With Fourteen Ideas for Peace
stories.hook: After the most terrible war the world had seen, a professor-president stood up with a list — fourteen ideas to help countries talk instead of fight.
text: In 1856, in Virginia, a boy named Woodrow Wilson was born. Reading was hard for him when he was little — the letters seemed to jump around — but he refused to give up, invented his own ways to study, and grew up to become a professor and then the president of a great university.

Then the professor became President of the United States. During his time, a terrible war spread across the world — so many countries fighting that people called it the World War. When it finally ended, Woodrow asked the question children ask and grown-ups forget: "How do we make sure this never happens again?"

His answer was a list of fourteen ideas for a fairer world — like ships sailing freely, countries choosing their own path, and most importantly, a big round table where nations could talk out their quarrels: the League of Nations.

The League was young and wobbly, like a first bicycle — but the idea did not die. It grew up to become the United Nations, where almost every country on Earth sits and talks today. Every peace meeting in the world carries a little echo of the professor's list.
textM: In the winter of 1856, in a quiet house in Virginia, a baby boy named Woodrow Wilson was born. His father was a minister with a great love of words, and the house was full of talking — long conversations at the supper table about books and ideas. It should have been the perfect home for a reader. But there was something that made young Woodrow's life hard, and nobody at the time understood what it was.

Letters would not sit still for him. When he looked at a page, the words seemed to shuffle and jump about. He was nine years old before he could read them properly, and some children thought he was slow. He was not slow at all. Today we would probably call it dyslexia, and we would know how to help him. Back then, he had to help himself.

So he did. He listened harder than anyone, because listening was easier than reading. He taught himself shorthand, a quick squiggly writing, so he could catch words as fast as they came. He read out loud, slowly, again and again, until the sentences stayed put. And in between he played baseball with his friends — he even started a little club, with rules he wrote himself.

The boy who could not read became a man who never stopped studying. He wrote books, and he became a professor, standing in front of students and explaining how countries are governed. He was so good at it that Princeton, a great university, asked him to be its president. Then the state of New Jersey asked him to be its governor. Then, in 1913, the whole country asked him to be President of the United States.

During his years in the White House, a terrible war spread across the world — so many countries fighting at once that people called it the World War. Woodrow watched the news arrive, day after day, and thought of all the families waiting at home. When at last the guns went quiet, he asked the question children ask and grown-ups forget: 'How do we make sure this never happens again?'

In January 1918 he stood before the lawmakers of his country and read out his answer: a list of fourteen ideas for a fairer world. Ships sailing freely. Fewer weapons. Countries choosing their own path. And, last and most important of all, a great round table where nations could talk out their quarrels instead of fighting them: the League of Nations.

He did not only write the list; he carried it himself. He sailed across the Atlantic to Europe — the first American president ever to do so while in office — and crowds filled the streets of Paris to cheer him and throw flowers, because they had had enough of fighting. For month after month he sat in long meetings, arguing patiently for his round table. It was slow, tiring work, and he was not a young man any more.

The League was new and wobbly, like a first bicycle, and it did not always work — even his own country decided not to join, which made him very sad. But the idea did not die. It grew up into the United Nations, where almost every country on Earth sits and talks today. Woodrow was given the Nobel Peace Prize. And the boy who once found words so hard had handed the world one of its most useful sentences: let us talk first.

stories.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
stories.title: The President by the Fireside
stories.hook: Illness took away his legs, but never his hope — and his warm voice on the radio helped a whole country be brave.
text: In 1882, in New York, a boy named Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born. He loved sailing, stamp collecting, and adventures. But when Franklin was a grown man, a sickness called polio took away the use of his legs. Some thought his life as a leader was over. Franklin thought differently.

From his wheelchair, he worked harder than ever — and the people chose him as President just when their country was in deep trouble: banks had failed, jobs had vanished, and families were afraid. Franklin spoke to them on the radio, calmly, like a friend sitting by the fireplace. "The only thing we have to fear," he said, "is fear itself."

He created jobs building parks, bridges, and roads, and hope slowly returned. Then an even bigger storm came — a world war — and Franklin led his country and its friends through it, working with allies across the oceans.

Before the war ended, Franklin helped plan something beautiful: the United Nations, a place for countries to solve problems with words instead of weapons. The man who could not walk helped the whole world take a step toward peace.
textM: In 1882, in a big house above the Hudson River in New York, a boy named Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born. He was an only child, and the outdoors was his playground. He sailed little boats on cold blue water. He watched birds through the trees and learned their names. And he collected stamps — thousands and thousands of them — because every tiny square was a window into a country far away.

Franklin grew up, married a thoughtful young woman named Eleanor, and went to work in politics. Then, when he was thirty-nine, he spent a summer day swimming and sailing at the family's island cottage. He went to bed tired. In the morning, his legs would not move. A sickness called polio had taken them away.

Some people whispered that his life as a leader was over. Franklin thought differently. Getting strong again was slow, patient work. He swam in warm springs where the water held him up. He wore heavy metal braces and practised standing, leaning on his son's arm. It was hard, and he was often tired — but he almost never let anyone see him sad. From his wheelchair, he worked harder than ever before.

The people chose him as President just when their country was in deep trouble. Banks had shut their doors. Jobs had vanished. Families stood in long lines for a bowl of soup. On his very first day, Franklin told them something they never forgot: "The only thing we have to fear," he said, "is fear itself."

Then he tried something nobody had tried before. He sat down beside a microphone, with just a few friends in the room, and talked to the whole country on the radio — slowly, simply, the way you explain something to a neighbour over the fence. All across the land, people pulled their chairs close to the wireless and listened in the warm dark. They called those talks his fireside chats, and it felt as though the President himself had come to sit by their fire.

He did not only talk; he made work. He sent young men out into the forests to plant trees — millions upon millions of trees — and to cut walking trails through the mountains. Others built parks, bridges, schools, and long ribbons of road that families still drive on today. Painters painted post offices. Writers wrote down the old songs before they were forgotten. Slowly, like light coming back after a storm, hope returned.

Then an even bigger storm arrived: a world war. Franklin led his country and its friends through it, meeting with allies from across the oceans, poring over maps late into the night. Eleanor travelled to the places he could not reach, shaking hands and listening, and brought their stories home to him. And wherever he worked, a small black dog called Fala trotted along beside the wheels of his chair and curled up under his desk.

Before the fighting ended, Franklin helped plan something beautiful. He even chose its name: the United Nations — a place where countries could bring their problems and solve them with words instead of weapons. It still meets today. The man who could not walk helped the whole world take a step toward peace, and he showed everyone that a body can be weak while a spirit stays enormously strong.

stories.name: Harry Truman
stories.title: The Farmer Who Helped Rebuild the World
stories.hook: An ordinary man from a small farm was handed the world's biggest job — and chose to help even yesterday's enemies rebuild.
text: In 1884, in Missouri, a boy named Harry Truman was born. He wore thick glasses, loved the piano and history books, and worked for years on his family's farm, plowing fields behind a team of horses. Nobody looked at Harry and said, "That boy will lead the world one day."

But Harry was steady, honest, and hardworking. He became a judge, then a senator, then vice-president — and suddenly, when President Roosevelt died, the farmer from Missouri was President, right at the end of the world's biggest war. On his desk he kept a little sign: "The buck stops here" — meaning, I don't pass my problems to someone else.

When the war ended, much of Europe lay in ruins — cities broken, people hungry. Harry could have said, "Not my problem." Instead, his country sent ships full of food, machines, and money to help rebuild — even to countries it had just been fighting. It was called the Marshall Plan, one of the kindest ideas ever to come from a war.

Harry also helped friendly countries join hands in a promise to protect each other, called NATO. The boy from the farm showed that you don't need to be dazzling to change the world — you need to be dependable, fair, and brave enough to help your neighbor stand up again.
textM: In 1884, in a tiny house in Missouri, a boy named Harry Truman was born. His eyes were so weak that he wore thick round glasses from the time he was eight. That meant no rough games with the other boys — so instead Harry read. He read history books one after another, all about kings and generals and ordinary people who had done brave things long ago.

He loved the piano too. Every morning he got up at five o'clock, while the house was still dark and quiet, and practised for two hours before school. Then, when his family needed him, Harry went to work on their farm. For eleven years he plowed the fields behind a team of horses, walking mile after mile in the dust, fixing fences and feeding pigs. Nobody looked at that young man and said, "He will lead the world one day."

Life did not go smoothly. Harry went away as a soldier in a great war and came home safe. He opened a little shop selling hats and shirts, and the shop failed, and he spent years paying back every penny he owned. He could have grown bitter. Instead he stayed steady, and he stayed honest, and people noticed.

So they gave him a job looking after the county's roads and buildings, and he built them well and did not waste a cent. Then they made him a senator. Then vice-president. And then, one spring afternoon, he was called to the White House and told that President Roosevelt had died. The farmer from Missouri was now President — right at the end of the world's biggest war. "Pray for me," he told the reporters. "I feel like the moon and the stars have fallen on me."

On his desk he kept a little sign that said "The buck stops here". It meant: I will not pass my problems along to somebody else. Whatever needs deciding, I decide it, and I take the blame if I am wrong.

When the war finally ended, much of Europe lay in ruins. Cities were broken. Bridges had fallen into rivers. Children were hungry, and a cold winter was coming. Harry could easily have said, "Not my problem — we have troubles of our own." Instead his country sent ships full of food, machines, seeds, and money to help rebuild — even to the countries it had just been fighting. It was called the Marshall Plan, and it may be the kindest idea ever to come out of a war.

Harry did more. He helped friendly nations join hands in a promise to protect one another, called NATO. And at home he signed an order saying that soldiers of every colour must serve together as equals — a fair and courageous thing to do at a time when many people were not ready for it.

When his years as President were over, Harry did not stay in the great city. He simply went home to Missouri, to the same old house with the porch, and took brisk morning walks around town, tipping his hat and saying hello to his neighbours as though he had never been away. The boy from the farm showed us something worth remembering: you do not have to be dazzling to change the world. You need to be dependable, fair, and brave enough to help your neighbour stand up again.

stories.name: John F. Kennedy
stories.title: The President Who Aimed for the Moon
stories.hook: A sickly boy who read adventure books in bed grew up to stay calm in the world's scariest moment — and to point at the Moon.
text: In 1917, in Massachusetts, a boy named John Fitzgerald Kennedy was born — everyone called him Jack. He was often sick as a child and spent long weeks in bed, where he devoured books about heroes and history. Later, as a young navy officer, his boat was wrecked at sea — and Jack, though injured, helped his crew swim to safety, towing one man by a strap held in his teeth.

Jack became President at only forty-three, full of energy and big dreams. He started the Peace Corps, sending young volunteers to teach and build in villages around the world. And he made a promise that made people gasp: "We choose to go to the Moon in this decade — not because it is easy, but because it is hard."

Then came thirteen terrifying days. Two mighty countries, each with dangerous weapons, stood eye to eye near the island of Cuba, and the whole world held its breath. Jack stayed calm. Instead of striking, he talked — quietly, carefully, letter by letter — until both sides stepped back. Talking had saved the world.

Jack did not live to see it, but six years later, people walked on the Moon, just as he had promised. His story whispers two lessons: stay calm when everyone is afraid, and aim for things that seem too far away.
textM: In 1917, in a busy house in Massachusetts, a boy named John Fitzgerald Kennedy was born. He was the second of nine children, and everybody called him Jack. The house was loud: brothers and sisters everywhere, football on the lawn before dinner, and a father who told them all to try to come first.

But Jack was often ill. He caught scarlet fever when he was two, and again and again through his childhood he had to stay in bed while the others ran about outside. So he read. He read stories of King Arthur and his knights, and books about explorers and kings and long-ago battles at sea. Lying still with a book was how Jack travelled, and history became his best friend.

When he was a young man he became an officer on a small, fast navy boat. One dark night at sea, a much bigger ship struck his boat and cut it in two. Jack hurt his back, but he gathered his crew in the water and led them swimming towards a speck of an island, hours away. One man was too badly burned to swim, so Jack gripped the strap of the man's life jacket in his teeth and towed him the whole way.
