She wrote a famous book called 'I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings', and one bright cold morning she stood before a whole country and read her poem at a president's inauguration. The girl who once said nothing had become a voice the world leaned in to hear.
textM: Maya Angelou was born in the United States in 1928, and her first name was not Maya at all. It was Marguerite. Her big brother Bailey could not say it properly when he was small, so he called her 'My', and then 'My-a' — and that name stayed with her for the rest of her life.

When she was little, she and Bailey went to live with their grandmother in a small town in Arkansas, where the road was dusty and the cotton fields went on and on. Their grandmother — everyone called her Momma — ran the general store. It smelled of flour and peppermint and new cloth. Maya helped weigh things out before the sun was up, while the cotton pickers walked past the door on their way to the fields, singing.

Then, while she was still very young, something so sad happened that Maya stopped speaking. For almost five whole years, she did not say a word out loud. Grown-ups did not always understand. But her grandmother was patient with her, and kept her close, and let her stay quiet for as long as she needed.

A quiet child is not an empty child. Maya listened to everything: the birds outside the window, the rain on the tin roof, the creak of the shop door, the way grown-ups sang when they thought nobody could hear them. She noticed how every single voice was different. And she read. She read her way through nearly every book she could reach, and the words gathered up inside her like water behind a wall.

Then a neighbour called Mrs. Flowers — the most elegant lady in town, who wore soft dresses and always had a book with her — invited Maya into her house. She gave her cool lemonade and sweet biscuits she had baked herself. Then she opened a book and read aloud. Maya had seen those words on the page before; she had never heard them sung by a human voice. Mrs. Flowers told her that written words are only half alive, and that it takes a voice to give them all their meaning.

Mrs. Flowers lent her books and asked her to come back and read them out loud. Little by little, Maya opened her mouth again. Her voice came back — and what a voice it was: deep, warm and slow, like honey pouring.

She grew up and did a hundred brave things. She became the first Black woman to work as a conductor on the streetcars of San Francisco. She danced, she sang, she lived in Ghana, she learned several languages. And she wrote. She wrote a famous book about her childhood called 'I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings', so that other children would know they were not alone.

One bright, freezing morning, Maya stood up in front of a whole country and read a poem she had written for a new president. Millions of people listened, and nobody moved. The girl who once said nothing had become a voice the world leaned in to hear. She reminds us that a quiet time is never a wasted time — and that everybody's voice is worth waiting for.

stories.name: Mahatma Gandhi
stories.title: The Gentle Man Who Made Salt
stories.hook: A shy little boy who showed the world that being gentle can be the bravest thing of all.
text: Long ago, in a little town called Porbandar beside the sea in India, a baby boy was born. His name was Mohandas Gandhi. He was such a shy little boy that when school finished he ran all the way home, so he would not have to talk to anybody.

When he grew up he sailed far away to London to learn about the law. Then he went to work in South Africa. One night he was put off a train, out into the cold, only because of the colour of his skin. Sitting alone on that dark platform, he made himself a quiet promise. He would stand up to everything that was unfair — but he would never hurt anybody to do it.

Back home in India, he showed millions of people how to be brave without fighting. He called it holding on to the truth: satyagraha. When the rulers said Indians could not even make their own salt, Gandhi simply started walking. He walked for weeks, all the way to the sea, and thousands of people walked with him. There he bent down and lifted a little salt from the shore, and the whole world was watching.

Gandhi spun his own cloth on a small wooden wheel and owned almost nothing at all. People loved him so much that they called him Bapu, which means father. India became free. And Gandhi left us an idea soft enough for bedtime: being gentle can be stronger than being loud or rough.
textM: Long ago, in a little town called Porbandar beside the sea in India, a baby boy was born. His name was Mohandas Gandhi. Porbandar was a place of white stone houses and salty wind, where you could hear the waves from the courtyard. Mohandas was such a shy little boy that when school finished he ran all the way home, so that he would not have to talk to anybody. He was afraid of the dark, too, and of ghosts, and of being laughed at.

But he loved stories. There was one play he saw about a king who told the truth no matter what it cost him, and it made young Mohandas cry. He watched it over and over in his mind. "I want to be like that," he thought. From then on, truth was the thing he cared about most.

When he grew up he sailed far away to London to learn about the law. He was terribly homesick. He wore a smart suit and tried to learn the violin and dancing, and gave both up rather quickly. And when he came home and stood in a courtroom for the very first time, he was so shy that no words came out at all. He had to sit back down. Not a very grand beginning.

Then he went to work in South Africa. One cold night he was riding on a train with a proper ticket in his pocket, and he was ordered off it and left on a dark platform, only because of the colour of his skin. He sat there all night, shivering, thinking. And there, in the cold, he made himself a quiet promise. He would stand up to everything that was unfair — but he would never hurt anybody to do it.

Back home in India, Gandhi wanted to know his own country properly, so he travelled in the cheapest, most crowded carriages of the trains, sitting on the floor with farmers and mothers and traders. He gave away his fine clothes and dressed as the poorest people dressed. Then he showed millions of people how to be brave without fighting. He called it holding on to the truth: satyagraha.

The rulers of India at that time had made a strange law: Indians were not allowed to make or gather their own salt, even though the sea was right there, and they had to pay a tax on every grain. Gandhi wrote a polite letter to say this was wrong. Nothing changed. So, at sixty-one years old, with a bamboo walking stick, he simply started walking to the sea.

He walked for twenty-four days, nearly four hundred kilometres, through village after village. People swept the dusty road in front of him. Some joined for an hour; some never went home again. By the end, thousands were walking behind him. On a bright morning by the water, Gandhi bent down and lifted a little salt from the shore — and the whole world was watching a very thin man holding nothing but salt in his hand.

Every day Gandhi spun his own cloth on a small wooden wheel, and he owned almost nothing: sandals, spectacles, a bowl, a watch. He laughed easily and teased his friends. People loved him so much that they called him Bapu, which means father. India became free. And his idea travelled on, all the way to Martin Luther King Jr. and Nelson Mandela — an idea soft enough for bedtime: being gentle can be stronger than being loud or rough.

stories.name: Viktor Frankl
stories.title: The Doctor Who Found Hope
stories.hook: A curious boy from Vienna who discovered that hope is something you can choose.
text: In the beautiful city of Vienna, in Austria, there lived a curious little boy named Viktor Frankl. While other children counted sheep, Viktor lay in his bed asking enormous questions. Why are we here? What makes a life matter?

He grew up to become a doctor — not a doctor of tummies or bones, but a doctor of the mind and the heart. People came to him feeling sad and lost, and Viktor listened to every one of them. He helped each person find one small reason to keep going, and slowly the heaviness lifted.

Then a very cruel time came to Europe. Viktor and his family were taken far from home, and he lost almost everyone he loved. Even through those dark years, Viktor kept watching and wondering. He noticed something quiet and true: the people who held on to a purpose — someone waiting for them, a piece of work still to finish, a song still to sing — found the strength to carry on.

When it was all over, Viktor wrote a small book called 'Man's Search for Meaning'. In it he gave the world his gift: nobody can ever take away your last freedom, the freedom to choose how you answer whatever happens to you. Even on the darkest night, he said, we can still choose hope.
textM: In the beautiful city of Vienna, in Austria, there lived a curious little boy named Viktor Frankl. Vienna was a city of cafés and music, of tall grey buildings and horses clip-clopping over the cobbles, full of people who liked to sit for hours and talk about ideas. Viktor fitted in perfectly. While other children counted sheep, he lay in his bed asking enormous questions. Why are we here? What makes a life matter?

When he was only three years old he announced to his family that he was going to be a doctor, and he never changed his mind. As a schoolboy he was so full of thoughts about how the mind works that he wrote a letter to the most famous thinker in Vienna, Sigmund Freud. Freud wrote back — and helped the schoolboy get his little paper printed in a real scientific journal.

He grew up to become a doctor — not a doctor of tummies or bones, but a doctor of the mind and the heart. He noticed that many young people in his city felt hopeless, so he opened free places where any young person could come and talk to someone, without paying a penny. People came to him feeling sad and lost, and Viktor listened to every one of them. He helped each person find one small reason to keep going, and slowly the heaviness lifted.

That was his big idea. Other doctors asked, 'What is the matter with you?' Viktor liked to ask a different question: 'What is still waiting for you?' A person who could answer that question, he found, could carry almost anything. He gave his idea a name that means 'healing through meaning'.

Then a very cruel time came to Europe. Viktor and his family were taken far from home, and he lost almost everyone he loved. Even through those dark years, Viktor kept watching and wondering. He noticed something quiet and true: the people who held on to a purpose — someone waiting for them, a piece of work still to finish, a song still to sing — found the strength to carry on.

Viktor had a purpose of his own. He had begun writing a book, and the pages had been taken away from him. So he kept the whole book alive inside his head. On any scrap of paper he could find, he wrote a few words to help himself remember. Some days, he said later, he would picture himself standing in a warm, bright hall, explaining everything he was learning to a room full of listening people. That picture was a light, and he walked towards it.

When it was all over, he came back to Vienna, to a city still putting itself together again, and he sat down and wrote. The little book took him only nine days. It is called 'Man's Search for Meaning', and in it he gave the world his gift: nobody can ever take away your last freedom, the freedom to choose how you answer whatever happens to you. Viktor lived a long life afterwards. He climbed mountains. He learned to fly an aeroplane when he was sixty-seven. He answered letters from strangers all over the world.

Millions of people have read that small book, and many of them say it helped them keep going on a hard day. That is why we still tell his story at bedtime. Even on the darkest night, Viktor said, we can still choose hope — and there is always something, however small, still waiting for us to do.

stories.name: Anne Frank
stories.title: The Girl and Her Diary
stories.hook: A chatty, funny, book-loving girl whose words became one of the most loved books in the world.
text: Anne Frank was born in Germany, and when she was very small her family moved to Amsterdam, a city full of canals and bicycles. Anne was funny and chatty — she talked so much in class that her teacher gave her the nickname Miss Quack-Quack. She loved cats, film stars and, most of all, books.

On her thirteenth birthday she was given a small notebook with a red-checked cover. It was the best present of all. Anne gave her diary a name, Kitty, and wrote to it almost every day, exactly as if she were writing to her very best friend.

Then a cruel time came, and Anne's family had to hide. They lived very quietly in a few secret rooms above her father's office, behind a door tucked away behind a bookcase, for two whole years. Anne kept writing all the while — about laughing and arguing and growing up, and about her dream of becoming a writer one day. And she wrote a line the world still remembers: that in spite of everything, she still believed people are really good at heart.

Anne did not live to see the end of that war. But her words did. Her father came home, found the little red-checked diary, and shared it with the world. Today Anne's diary has been read by millions of people in more than seventy languages — a girl's gentle voice, still talking, still hoping, long after the dark days ended.
textM: Anne Frank was born in Germany in the summer of 1929, in a city called Frankfurt. When she was still very small, her family packed their suitcases and moved to Amsterdam, in the Netherlands. It was a city of canals and church bells, of narrow houses standing shoulder to shoulder, and of bicycles ringing along the streets from morning until night. Anne learned a new language, made new friends, and very soon it felt like home.

At school, Anne was the one everybody noticed. She was funny, she was clever, and above all she was chatty — she talked so much in class that her teacher gave her a nickname: Miss Quack-Quack. He even set her the task of writing an essay about why chatterboxes chatter. Anne wrote the whole thing in rhyme, and the class laughed, and so did the teacher. She loved cats. She pinned pictures of film stars on the wall beside her bed. But most of all, she loved books and stories and words.

On the morning of her thirteenth birthday, Anne woke up very early, far too excited to sleep. Downstairs on the table lay a small notebook with a red-checked cover and a little clasp. Of all her presents, it was the one she loved best. She decided that her diary would not really be a book at all — it would be a friend. So she gave it a name: Kitty. “Dear Kitty,” she began, and after that she wrote to her almost every single day.

Then a cruel time came to Europe, and Anne's family had to hide. They moved into a few small rooms above her father's office, and a kind helper built a swinging bookcase in front of the doorway so that nobody would ever guess the rooms were there. Four other people came to hide with them. They stayed for two whole years.

Life in those rooms was very, very quiet. During the day, while people worked in the offices below, nobody upstairs could run, or cough loudly, or even turn on a tap. Anne learned to walk about in her socks. She listened to the bells of the Westerkerk church chiming the hours, and she loved that sound. From the attic window she could see a patch of sky, a bird flying past, and the top of an old chestnut tree that changed with the seasons — green, then gold, then bare, then green again.

And all that time, she wrote. She wrote about laughing and arguing, about her sister Margot, about the cat who lived with them, about missing her friends and the wind and the rain. She wrote about being thirteen, then fourteen, then fifteen. She wrote about what she wanted to be when it was all over: a writer, with real books on real shelves. “I want to go on living even after my death,” she wrote one day. And she wrote a line the world still remembers — that in spite of everything, she still believed that people are really good at heart.

Anne did not live to see the end of that war. But her words did. A brave friend of the family named Miep Gies gathered the scattered pages up off the floor and kept them safe in a drawer, without ever reading a single one. And when Anne's father came home at last, Miep put them gently into his hands.

He read them, and he cried, and then he did the thing Anne had dreamed of: he turned her diary into a book. Today it has been read by millions of people in more than seventy languages, and the house with the swinging bookcase is a museum where visitors walk very softly. Anne wanted her writing to matter, and it does. Her voice is still talking, still noticing small things, still hoping — reminding everyone who reads her that one ordinary girl with a notebook can be heard by the whole world.

stories.name: The 14th Dalai Lama (Tenzin Gyatso)
stories.title: The Boy Who Chose Kindness
stories.hook: A farmer's son who lost his homeland and still says his religion is simply kindness.
text: High up among the snowy mountains of Tibet, in a small farming village, a baby boy was born to a family who grew barley and looked after horses. When he was only two years old, wise old monks came looking for him. They said this little boy was the next Dalai Lama, and they carried him away to a palace with a thousand rooms.

It was a very big home for a very small boy. He wore red robes and learned to sit still, but oh, he was curious. He took clocks and watches to pieces just to see how they ticked inside, though he could not always put them back together again. At night he pointed his telescope at the city far below, watching the little lights and wishing he could run about in the streets like other children.

When he was a young man, a hard time came and he had to leave his homeland. He crossed the mountains on foot, and ever since that day he has lived far from home. He could have let his heart turn bitter. Instead he chose something braver. He decided to spend his whole life teaching people to be kind to one another.

Today he travels the world with his big warm laugh, telling everyone that we all belong to one human family. He was given the Nobel Peace Prize for it. And when people ask him what he believes, he smiles and says something small enough for any child to carry: 'My religion is very simple. My religion is kindness.'
textM: High up among the snowy mountains of Tibet, in a village of flat-roofed houses called Taktser, a baby boy was born to a family of farmers. They grew barley and buckwheat and potatoes, and they looked after horses, sheep and a few shaggy yaks. They named him Lhamo Thondup. The air up there is thin and bright, and in winter the whole world turns white and very, very quiet.

When he was two years old, some travellers stopped at the house. They looked like ordinary men, but they were wise old monks, and they had come a very long way, searching. They laid some old things out on a table — a walking stick, a small drum, a string of beads — mixed in with new ones that looked exactly the same. The little boy reached straight for the old ones. "That's mine," he said. The monks looked at one another, and their eyes filled with tears.

They told his parents that this small farm boy was the next Dalai Lama, the teacher his people had been waiting for. So he travelled for months across the mountains to the city of Lhasa, and went to live in the Potala Palace — a building so vast it had a thousand rooms, with dark stairways and butter lamps that flickered all night long.

It was a very big home for a very small boy. He wore red robes, learned to sit still, and studied for hours and hours with his teachers. But oh, he was curious. He took clocks and watches to pieces just to see what made them tick, and he was much better at taking them apart than at putting them back together. He mended a film projector all by himself. He loved maps and picture books of faraway countries, and taught himself the names of places he had never seen. And at night he pointed his telescope down at the city below, watching the little lights and the people going home, wishing he could run about in the streets like other children.

When he was a young man, a hard time came, and he had to leave his homeland. He slipped away in the night and crossed the great mountains on foot and on horseback, through snow and thin cold air, until he reached India. He was twenty-three years old. He has lived far from home ever since, and so have many of his people.

He could have let his heart turn bitter. It would have been easy. Instead he chose something braver. He made a new home in a green town in the hills, opened schools for the children who had come with him, and decided to spend his whole life teaching people to be kind to one another. He still gets up at three in the morning to sit quietly and wish everybody well — even the people who were unkind to him.

Today he travels the world with his big warm laugh — a laugh that starts somewhere down in his shoulders — telling everyone that we all belong to one human family, and that a happier world begins with a happier heart. He was given the Nobel Peace Prize for it. And when people ask him what he believes, he smiles and says something small enough for any child to carry: 'My religion is very simple. My religion is kindness.'

stories.name: Michelle Obama
stories.title: The Girl Behind the Curtain
stories.hook: A girl from a tiny Chicago apartment who grew up to plant a garden at the White House.
text: On the South Side of Chicago, in a little apartment with just one bedroom, lived a girl named Michelle. She and her big brother Craig slept in the living room, with a curtain hung down the middle so that each of them could have a room of their own.

Her father went to work at the city water plant every single day, even when his legs hurt and walking was hard, and he almost never complained. Her mother taught Michelle to read before she had even started school. At dinner the family talked and laughed and argued about everything, and Michelle learned that her voice mattered.

Michelle worked hard and loved to learn. One day somebody told her she was not clever enough for a famous university called Princeton. Michelle did not shout. She simply studied, and she went to Princeton — and then to Harvard as well — and she became a lawyer.

Years later, that girl from behind the curtain became the first Black First Lady of the United States. She dug a vegetable garden at the White House and invited children to plant it and taste it, telling girls and boys everywhere to learn, to move, to eat well and to keep becoming. And she gave the world a rule worth remembering: when they go low, we go high.
textM: On the South Side of Chicago, on a street called Euclid Avenue, stood a small brick house. Upstairs, in an apartment with just one bedroom, lived a girl named Michelle Robinson. She was born in 1964. She and her big brother Craig slept in the living room, where their parents had put up a wooden curtain down the middle, so that each of them could have a little room of their own.

Her father, Fraser, looked after the boilers at the city water plant. He had an illness that slowly made his legs weak, so every morning took him a little longer than the morning before. He would button his shirt slowly, take up his canes, and go to work anyway. He hardly ever complained. Watching him, Michelle learned something she never forgot: you can be tired and still be steady.

Her mother, Marian, taught her to read before she had even started school. Downstairs lived her great-aunt Robbie, who gave piano lessons. Michelle practised on Robbie's old piano, which had one chipped key — and that little chip was how her fingers always found the middle note. Then came a recital on a shiny grand piano with no chip anywhere. Michelle froze. Gently, Aunt Robbie reached over and placed her finger on the right key. Michelle breathed, and played.

At dinner the Robinsons talked and laughed and argued about everything — school, the news, whose turn it was to wash the dishes. Nobody was told to be quiet. Michelle learned that her voice mattered. She loved learning so much that she skipped a whole grade, and later she rode buses and trains for an hour and a half each way to reach a good high school on the far side of the city.

One day an adviser at school looked at her and said she was not really Princeton material. Michelle did not shout. She went home, and she studied. She got into Princeton. Then she went to Harvard to learn law, and she became a lawyer. At her law firm she was asked to look after a new young lawyer for the summer. His name was Barack Obama. They talked, and talked, and later they married.

But a fine office was not enough for Michelle. She left it to do work that helped her own city: showing young people how to serve their neighbourhoods, and helping a big hospital open its doors wider to the families living all around it. Whatever job she was doing, she kept coming back to the same question: who is this actually helping?

Then, in 2009, the girl from behind the curtain walked into the White House as the first Black First Lady of the United States. She looked out at the huge lawn and asked for something surprisingly simple: a garden. Children came with little spades and muddy knees to plant lettuce and carrots and sweet potatoes, and to taste what they had grown.

From that garden grew bigger things. Michelle told children everywhere to move, to eat well, to stay in school and to reach higher, and she worked so that girls in many countries could keep learning. She wrote her life story in a book called Becoming, because she believes nobody is ever finished growing. And she gave the world a rule worth remembering at bedtime: when they go low, we go high.

stories.name: Malala Yousafzai
stories.title: The Girl with the Book
stories.hook: A girl from a green valley who taught the world that one book and one pen can change everything.
text: In the Swat Valley in Pakistan, where the mountains are green and the rivers run cold and clear, a girl named Malala was born. Her father ran a school, and Malala grew up among chalk and books and children's voices. She loved learning so much that she was nearly always top of her class.

Then some dangerous men came to the valley and said that girls must stop going to school. Many people were too frightened to speak. Malala was only eleven, but she spoke anyway. She wrote a diary telling the world why every girl deserves to learn, and she said it out loud on the radio and on television.

One day, because she had spoken, Malala was badly hurt. Many doctors worked hard, for a long time, to make her well again. Slowly she got better. And the very first thing she did when she was strong enough was to pick up her books and start speaking again.

The world listened. At just seventeen, Malala became the youngest person ever to win the Nobel Peace Prize, and she has helped build schools for girls in many countries. She gave everyone the simplest and biggest idea of all: one child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world.
textM: In the Swat Valley in Pakistan, the mountains are green and the rivers run cold and clear over smooth stones. In summer the apricot trees hang heavy with fruit. In a town there called Mingora, in 1997, a girl was born, and her father named her Malala, after a brave young woman from long ago who was remembered for her voice.

Her father ran a school, and the family lived close beside it, so Malala grew up in a world of chalk dust, ink, and children's voices carrying down the corridor. Long before she could read, she liked to creep into the back of the big children's lessons and listen. When the school was empty she would stand at the blackboard and pretend to be the teacher.

She grew into a girl who loved learning more than almost anything. There was another very clever girl in her class, and the two of them took turns being first — which only made Malala study harder. She had a best friend called Moniba, and they walked to school together, talking the whole way about lessons and exams and what they would be one day. Malala thought she might become a doctor. Her father thought she might become something even larger, and told her so.

Then some dangerous men came to the valley, and they said that girls must stop going to school. Many people were too frightened to say anything at all. Malala's father said quietly that they would not close the school. Malala was only eleven, but she spoke too. She asked a question that travelled a long way: how dare anyone take away my right to learn?

She began writing a secret diary for the radio, under a made-up name that means cornflower. She wrote about small ordinary things — hiding her books under her shawl on the way to school, wondering each morning whether the classroom would still be open. Then she stopped hiding. She spoke on television with her own name and her own face, calmly, again and again. She was small, and her voice was still a child's voice, and people all over her country began to listen to it.

One day, because she had spoken, Malala was badly hurt. Many doctors worked hard, for a long time, to make her well again, and she woke up in a hospital far from home, in England. Slowly, slowly, she got better. And the very first thing she did when she was strong enough was to pick up her books and start speaking again.

On her sixteenth birthday she stood up in front of leaders from all over the world and gave them the simplest and biggest idea of all: one child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world. The next year, at just seventeen, she became the youngest person ever to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.

Malala went on to study at Oxford University in England, and she and her father built a fund that helps girls go to school in many countries — girls in refugee camps, girls in mountain villages, girls whose families had never sent a daughter to a classroom. She still says the same thing she said at eleven: every girl deserves to learn. And every day, more of them do.

stories.name: Plutarch
stories.title: The Man Who Collected Lives
stories.hook: He loved his little town so much he never left it — but he brought the whole world into it, one story at a time.
text: Long, long ago in Greece there was a small town called Chaeronea, with quiet streets and hills all around. A boy named Plutarch was born there. Other clever people left small towns for big cities. Plutarch stayed. 'If I leave,' he said with a smile, 'my little town would be one person smaller.'

Plutarch was a great listener. He served as a priest at Delphi, where travellers came from far away, and he asked them questions and wrote down what they said. He collected stories the way some children collect shells or stones — carefully, and never throwing a good one away.

Then he wrote a wonderful book called Parallel Lives. He put one famous Greek beside one famous Roman, two lives side by side, so you could see how each person grew up and what they chose to do. It was the first great book of biographies — the first big book of true life stories.

Plutarch believed that a tiny thing — a kind word, a small joke, the way someone treats a friend — can tell you more about a person than a huge battle. Because he wrote them down, people from long ago still feel real to us. Every time someone tells the story of a life, they are doing what Plutarch taught the world to do.
textM: Long, long ago in Greece there was a small town called Chaeronea, with quiet streets, olive trees and green hills all around it. It was the sort of place where everybody knew everybody, and where nothing very grand ever happened. About two thousand years ago, a boy named Plutarch was born there.

He grew up asking questions, so his family sent him to study in the great city of Athens. Later he travelled all the way to Rome, where the streets were packed with people and where crowds came to hear him give talks. He learned Latin there as a grown-up, which was slow, difficult work, and he cheerfully admitted how difficult it was. He could easily have stayed in a big city. Clever people usually did. But Plutarch went home to his little town, and he never moved away again. 'If I left,' he said with a smile, 'my little town would be one person smaller.'

At home he taught young people in his own house, and he loved long suppers where everyone talked and asked questions and laughed until late. He wrote those conversations down too — questions like why the sea is salty, and why we remember dreams. Plutarch thought a good question at the table was as fine as a feast.

For many years he was a priest at Delphi, high on a mountainside, where travellers came from all over the world to ask what their future would hold. Plutarch asked them things instead. Where are you from? What happened there? Who was your grandmother? Then he wrote it all down. He collected stories the way some children collect shells or smooth stones — carefully, and never throwing away a good one.

Out of all that collecting came a wonderful book called Parallel Lives. He placed one famous Greek beside one famous Roman, two lives side by side, so that you could hold them up and compare them: how each one grew up, what each one was afraid of, and what each one chose to do. He wrote dozens of these pairs, filling page after page, and many of them we can still read today. It was the first great book of biographies — true stories of real lives.

He wrote them differently from everybody else. Other writers filled their pages with battles and dates. Plutarch wanted to know what a person was really like. He said that a tiny thing — a joke, a kind word, the way somebody treats a friend — often shows you a person's heart far better than an enormous battle does.

So his pages are full of small bright moments. A boy who calms a wild horse that nobody else dares to ride. A general who eats the same plain supper as his soldiers. Somebody who keeps a promise on a day when keeping it is hard. Little things, remembered and written down, so that they would not be lost.

Because Plutarch wrote them, people from long ago still feel real to us. Hundreds of years later, a writer called Shakespeare read his book and turned those lives into plays that are still performed today. And every time somebody tells the story of a life — in a book, in a film, or at bedtime, like tonight — they are doing exactly what Plutarch taught the world to do.

stories.name: Charles Dickens
stories.title: The Boy Who Turned Sad Days Into Stories
stories.hook: He walked London at night, remembering every face — and then he wrote them all down.
text: In England, long ago, a small boy named Charles loved books more than almost anything. He was thin and quiet, with big eyes that noticed everything. He read the same stories again and again, and made up new ones for himself in the corner of a room.

When Charles was twelve, his family ran out of money and everything changed. He had to leave school and go to work in a factory, sticking labels on pots of shoe polish, long day after long day. He was lonely, and he was sad. But he never forgot how it felt — and he never forgot the other children working beside him.

Later Charles walked the streets of London at night, mile after mile, watching. He remembered every face: the cheerful cook, the tired boy, the old man with holes in his coat. All of them went into his notebook of the mind. Then he began to write, and people could not stop reading.

He wrote Oliver Twist and A Christmas Carol, and became the most loved storyteller of his time. His stories about poor and hungry children made rich and powerful people ashamed — and they changed the laws to help. Charles took his hardest days and turned them into stories that made the whole world a little kinder.
textM: Long ago in England, a small boy named Charles Dickens loved books more than almost anything. He was thin and quiet, with big eyes that noticed everything. For a while he lived in a town by the dockyards, where sailors sang and ships were mended, and he would climb up to a little attic room where a shelf of old books sat waiting for him.

He read them until he knew them by heart. Then he made up stories of his own in the corner of a room, and sometimes his father stood him on a table to sing a comic song for the neighbours. Charles liked that very much. He decided, secretly, that one day he would be somebody. It was a big thought for a small boy in a small room.

When Charles was twelve, his family ran out of money, and everything changed. He had to leave school and go to work in a riverside factory, sticking labels on pots of shoe polish. He worked from morning until night, six days a week, and ate his dinner alone. He was lonely, and he was sad. He never forgot how it felt — and he never forgot the other children working beside him.

It lasted about a year, but he kept it a secret for almost his whole life. He told no one, not even his own children. Later he wrote about a boy in the very same trouble, and gave him a happier ending. Charles went back to school, learned to write astonishingly fast, and got a job writing down what people said in Parliament — the quickest, sharpest reporter in the room.

In the evenings, he walked. Charles walked the streets of London mile after mile, sometimes twelve or twenty miles in one night, past lamplighters and pie stalls and windows glowing yellow. He remembered every face: the cheerful cook, the tired boy, the old man with holes in his coat. All of them went into the notebook of his mind. Some nights he could not settle at all, and he said that if he could not walk fast and far, he thought he would simply burst.

Then he began to write, and people could not stop reading. His stories came out a few chapters at a time, like a programme you wait for each week. Crowds gathered on the docks in New York and shouted up to the arriving ships to ask what happened next. Charles read his own stories aloud to packed halls, doing all the voices. He wrote with a goose-quill pen and blue ink, and he could not begin until everything on his desk was arranged just so.

He wrote Oliver Twist, about a hungry orphan who dared to ask for more, and A Christmas Carol, written in only six weeks, about a cold-hearted man who learns to be generous. He gave his people wonderful names — Fagin, Scrooge, Tiny Tim — and once he had named them, he said, they seemed to come and stand beside him while he wrote. He walked through the poorest streets and visited schools for children who had nothing at all, and then he put everything he saw into his books.

His stories made rich and powerful people feel ashamed, and things began to change: better schools, better rules, and a hospital for sick children that he helped to rescue with a single evening's reading. We still tell his tales at Christmas. Charles took his hardest days and turned them into stories that made the whole world a little kinder.

stories.name: Steve Jobs
stories.title: Even the Back of the Cabinet
stories.hook: His father taught him that the part nobody sees should still be beautiful.
text: In America, a baby boy was adopted by Paul and Clara Jobs, who loved him very much. They made one big promise the day they brought him home: this boy would go to university one day. They called him Steve.

Steve's father worked in the garage, and Steve stood beside him and watched. His father showed him how to build things carefully, right to the very end. 'Even the back of the cabinet,' he said, 'where nobody can see — make it beautiful.' Steve never forgot that lesson.

When he grew up, Steve and his friend Steve Wozniak built a computer in that same garage. They started a company called Apple. In those days computers were big, grey and confusing. Steve wanted them simple and friendly, so that anyone — even a child — could use one.

It was not always easy. Once he was even asked to leave the company he had started. He used those years to learn new things and come back stronger, and later he helped make the iPhone. He also once took a class in beautiful handwriting, just because he was curious — and years later that class made the letters on computer screens lovely. Care about the small things, and stay curious.
textM: In February 1955, in California, in the United States, a baby boy needed a family. Paul and Clara Jobs brought him home and loved him with all their hearts. They made one big promise that day: this boy would go to university when he grew up. They called him Steve. The valley where they lived was still full of apricot orchards then — warm, quiet, with rows of small houses and long green afternoons.

Paul Jobs worked with his hands. He could mend cars and build furniture, and his workshop was the garage, which smelled of oil and sawdust. One day he cleared a space on his workbench and said, 'Steve, this bench is yours now.' Then he gave his son some of his own tools, and taught him how to use them slowly and properly.

Paul showed him how to finish a job right to the very end. 'Even the back of the cabinet,' he said — the side that faces the wall, where nobody will ever look — 'make it beautiful.' Steve asked why. Because you will know, said his father. A real craftsman cares about the parts nobody sees. Steve never forgot that, not once in his whole life.

Steve was curious almost to the point of cheek. When he was twelve he needed spare parts for a machine he was building, so he found the telephone number of a famous engineer named Bill Hewlett and simply rang him at home. They talked for twenty minutes. Steve got his parts — and a summer job at the man's factory as well.

He went to university, just as his parents had promised, but it cost a great deal of money. So he stopped taking the classes he was supposed to take, and quietly sat in on the ones he loved instead. One of them was calligraphy: the art of beautiful letters, drawn slowly with a wide pen. It seemed completely useless. He learned it because it was lovely.

Back home, Steve and his friend Steve Wozniak built a computer in that same garage, and in 1976 they started a company called Apple. In those days computers were big grey machines that only experts understood. Steve wanted them small, friendly and simple, so that anyone — even a child — could switch one on and know what to do.

When he helped build a computer called the Macintosh, he remembered that calligraphy class and gave the screen beautiful letters. Nothing you learn is ever wasted. But things did not always go well. One day he was asked to leave the very company he had started. He was sad — and then he began again. He helped a small animation studio make Toy Story, the first film ever drawn entirely by computers. Years later, Apple asked him to come back.

Back at Apple he helped make the iPod, and then the iPhone, a computer small enough to fit in a pocket, which changed how people all over the world talk, learn and take pictures. And inside those machines, in places you will never see, the wires were tidy and the parts were neat. Because his father was right: care about the small things, do good work even when nobody is looking, and stay curious about everything.

stories.name: Viola Davis
stories.title: The Girl Who Found Herself on a Stage
stories.hook: Where you begin does not decide where you will end.
text: Viola Davis was born on her grandmother's farm in South Carolina, in America. When she was still tiny, her family moved north to a small town called Central Falls. Their apartment was old and falling apart, and there was often not enough food. Some children teased her for the colour of her skin.

But Viola had a big imagination. She and her sisters made up plays and acted them out for each other. Then one day at school a teacher put her in a real play, on a real stage, with lights. Standing there, saying the words, Viola felt something new and wonderful: for the first time she felt fully alive, and fully seen.

So she worked. She studied acting for years and years, saying lines over and over, learning from every teacher she could find. There were many days when nobody chose her. She kept going anyway, because she knew what she had felt on that first stage.

Viola became one of the greatest actors in the world. She is the first Black woman to win acting's 'triple crown' — an Oscar, an Emmy and a Tony. She wrote a book about her life called Finding Me, so that other children would know: where you start is not where you have to stay.
textM: Viola Davis was born in 1965 on her grandmother's farm in South Carolina, in America, in a little house where the floors creaked and the fields went on and on. She was still tiny when her family packed up and travelled north, to a small mill town in Rhode Island called Central Falls, where the winters were long and the wind came off the river cold. The farmhouse she left behind was barely more than one room, with a porch where the family sat when the day finally cooled.

Their apartment was old and falling apart, and the heating often did not work. There was frequently not enough food, and Viola and her sisters sometimes went to bed hungry. Some children teased her for the colour of her skin. She was a fast runner, and for a long time running away felt easier than standing still. But her mother worked and worked, and stood up for what was right, and taught her daughters to hold their heads up.

But Viola had an enormous imagination, and that was something nobody could take. She and her sisters made up plays in the flat, using blankets for costumes and the sofa for a castle. Her big sister would invent the story, and Viola would act it out with her whole body, and for a little while the cold room turned into somewhere else entirely.

One evening the television was on, and Viola saw an actress named Cicely Tyson playing a woman who was proud and strong and had skin like her own. Viola sat up. Something inside her said: that. She turned to her mother and told her, in a small clear voice, that this was what she wanted to do when she grew up.

Then at school a teacher put her in a real play, on a real stage, under real lights. Viola stood there in the warm brightness and said the words she had practised. Something new and wonderful happened. For the first time in her life she felt fully alive, and fully seen. After that, she joined every drama club and holiday programme she could find.

So she worked. She studied acting at college, and then for four more years at a famous school in New York, saying lines over and over until they lived in her bones. She learned how to breathe, how to stand still, how to listen. There were many, many days when she went to an audition and nobody chose her. Some nights she wondered whether she had picked an impossible dream. Then she would get up and say the lines one more time.

She kept going anyway, because she remembered exactly how she had felt on that first stage. Slowly the parts came, and then the great parts. Viola became one of the finest actors in the world, and the first Black woman to win acting's triple crown — an Oscar, an Emmy and a Tony. Later she won a Grammy too, for reading her own life story out loud.

That story is a book called Finding Me. She wrote it for the hungry girl in the cold apartment, and for every child who feels small and unseen. It says the thing Viola most wants children to hear: where you begin is not where you have to stay, and the person you are becoming is already inside you.

stories.name: Tara Westover
stories.title: The Girl Who Taught Herself
stories.hook: She was seventeen the first time she ever sat in a classroom.
text: Tara Westover grew up on a mountain in Idaho, in America, with pine trees and wide open sky. Her family believed differently about school than most families did, so Tara and her brothers and sisters did not go to one. She learned by helping at home, and the mountain was her whole world.

She worked in her father's scrapyard, sorting metal, and she helped her mother make herbal medicines from plants. She was strong and hard-working. But she was also very curious, and she began to wonder what was written in all the books she had never read.

So Tara taught herself. She borrowed books and worked through them alone — mathematics, grammar, page after page, sometimes late into the night. It was slow and it was hard. At seventeen she sat an exam, and she passed, and she won a place at university. On her first day she walked into a classroom for the very first time in her life.

She did not stop there. She kept studying and studying, all the way to a doctorate at Cambridge in England. Then she wrote a book about it all called Educated, which people around the world have read. Her story says something lovely: it is never too late to learn, and learning can open the whole wide world.
textM: Tara Westover was born in 1986, the youngest of seven children, on a mountain in Idaho, in America. Her family called their mountain Buck's Peak. There were pine trees, and wind, and a sky so wide it made you feel small in a good way. Her family believed differently about school than most families did, so Tara and her brothers and sisters never went to one.

Instead she learned by helping. Her mother made medicines from plants, and the kitchen smelled of lavender and mint and clove. Tara sorted leaves, filled little bottles and stuck on the labels. Her mother also helped babies to be born, so sometimes the telephone rang in the middle of the night and Tara would wake to headlights swinging across the ceiling.

By day she worked in her father's scrapyard, sorting iron from copper, with the clang of metal ringing across the valley and her hands black to the wrist. She was strong and she was fast, and she was proud of both. She also loved to sing, and once she sang on a stage in a town play, and discovered she liked the feeling of an audience listening. Standing up there, she felt for a moment like somebody with a life of her own choosing.

Her older brother Tyler had left the mountain to go to college. When he came home he brought books, and music that filled the house with violins. One day he told Tara, gently, that there was a whole world out there, and that she could go and look at it if she wanted. Tara said the mountain was her world. But afterwards she could not stop thinking about it.

So Tara taught herself. She borrowed textbooks and worked through them alone at the kitchen table — algebra, trigonometry, grammar, page after page, often late into the night with the wind pushing at the windows. Nobody explained anything. She simply read a rule, tried it, got it wrong, and tried again. It was slow and it was hard and sometimes she cried. But every so often a rule would suddenly make sense, and the whole page would light up, and that feeling kept her going.

At seventeen she sat a big university entrance exam. She did not do well enough. So she went back to the books, studied harder, and sat it again — and this time she passed, and won a place at university. On her first day she walked into a classroom for the very first time in her life and quietly found a seat.

Those first weeks were bewildering. Everyone seemed to know things she had never heard of, and she had to ask questions that made her feel foolish. She asked them anyway. She read and read, and her teachers noticed how hard she worked, and one of them helped her win a scholarship to Cambridge, in England, where the libraries are older than her whole country.

She kept going all the way to a doctorate in history. Then she wrote a book about it all, called Educated, which people around the world have read and loved. Her story says something worth carrying to sleep: it is never too late to start learning, questions are nothing to be ashamed of, and learning can open the whole wide world.

stories.name: Elon Musk
stories.title: The Boy Who Read the Whole Encyclopedia
stories.hook: A dreamy boy from Pretoria read so deeply that his family had to shout to reach him.
text: In a sunny city called Pretoria, in South Africa, a quiet boy named Elon was born. He liked to sit in a corner with a book and disappear inside it. Sometimes his family had to call his name three times before he heard them. His mind was busy somewhere far away.

Elon loved books so much that he read a whole encyclopedia — every page, from A all the way to Z. When he was about ten, he found a computer and taught himself how to write programs. Nobody showed him how. He read the instructions, he tried, and he tried again.

At twelve, he made a little space game of his very own and sold it. Later he travelled far away — first to Canada, then to America — carrying almost nothing except his ideas. He kept asking a question grown-ups had stopped asking: 'Why not?' Why not cars that run on electricity? Why not rockets that come home?

Today, rockets he helped build fly up towards the stars and then land gently back on their legs, ready to fly again. Elon's secret was simple. Read a lot. Teach yourself. And when someone says something is impossible, ask 'why not?' — then keep on trying.
textM: In a sunny city called Pretoria, in South Africa, a quiet boy named Elon was born in 1971. In spring the streets there turn purple, because the jacaranda trees all flower at once. Elon hardly noticed. He liked to sit in a corner with a book and disappear inside it. Sometimes his family had to call his name three times before he heard them. His mind was busy somewhere far away.

School days were not always easy for him, but books were faithful friends. He read adventure stories and comics and science fiction about ships that sail between the stars. When he had read everything in the house, he started on the encyclopedia — every page, from A all the way to Z — and he remembered a surprising amount of it. He wanted to know how things were put together, and he would take an idea apart the way another child takes apart a toy.

When he was about ten, his family got a small computer. It came with a fat manual that said the lessons inside would take about six months. Elon opened it, and barely slept, and finished it in a few days. Nobody showed him how to write programs. He read the instructions, he tried, and he tried again.

At twelve he made a little space game of his very own, called Blastar. It had a small spaceship that had to clear a path through space, drawn in the simple bright blocks that computers made in those days. He sold it to a computer magazine for about five hundred dollars. Imagine that: a boy in Pretoria, typing a game into a machine at night, and someone paying him for the ideas in his head.

At seventeen he flew across the world alone, first to Canada, then to America, carrying almost nothing except those ideas. He worked hard, sometimes at rough jobs, and studied at university. And all the while he kept asking a question grown-ups had stopped asking: 'Why not?' Why not cars that run on electricity? Why not rockets that come home instead of being thrown away?

Rockets are hard. His first rocket failed. The second failed. The third failed too, and the money was almost gone. Many people would have stopped there. Instead, each time, the team gathered up the pieces, worked out exactly what had gone wrong, and began again. They built a fourth rocket, and in 2008 it climbed all the way up into space. Elon later said the failures were not the end of the story — they were how the team learned what the rocket needed.

Today, rockets he helped build fly up towards the stars and then come down and land gently on their legs, standing upright like a bird settling on a branch, ready to fly again. The first time one did that, the engineers watching cheered so loudly that you could hear them right through the video. Electric cars hum quietly along roads where everyone once said only petrol engines could go.

Elon's secret was simple, and it is a secret any child can borrow. Read a lot. Teach yourself. And when someone says something is impossible, ask 'why not?' — then keep on trying, even after the first three tries do not work.

stories.name: Warren Buffett
stories.title: The Boy Who Loved Counting
stories.hook: A boy in Omaha counted everything, saved every coin, and learned that patience is the greatest secret of all.
text: In a quiet town called Omaha, in the United States, a boy named Warren was born. He loved numbers the way other children love sweets. He counted everything. He even counted how many times each letter appeared on the pages of the Bible.

When Warren was six, he bought a pack of cola bottles and sold them one by one, keeping a few small coins. Then he sold chewing gum and newspapers from door to door. He saved every coin in a little drawer. At eleven, he bought his very first tiny share of a company.

The share went down before it went up, and Warren learned the biggest secret of all: patience. Good things grow slowly, like a tree. You plant a small seed, and then you wait — not for a few days, but for many, many years. Warren waited better than almost anyone.

Warren grew up to be one of the wisest money-minders in the world, and yet he still lives in the same simple house he bought long ago. He tells jokes, and he has promised to give away almost everything he has. Be patient, save a little, and stay humble and kind.
textM: In a quiet town called Omaha, in the middle of the United States, a boy named Warren was born in 1930. Omaha had wide streets, wide skies, and long freight trains that rumbled through at night. It was a hard time for money; grown-ups spoke about it in worried voices. But Warren had found something that made him happy, and it cost nothing at all. He loved numbers the way other children love sweets.

He counted everything. Sitting on the front steps with a friend, he wrote down the numbers on the licence plates of passing cars. He learned the sizes of cities by heart. He and his friend even counted how many times each letter appeared on the pages of the Bible, just to see which one won. To Warren, numbers were not homework. Numbers were a game he never got bored of playing.

When Warren was six, he had an idea. He bought a pack of six cola bottles from his grandfather's little shop for twenty-five cents. Then he walked around and sold them one at a time, five cents each, and came home with thirty. Five cents left over. It was a tiny amount — but it was his, and he had made it appear out of an idea.

After that he never stopped. He sold chewing gum from door to door with a tray hung round his neck. He fished lost golf balls out of ponds, cleaned them, and sold them. He got up before dawn to deliver newspapers, hundreds of them, before school. He and a friend bought a second-hand pinball machine and put it in a barber's shop, and shared the coins. He kept every penny in a little drawer and counted it often.

At eleven, Warren bought his very first tiny share of a company — three of them, with money he had saved himself. Almost at once, the price went down. Warren felt worried every single day until it climbed back up, and the moment it did he sold it, glad to escape. Then he watched from the outside as that share went up, and up, and up — far higher than the price he sold it for.

That is when he learned the biggest secret of all: patience. Good things grow slowly, like a tree. You plant a small seed, and then you wait — not for a few days, but for many, many years. And each year, the tree grows a little from what it grew the year before. It is a snowball rolling downhill: small at the top, enormous at the bottom, if you only let it roll. Warren waited better than almost anyone alive.

He grew up to be one of the wisest money-minders in the world. And yet he still lives in the same simple house in Omaha that he bought long ago, on an ordinary street with ordinary neighbours. He reads for hours every day — reports, newspapers, books — because he says the more you understand, the fewer mistakes you make. He tells jokes. He plays the ukulele. He is famous for being cheerful.

And here is the best part. Warren has promised to give away almost everything he has, so that it can go to schools and doctors and children who need it. He says money was never really the point; the point was the puzzle, and the friends, and being useful. So the lesson from the boy who counted licence plates is a gentle one. Be curious. Save a little. Wait longer than everyone else. And stay humble and kind.

stories.name: Oprah Winfrey
stories.title: The Little Girl They Called 'The Preacher'
stories.hook: A poor country girl who could recite poems so beautifully that the whole church smiled grew up to listen to the world.
text: In the green countryside of Mississippi, in the United States, a baby girl named Oprah was born. Her family had very little money. She lived with her grandmother, who was strict and loving, and who taught her to read before she was even three years old.

Oprah wore dresses her grandmother sewed from empty potato sacks, and some children laughed at her. But when she stood up in church, something wonderful happened. She said poems and speeches so beautifully that the grown-ups smiled and nodded and called her 'The Preacher'.

Her early years were hard, and there were days when she felt very alone. But she held on to two things: books and her own voice. She read and read. She practised speaking out loud. Slowly she grew strong, and she became a young woman who read the news on television.

Then Oprah made her own show, where she did the kindest thing of all — she listened to people's stories. Millions of families watched her every day. She also built a school for girls in South Africa, so that they could dream too. Your voice and your kindness can lift other people up.
textM: In the green countryside of Mississippi, in the United States, a baby girl was born and named Oprah. Her family had very little money. She lived on a small farm with her grandmother, Hattie Mae, in a house with no running water. There were pigs and chickens in the yard, a well outside, and the smell of woodsmoke in the evening.

Hattie Mae was strict and loving. She taught Oprah her letters from the Bible before Oprah was even three years old. Soon Oprah could read almost anything, and her grandmother told the neighbours, 'This child can talk.' In a house with no other children, Oprah made her own audience. She lined up the crows sitting on the fence and the animals in the yard, and she interviewed her corncob doll.

Her grandmother sewed her dresses out of empty potato sacks, and some children laughed at her clothes. But when Oprah stood up in church on a Sunday, something wonderful happened. She recited poems and long speeches without a single mistake, in a voice that filled the whole room. The grown-ups smiled and nodded and called her 'The Preacher'.

Her childhood was not easy. She moved between her grandmother's farm, her mother's home in a northern city, and her father's house in Nashville. There were long stretches when she felt very alone. But she held on to two things: books, and her own voice. Books, she said later, showed her that there was a whole world beyond the front porch.

Her father was strict about reading. Every week Oprah had to finish a book and write about what was in it. She read and read. She practised speaking out loud, standing tall, saying every word clearly. She won speaking contests, and one of them won her a place at university. At seventeen she won a contest in Nashville, and a local radio station heard her voice and asked her to read the news after school. She was still a schoolgirl, and already she was on the radio.

At nineteen, still a student, Oprah was asked to read the news, first on the radio and then on television. She was the youngest news reader at that station, and one of the first Black women to sit in that chair. But reading the news did not quite fit her. She kept wanting to put the paper down and ask people how they were feeling.

So Oprah made her own show. And there she did the kindest thing of all — she listened. She let ordinary people tell their own stories. She cried with them and laughed with them, and millions of families watched her every day for twenty-five years. When she talked about a book she loved, whole countries went out and read it.

Oprah used what she earned to help other people. She built a school for girls in South Africa, so that clever girls with very little money could learn and dream, just as she once did. She calls them her daughters, and many of them have grown up to be doctors and engineers and teachers. Her life whispers something to every child: your voice is worth practising, and listening to somebody else is one of the kindest gifts you can give.

stories.name: Richard Branson
stories.title: The Boy Who Found His Own Way Home
stories.hook: Letters danced on the page for him, but he was full of brave ideas — and one day his mother asked him to find his own way home.
text: In England, a boy named Richard was born with a head full of ideas. But the letters on a page danced and jumped in front of his eyes. This is called dyslexia. Reading and writing felt very hard, and he was often near the bottom of his class.

One day his mother stopped the car a few miles from home. 'Find your own way back,' she said kindly. Richard walked across the fields, past cows and hedges, and arrived home tired but very proud. His mother was teaching him confidence — that he could work things out by himself.

At sixteen, Richard started a magazine written by students, for students. Then he opened a shop that sold records. Later, when a flight was cancelled and all the passengers were stuck, he hired a plane himself to take everybody home — and one day he started a whole airline.

Richard loves adventure. He has crossed oceans in fast boats and floated over the world in hot-air balloons, and he even built a company for flying to the edge of space. He shows us something important: school is not the only kind of clever. Be bold, be curious, and be kind.
textM: In England, in 1950, a boy named Richard was born with a head full of ideas. But when he opened a school book, the letters danced and jumped and swapped places in front of his eyes. This is called dyslexia. Reading out loud in class made his cheeks burn. He was often near the bottom of every list, and some teachers thought he simply was not trying. He was sent away to boarding school when he was eight, and he missed home very much.

But Richard's mother, Eve, was certain her son could do difficult things. One day, driving home, she stopped the car a few miles from the house. 'Find your own way back,' she said kindly, and drove off. Richard set out across the fields. He passed cows and hedges and gates, asked a farmer for directions, and arrived home hours later — tired, muddy and enormously proud.

That was his mother's lesson. Not 'be careful', but 'you can work things out'. It gave Richard something school had never given him: confidence. He discovered that he was clever in a different way. He could not spell very well, but he could listen to people, spot a good idea, and talk to almost anybody.

At sixteen he started a magazine called Student, written by young people for young people. He ran it from a basement with a borrowed telephone, ringing up famous people and asking them for interviews. Sometimes, to his amazement, they said yes. Then he began selling records by post, cheaper than the shops, and soon he opened a record shop of his own on a busy London street. The little team needed a name. 'We are complete beginners at all of this,' somebody laughed. 'We are virgins.' And that is how the name Virgin was chosen.

Years later, Richard was in the Caribbean, trying to reach another island, when his flight was cancelled. Everybody sat down to wait. Richard did not. He made a phone call and hired a whole aeroplane, borrowed a blackboard, chalked a price on it, and walked round the airport selling seats to the other stranded passengers. The plane took off full. On the way he thought: perhaps I could do this properly. A few years later he started a real airline.

Richard also loves adventure. He has raced across the Atlantic Ocean in a fast boat. He has floated over the sea in giant hot-air balloons, higher than the clouds, where the air is icy and the world below looks like a map. Not everything worked. A boat sank and balloons came down in the water. Every time, help arrived — and after a while, he tried again.

He has built companies for trains and telephones, and even one for flying to the edge of space, where the sky turns black and you can see the curve of the Earth. He also gives a great deal of his money away, to help people and to protect the sea and the air.

Richard says his dyslexia was never his weakness. It taught him to keep things simple, and to ask for help. School is not the only kind of clever. If reading feels hard for you, that does not mean your ideas are small. Be bold, be curious, and be kind.

stories.name: Tony Robbins
stories.title: The Knock at the Door
stories.hook: A stranger once brought food to a hungry family, and that single kindness changed a boy's whole life.
text: In sunny California, in the United States, a boy named Tony was growing up. His family did not have much money, and his home was not always a happy place. Tony was tall and quiet, and he wondered a great deal about people and how they feel.

One Thanksgiving, when there was almost no food in the house, somebody knocked at the door. A stranger stood there holding baskets of food for the whole family. Tony never forgot it. That one act of kindness made him believe that even strangers can care.

As a teenager, Tony worked as a cleaner, sweeping floors at night. But he read too — hundreds and hundreds of books about how people find courage when life is hard. He read faster and faster, filling his head with hopeful ideas.

Tony grew up to be a coach, standing in front of huge crowds and helping people believe in themselves again. And he never forgot that knock at the door: he has helped give millions of meals to hungry families. One small kindness can change a life — and you can pass it on.
textM: In 1960, in sunny California, in the United States, a boy named Tony was born. His family did not have much money, and his home was not always a happy place. Tony was a quiet child who watched people carefully, and who wondered a great deal about how they feel and why.

He was the eldest, so he looked after his younger brother and sister. He learned to read a room — to notice when a grown-up's voice changed, to make a joke at exactly the right moment, to keep things calm. It was a hard way to learn, but he was learning something real: that the way we feel can change, and that words can help change it.

One Thanksgiving, when Tony was eleven, there was almost no food in the house. Everyone was hungry and everyone was tense. Then somebody knocked at the door. Tony was the one who opened it. A stranger stood there holding boxes and baskets — a whole dinner for the family, enough for every single person. He said it came from someone who cared. Then he went away, and nobody ever learned his name.

Tony never forgot that knock. It taught him something he carried for the rest of his life: strangers can care about you. People you will never meet can simply decide to be kind. And if somebody out there could do that for his family, then one day he would do it for somebody else's.

Tony grew very tall very fast — nearly a head taller in a single year, so that his hands and feet felt too big and he did not always fit in. As a teenager he worked as a cleaner, sweeping floors and emptying bins at night. But he read as well: hundreds and hundreds of books about how people find courage when life is hard. He even took a course in reading quickly, so that he could read more.

At seventeen he went to hear a speaker he admired, and afterwards he asked the man for a job. He carried chairs. He handed out leaflets. He told people about the talks. And he listened to every single word. He was never the loudest person in the room; he was the one paying attention. Slowly he began to speak himself — first in small rooms, then in bigger ones, and later in halls with thousands of people in them.

Tony became a coach: someone who helps other people believe in themselves again. He asks questions. He listens. He tells people that a life can begin to change in a single moment, if you decide that it can. And all that time, he never forgot that one Thanksgiving.

So he began carrying baskets of food to families himself, saying exactly what the stranger had said: this is from someone who cares. Then he asked his friends to help, and they asked their friends. It grew, and grew, and he has now helped provide many millions of meals to hungry families around the world. That is why his story still matters tonight: one small kindness can change a whole life — and you can be the one who passes it on.

stories.name: Indra Nooyi
stories.title: The Girl Who Gave Speeches at Dinner
stories.hook: Every night at dinner her mother asked her what she would do if she led the country — and the family voted.
text: In a warm city called Madras — today it is called Chennai — in India, a girl named Indra grew up in a close and busy family. Every evening they all ate dinner together, and something rather unusual happened at the table.

Her mother would ask each daughter, 'If you were the prime minister, what would you do?' The girls had to stand up and give a speech. Then the whole family voted for the best one. Indra learned to say her big dreams out loud, without ever feeling shy.

Indra also played cricket in the street and the guitar in an all-girl rock band — something not many girls did back then. She studied very hard as well. One day she flew all the way to America with very little money in her pocket.

To pay for school, she worked at night as a receptionist while the other students slept. Years later, she became the leader of one of the biggest food companies in the world. And she did a lovely thing: she wrote thank-you letters to the parents of the people who worked with her.
textM: In a warm city beside the sea called Madras — today it is called Chennai — in India, a girl named Indra was growing up. The mornings smelled of coffee and jasmine. Crows sat along the wall and complained. In her house lived her parents, her sister, her little brother, and her grandfather, who had once been a judge and who checked everybody's homework. Outside, the street rang with bicycle bells, and the sea was never very far away.

Every evening the whole family ate dinner together, and something rather unusual happened at the table. Her mother would look at her daughters and say, 'Tonight you are the prime minister. What would you do?' Each girl had to stand up and give a speech. Then the whole family voted for the best one, and the winner was very proud indeed.

So Indra learned to say her biggest dreams out loud, without feeling shy at all. Her mother believed her daughters could grow up to lead a whole country — even though, in those days, hardly anyone expected girls to lead anything. And her grandfather taught her something else: work carefully, and never be satisfied with a half-finished answer.

Indra was not only a studious girl. She played cricket in the street with the boys, and she played the guitar in an all-girl rock band, which was almost unheard of for girls in India then. She studied physics, chemistry and mathematics, and afterwards she studied business at a famous college in Calcutta. Very often she was the only girl in a room full of boys, and she did not mind that one bit.

Then a letter arrived. A university in America called Yale had said yes. She flew across the world with one suitcase and about five hundred dollars in her pocket, and everything there was new — the cold, the food, the way people spoke. To pay for her studies she took a night job as a receptionist, from midnight until five in the morning, while the other students slept.

When it was time for job interviews, she had no money for a smart suit, so she bought a cheap one that did not fit properly. She felt awkward in it, and the interview went badly. A teacher gave her gentle advice: be yourself. So for the next interview she wore her sari, the clothes she felt at home in. That company said yes.

Years later, Indra became the leader of PepsiCo, one of the biggest food and drink companies in the world, and one of very few women anywhere doing such a job. She led it for twelve years. She asked her company to make food a little healthier, to use less water and less packaging, and to think about the future — not only about this year.

And she did one lovely thing that nobody had thought of before. She wrote thank-you letters to the mothers and fathers of the people who worked with her, to say: thank you for the gift of your child. Some parents cried when they read them. Indra still tells children the same three things: speak up, work hard, and never forget the people who helped you get there.

stories.name: David Attenborough
stories.title: The Boy With a Museum in His Bedroom
stories.hook: He filled his room with stones and feathers — then he filled the world with wonder.
text: Long ago in England, a boy named David rode his bicycle out to the old stone quarries. He came home with his pockets full of fossils, bright stones and speckled bird eggs. He laid them out neatly on his shelves and called it his own little museum.

David never stopped looking closely at things. He learned that a beetle's back can shine like a jewel, and that a snail carries its house wherever it goes. Nothing was too small for him to notice. Everything, he thought, had a story hiding inside it.

When he grew up, David travelled to every corner of the Earth with a camera. He sat with gorillas in the misty mountains. He filmed tiny insects, singing birds and whales as big as buses. And he told their stories in a soft, gentle whisper, as if the animals were sleeping nearby.

More children have met the wild animals of the world through David than through anyone who ever lived. Now, with white hair and the same kind eyes, he asks us all to protect nature. Look closely at the world, he says — and love what you find.
textM: Long ago in England, in a town called Leicester, a boy named David grew up in a big house on the edge of a university, with two brothers and a garden. He was the middle one. What he loved best was riding out alone on his bicycle to the old stone quarries, where the rock had been cut wide open.

There, if you split a stone in just the right place, you might find an ammonite — a curled shell that had been asleep inside the rock for millions of years. David came home with his pockets heavy with fossils, bright stones and speckled bird eggs. He laid them out neatly on his shelves with little labels, and called it his own museum.

He was a practical boy too. There was a pond nearby full of newts, and the university needed newts for its science lessons. David caught them and sold them for a few pennies each — and never once mentioned that the pond was only a few steps from the door.
