He walked to school barefoot along red dusty paths, and when it rained the red dust turned to red mud and squeezed up between his toes.

The best part of the day came at night. Everyone gathered around the fire, and his mother and the elders told stories in Gikuyu, their mother tongue. There were stories about clever hares and greedy ogres. There were riddles, and everyone tried to tell the story better than the last person. Ngũgĩ learned something there that he never forgot: a story is not only what happened. It is also how you tell it.

At school it was different. Children who spoke Gikuyu in the school yard were shamed and made to wear a sign around their neck, while English was praised as the language of clever people. Ngũgĩ was quick, so he learned English very well indeed. But a small question stayed with him, year after year: why should my own language, the one my mother sings in, make me feel small?

One day he came home from a long time away and found that his whole village had been moved somewhere else. Where his home had stood there was only an empty patch of ground and the smell of dust. The place of the fire stories was gone. He stood there a long while without saying anything. He kept that ache inside him, and years later it would come out on paper, in book after book.

He worked hard, went to a famous school and then to university, and while he was still a young man he wrote a novel. It was published when he was only twenty-six, and people read it all around the world. He had become a famous writer — in English. Then he made two brave choices. First he gave up the English name he had been given and took back his own: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o.

Then he made an even braver choice. He decided to write his stories in Gikuyu — because a language carries a people's songs, their jokes, their grandmothers and their memory, and because he wanted the farmers and mothers of Limuru to read him first, before anybody else in the world. He and his neighbours even built an open-air theatre in the village and performed a play together, with ordinary workers acting the parts.

That play was in his mother tongue, and because of it he was locked away for a year. Even there he kept writing. He had no notebook, so he wrote a whole novel on sheets of toilet paper. The paper there was rough and hard, which turned out to be lucky: rough paper takes ink and does not tear. Page by hidden page, the book grew — because paper is paper, and a story always finds its way out.

He came home, and he kept writing, and he kept telling anyone who would listen: no language in the world is better than another. Today, all over Africa and far beyond, children are learning to read in the languages their grandmothers speak, and teachers point to Ngũgĩ when they explain why. Your mother tongue is not something to hide. It is a treasure.

stories.name: Aesop
stories.title: The Storyteller Whose Animals Could Talk
stories.hook: The man who taught the whole world that a slow tortoise can beat a fast hare.
text: Long, long ago, in a land called Greece, there lived a man named Aesop. He was born more than two thousand five hundred years ago. He was an enslaved man, which means he was not free. Some old writers said he came from Africa. Nobody knows for certain. His life is half history, half legend.

But everyone agreed on one thing: Aesop was clever. He could answer a hard question with one tiny tale, and the whole room would laugh and nod and understand. His cleverness became so famous that he was given his freedom. Then he walked from town to town, telling his stories to anyone who would listen.

In his stories, the animals talk. A slow tortoise races a boastful hare, and while the hare stops for a nap, the tortoise plods on and on and wins. A busy ant gathers food all summer while the grasshopper only sings. A great lion lets a little mouse go free, and one day that same mouse nibbles through the ropes and sets the lion free. Real tortoises really are slow and steady, and they can live for a hundred years.

Aesop never wrote a single one of them down. People remembered them and said them out loud, mouth to mouth, for hundreds and hundreds of years. That is why tonight, so very far away, you are still hearing them. They are the oldest animal stories in the world.
textM: Long, long ago, in a land called Greece, the hills were covered in olive trees and the roads were white with dust. Little donkeys carried baskets down to the market. In that land, more than two thousand five hundred years ago, there lived a man named Aesop. He was an enslaved man, which means he was not free. He could not choose where to live or how to spend his days. Some old writers said he came from Africa. Nobody knows for certain. His life is half history, half legend.

Aesop owned almost nothing. No house. Not one coin in his pocket. But he had something nobody could ever take away from him: a head full of stories. When the people around him argued and shouted, Aesop would wait quietly until the noise dropped. Then he would say, 'Shall I tell you about a fox I once heard of?' And everyone would go still, and listen.

Everybody agreed on one thing. Aesop was clever. He could answer the hardest question with one tiny tale, and the whole room would laugh, and nod, and understand. Word of his cleverness travelled from town to town, the way good news does. And in the end he was given his freedom. Imagine that day. Imagine stepping out into the sunshine and knowing that your feet could carry you anywhere they liked.

So he walked. From village to village, from market to market, telling his stories to anyone who would listen — farmers, sailors, and children sitting in the shade. And in his stories, the animals talk. A boastful hare laughs at a slow tortoise and dares him to a race. The hare shoots ahead, so far ahead that he decides there is plenty of time for a nap. But the tortoise keeps going. Plod. Plod. Plod. When the hare wakes up, the tortoise is already at the finish line. Real tortoises really are slow and steady, and some of them live for a hundred years.

There were many more. A busy ant gathers seeds all summer long while the grasshopper only sings, and when the cold comes the ant has a full cupboard. A great lion catches a tiny mouse and then lets her go, and everyone laughs — what use is a mouse to a lion? But one day the lion is caught in a hunter's ropes, and the little mouse nibbles, and nibbles, and nibbles until he is free again.

Why animals? Because a story lets you say a true thing gently. It is very hard to tell a proud person that they are being proud. But anyone can smile at a boastful fox or a show-off crow — and then think, quietly, about themselves. That was Aesop's magic. He never told anybody off. He simply told a story, and let each person find the lesson on their own.

And here is the most surprising part. Aesop never wrote a single one of his fables down. Not one word. People just remembered them and said them out loud, mouth to mouth, parent to child, night after night, for hundreds of years. Long after Aesop was gone, other people finally gathered them up and put them into books.

The stories never stopped travelling. They crossed seas and mountains, and were retold in language after language after language. That is why tonight, so very far away from Greece, you are hearing them too. They are the oldest animal stories in the world, and they still teach the same gentle things they always did. Slow and steady wins the race. And even the smallest friend can turn out to be the biggest help of all.

stories.name: Jean de La Fontaine
stories.title: The Boy Who Made Fables Sing
stories.hook: A dreamy boy from the woods who made Aesop's animals sing in French.
text: In France, a long time ago, a boy named Jean de La Fontaine was born in a small town beside a great forest. He was supposed to sit still and study his books. Instead he wandered under the tall trees, watching birds and listening to the wind. The grown-ups shook their heads and called him a dreamer.

But all that dreaming turned out to be useful. Jean watched real animals very closely: the way a fox tilts its head to listen, the way ants hurry along in a busy line, the way a crow shines blue-black in the sunshine. He remembered every small, true detail.

Then he took Aesop's old animal tales and turned them into poems in French, so lovely that they sound like songs. In 'Le Corbeau et le Renard', a crow sits high in a tree with a fine piece of cheese in his beak. The fox below says, 'Oh, what beautiful feathers! Surely you sing beautifully too?' The proud crow opens his mouth to sing, and the cheese drops straight down to the waiting fox. Real foxes truly are clever: they can hear a mouse moving under the snow.
Children in France still learn his poems by heart, hundreds of years later. Jean de La Fontaine gave Aesop's animals a new voice. He made animal wisdom sing.
textM: In France, a long time ago, a boy named Jean de La Fontaine was born in a small town called Château-Thierry, right beside a great forest. The trees began almost at the end of his street. His father's job was to look after those woods — the trees, the streams, the deer — so the forest was almost part of the family.

Jean was supposed to sit still and study serious books. He tried being a lawyer. He tried a few other things too. But he kept slipping away under the tall trees, watching birds and listening to the wind move through the leaves. The grown-ups shook their heads and called him a dreamer. He was not lazy at all. He was simply looking at the wrong things, as far as the grown-ups could tell.

All that dreaming turned out to be useful. Jean watched real animals very closely. He noticed the way a fox tilts its head to listen. The way ants hurry along in a busy line, each one carrying something. The way a crow shines blue-black when the sun catches its feathers. And he noticed that animals have habits, just as people do: the greedy ones, the careful ones, the ones who cannot resist showing off.

Then he had a wonderful idea. There were very old animal tales, told long ago by a storyteller called Aesop. Jean took those tales and turned them into poems in French — poems with rhythm and rhyme, so lovely that when you say them out loud they sound like little songs. It took him years and years. In the end he wrote more than two hundred of them, gathered together into twelve small books.

In 'The Crow and the Fox', a crow sits high in a tree with a fine piece of cheese in his beak. The fox below looks up and says, 'Oh, what beautiful feathers! Surely you sing beautifully too?' You can almost hear the fox smiling as he speaks. The proud crow opens his mouth to sing — and the cheese drops straight down to the waiting fox. The fox trots away with his supper, and the poem says the crow promised himself, a little too late, that he would never be caught like that again.

Real foxes truly are that clever. A fox can hear a mouse moving about under the snow, and leap high in the air to land right on top of it. Ants really do carry crumbs many times bigger than themselves. Jean knew small true things like that, and it is why his animals still feel so alive on the page, hundreds of years after he put down his pen.

He wrote about the hare who ran too fast and lost the race to a slow, steady tortoise. He wrote about the cicada who sang all summer while the ant quietly put food away. Each poem ends with a small idea you can carry about in your pocket. And the fable never scolds you. It simply lets you watch, and smile, and think for yourself.

Children in France still learn his poems by heart, hundreds of years later, and stand up in class to say them. Grown-ups remember them too, which means a whole country shares the same animals in its memory. Jean de La Fontaine gave Aesop's animals a brand-new voice. He made animal wisdom sing.

stories.name: Anna Sewell
stories.title: The Horse Who Told His Own Story
stories.hook: She let a horse tell his own life story, and the whole world listened.
text: Anna Sewell was born in England, in a house near the sea. When she was fourteen, she ran home in the rain, slipped, and hurt both her ankles badly. They never healed properly. After that day, she could not walk very far at all.

So Anna went everywhere by horse. She drove her own little pony carriage, and she learned to guide her pony with her voice alone, hardly touching the reins. She could tell when a horse was tired, or worried, or happy. Horses became her closest friends in the world.

But out on the roads she saw sad things: drivers whipping worn-out horses, and a hard strap called the bearing rein that forced a horse's head high until its neck ached. So Anna wrote a book called 'Black Beauty', and she let the horse tell it himself, in his own voice. Black Beauty remembers his mother's gentle advice, the green meadow where he was a foal, the kind hands and the unkind ones. Real horses do remember: they know a kind voice for years and years.

Anna wrote it lying on a couch, very ill, and she left us only a few months after the book appeared. She never knew it became one of the best-loved books ever written, or that it changed the law and made people gentler to horses everywhere.
textM: Anna Sewell was born in 1820 in a little town beside the sea in England, where the wind smelled of salt and the fishing boats came in at dawn. Her family were Quakers — quiet, kind people who believed in being gentle to every living thing. Her mother wrote stories for children and taught Anna at home, and the two of them were the very best of friends. Anna loved being outdoors, and as a girl she could walk for miles.

When Anna was fourteen, she stayed late at school and hurried home through the rain. She slipped on the wet path and hurt both her ankles badly. They never healed properly. After that day she could not walk far at all, and for the rest of her life she needed a stick, or a helping arm, or a carriage.

So Anna went everywhere by horse. She drove her own little pony chaise, taking her father to the station every morning and fetching him home every evening. She learned to guide her pony with her voice alone — a click, a word, a soft 'steady now' — hardly touching the reins, and never, ever using a whip. She could tell just by looking whether a horse was tired, or worried, or happy.

Horses became her closest friends. She would stop the carriage to say hello to a horse she did not even know, the way you might greet a neighbour's dog. But out on the roads she saw sad things too: drivers whipping worn-out horses up steep hills, and a hard strap called the bearing rein, which forced a horse's head high and stiff until its neck ached. Anna never spoke roughly to any animal, and she hoped nobody else would either. Sometimes she stopped her carriage and told a driver, very politely, that his horse had had enough for one day.

By then Anna was often too ill to leave the house. So she lay on the sofa by the window and began to write a book. On some days she wrote in pencil on scraps of paper; on days when even that was too tiring, she said the words aloud and her mother wrote them down for her. It took her six years.

The book was called 'Black Beauty', and Anna did something nobody had done before: she let the horse tell his own story, in his own voice. Black Beauty remembers the green meadow where he was a foal, and his mother's gentle advice, and the kind hands, and the unkind ones. Real horses do remember. They know a kind voice for years and years. The whole book is told as if the horse is looking back at the end of a long life, quietly, from a warm stable full of straw.

A publisher bought the book for twenty pounds — not very much, even then. It came out in the winter, and Anna left us only a few months later. She never knew what happened next. She never knew that it sold in the millions, in dozens of languages, and that it is still being read tonight, somewhere, by someone your age.

And she never knew that the people who read it began to change their minds. The bearing rein went out of use. New laws were made to protect working animals. One quiet woman, lying on a sofa, made the whole world gentler towards horses — simply by asking us to imagine what it feels like to be somebody else. That is what a story can do: it lends you another's eyes for a little while.

stories.name: Beatrix Potter
stories.title: The Girl and the Four Little Rabbits
stories.hook: A quiet girl with a secret zoo upstairs who wrote about four little rabbits.
text: Beatrix Potter grew up in a big, quiet house in London. She did not go to school. She learned at home, upstairs in the nursery. And up there she kept a secret little zoo: rabbits, mice, a hedgehog, frogs, and even a bat. Her pet rabbit Peter wore a small lead and went for walks with her.

Beatrix drew them all, again and again, for hours and hours. She learned exactly how a rabbit's ear folds over, and how a mouse holds a crumb in both little paws. She also loved mushrooms and studied how they grow, painting hundreds of them. She was a real scientist, though in those days very few grown-ups would listen to a woman.

One day she wrote a letter to a little boy who was ill. 'I shall tell you a story about four little rabbits, whose names were Flopsy, Mopsy, Cottontail and Peter,' she began, and she drew pictures all along the edges. That letter became 'The Tale of Peter Rabbit', about a naughty rabbit who squeezes under a garden gate, loses his little blue jacket, and hurries home to his mother for a cup of warm herb tea.

With the money her books earned, Beatrix bought farms and hills and flocks of sheep, and she gave the land away so that it would stay green forever. Her animals still feel alive on the page, because she truly knew them.
textM: Beatrix Potter was born in 1866 and grew up in a big, quiet house in London. It was the sort of house where the clocks ticked loudly and grown-ups spoke softly. She did not go to school. She learned at home, right at the top of the house, in the nursery, with a governess and a great many books. She was often alone up there. But she was almost never lonely.

Because up in that nursery Beatrix kept a secret little zoo. There were rabbits, mice, a hedgehog, frogs, newts, and even a bat. Her rabbit Peter went for walks on a small lead, and she taught him to jump through a hoop and to ring a little bell. When the family travelled, Peter travelled too, in a basket. Nobody minded very much, so long as everything stayed upstairs.

Beatrix drew her animals again and again, for hours and hours, until she knew them by heart. She learned exactly how a rabbit's ear folds over when it listens. She learned how a mouse holds a crumb in both little paws, sitting up very straight. She learned the way a hedgehog's spines lie down flat when it is comfortable. Nothing in her pictures is guessed. She had watched it all.

Every summer the family left the grey city for the hills of Scotland or the Lake District. Beatrix would step off the train into air that smelled of rain and grass, and she was so happy she could hardly speak. She collected beetles, fossils, feathers and leaves, and filled her sketchbooks all summer long.

She also loved mushrooms. Most people walked straight past them. Beatrix knelt down. She painted hundreds of them, so carefully that scientists still use her pictures today, and she looked at their tiny dust-fine spores under a microscope to work out how new mushrooms begin. She even wrote a scientific paper about it. But in those days women were not allowed into the learned society's meeting room, so a man had to read her paper aloud for her while she waited outside.

One September, Beatrix sat down to write a letter to a little boy called Noel, who was ill in bed and needed cheering up. She could not think of any news. So she wrote: "I shall tell you a story about four little rabbits, whose names were Flopsy, Mopsy, Cottontail and Peter." Then she drew pictures all along the edges of the page.

That letter became 'The Tale of Peter Rabbit' — the story of a naughty rabbit who squeezes under a garden gate, loses his little blue jacket, and hurries home to his mother for a cup of warm herb tea. At first, publisher after publisher said no. So Beatrix printed the book herself, a small pile of copies, to give to friends. Then a publisher changed his mind, and children everywhere fell in love with Peter.

With the money her books earned, Beatrix bought a farm among the hills, and then more farms, and hills, and flocks of tough grey sheep. She became a real farmer and won prizes at country shows. And when she was old she gave the land away, thousands of acres of it, so that it would stay green and open for children she would never meet. You can walk there today. And her animals still feel alive on the page, because she truly knew them.

stories.name: Jean-Henri Fabre
stories.title: The Man Who Listened to Insects
stories.hook: He lay in the grass for years and turned tiny insects into heroes.
text: Jean-Henri Fabre was born in a poor farming village in the south of France. There were no toys, so the fields became his playground. He would lie in the grass for hours, his nose close to the ground, watching tiny things move. Once, as a very small boy, he shut his eyes and then his mouth, trying to work out which one he saw the sun with.

He grew up and became a teacher, and he studied insects in a brand-new way. Other scientists pinned dead insects inside boxes. Fabre watched living ones instead, for years and years, in his own stony little garden. He gave that garden a name: the harmas.

And what he saw there! A dung beetle rolling a ball bigger than himself, walking backwards, pushing with his strong back legs all the way home. A hunting wasp digging a neat burrow in the sand. A cicada singing in the hot afternoon; he has tiny drums in his sides, and he can sing loudly enough to fill a whole valley. Fabre wrote about them so warmly that people called him 'the insect's Homer'.

Fabre showed us something simple and wonderful: watch one small creature long enough, and it becomes a whole world. So the next time an ant crosses your path, stop. Look closely. There is a story there.
textM: Jean-Henri Fabre was born in a poor farming village in the south of France, where the houses were made of grey stone and the hills smelled of thyme. His family had almost nothing, so when he was very small he was sent to live with his grandparents on their farm. There were no toys there. Instead there were ducks and calves, a big fire in the evening, and fields that went on forever. The fields became his playground.

He would lie in the grass for hours, his nose close to the ground, watching tiny things move. Once, as a very small boy, he shut his eyes and then his mouth, trying to work out which one he saw the sun with. He filled his pockets with beetles and snail shells, and came home late, and got into gentle trouble for it.

Growing up was hard. The family moved from town to town looking for work, and for a while young Henri had to leave school. He sold lemons at a busy fair and worked on a railway line, sleeping under the stars and spending his few coins on books. Then he won a place at a college for teachers, and at nineteen he stood in front of his very first class. He taught himself mathematics at night, by candlelight, one chapter ahead of his pupils.

One day he read a small book about a wasp that hunts beetles, and something inside him lit up like a lamp. He became a teacher who studied insects in a brand-new way. Other scientists pinned dead insects inside boxes and gave them long Latin names. Fabre watched living ones instead, for years and years, on his knees, with a notebook.

For most of his life he was poor, and he wrote simple school books to feed his children. But at last, when he was fifty-five, he bought a stony scrap of land at Sérignan — too rocky to farm, full of thistles and wasps and warm flat stones. To everyone else it was waste ground. To Fabre it was heaven. He gave that garden a name: the harmas, and he never needed to go anywhere else again.

And what he saw there! A dung beetle rolling a ball bigger than himself, walking backwards, pushing with his strong back legs all the way home. A hunting wasp digging a neat burrow in the sand, then finding her own doorway again among a hundred others. A cicada singing in the hot afternoon; he has tiny drums in his sides, and he can sing loudly enough to fill a whole valley.

Fabre loved to ask a question and then find a way to answer it. Do cicadas hear their own song? He borrowed the village cannon and let it off beneath the tree — bang! — and the cicadas sang on without missing a note. He put a line of little processionary caterpillars around the rim of a flowerpot, each following the silk thread of the one in front, and they walked round and round for days. And on warm nights, great peacock moths came flying through his open window from far across the fields, dozens of them, to visit one single moth in a cage.

He wrote it all down in ten books, so warmly that people called him 'the Homer of insects'. He stayed poor for a long time, until at last, when he was very old, friends and admirers came from all over the world to thank him. Fabre showed us something simple and wonderful: watch one small creature long enough, and it becomes a whole world. So the next time an ant crosses your path, stop. Look closely. There is a story there.

stories.name: E. B. White
stories.title: The Spider Who Could Write
stories.hook: He was too shy to speak in front of people — so he spoke to animals instead.
text: Long ago, in a big house in New York, lived a quiet boy named Elwyn. He was so shy that standing up to speak made his knees shake. But behind the house was a stable, warm and full of hay, and there he was never afraid. He talked to the horses. He watched the mice. Animals never asked him to make a speech.

When he grew up, he bought a farm by the sea in Maine. He kept geese who honked at the gate, sheep with soft grey wool, and pigs in the barn. One morning he stopped in the barn doorway and saw a grey spider spinning something round and silky — an egg sac, full of hundreds of tiny babies waiting to hatch. He stood and watched for a very long time.

Then a small runty piglet came to his farm, and he wished with all his heart that someone could save it. So he wrote a story. In 'Charlotte's Web', a little pig named Wilbur is in trouble — until a clever grey spider called Charlotte spins words right into her web. 'SOME PIG,' she writes. 'TERRIFIC.' Everyone comes to look, and nobody can bear to lose a pig so famous. E. B. White studied real spiders carefully, so Charlotte would spin and climb exactly as a true spider does.

At the end, Charlotte grows old and tired, the way spiders do. But her babies hatch and float into the barn on tiny silk threads, and some of them stay with Wilbur forever. That is why children still read the book today: it says that a friend can change your whole life, and that the smallest creature in the barn — a spider in a corner — may be the most wonderful of all.
textM: Long ago, in a big house in a town called Mount Vernon, near New York, lived a quiet boy named Elwyn. He had six brothers and sisters and a piano in the parlour, but what he loved best was the stable behind the house. It was warm there, and dim, and it smelled of hay and horses. He talked to the horses. He watched the mice run along the beams. Elwyn was so shy that standing up to speak in class made his knees shake — but animals never asked him to make a speech.

He was afraid of a great many things, and he wrote about them in a diary, and then he discovered something useful: writing made the fear smaller. When he grew up he wrote for a magazine in New York, and everyone said his sentences were as clear as pond water. But the city was noisy, and he kept dreaming of barns.

So he bought a farm by the sea in Maine. He kept geese who honked at the gate, sheep with soft grey wool, and pigs in the barn. He had a dachshund named Fred who followed him everywhere and disagreed with everything. Every evening he carried a pail down to the pigpen and stood there while the pig ate, thinking.

One autumn a pig on his farm fell ill, and though he sat up with it and did everything he could, he could not save it. It made him very sad. He kept thinking the same thought over and over: if only somebody had been able to save that pig.

Then one day, in the doorway of the barn, he saw a grey spider spinning something round and silky — an egg sac, full of hundreds of tiny babies waiting to hatch. He stood and watched for a very long time. When it was time to go back to the city, he cut the sac down, put it in a box, and took it with him. Weeks later hundreds of tiny spiders came out of it in his bedroom and spun their threads across his hairbrush and his mirror. He was delighted.

He read books about real spiders until he knew exactly how they spin and climb and hunt. And then he wrote 'Charlotte's Web'. In it, a small pig named Wilbur is in trouble, until a clever grey spider called Charlotte writes words right into her web above his pen. 'SOME PIG,' the web says one morning. Later: 'TERRIFIC.' 'RADIANT.' 'HUMBLE.' People come from miles around to see it, and nobody can bear to lose a pig so famous.

At the end, Charlotte grows old and tired, the way spiders do, and her babies hatch and float into the barn on tiny silk threads. Three of them stay with Wilbur forever. Years later, when E. B. White read the story aloud so it could be recorded, he reached that part and his voice trembled, and he had to start again, and again, and again. He had written it himself, and it still moved him.

That is why children all over the world still read the book today. It says that a friend can change your whole life; that being small is not the same as being unimportant; and that the most wonderful creature in the barn might be a quiet grey spider in a corner, whom nobody had bothered to notice.

stories.name: Birago Diop
stories.title: The Doctor Who Kept the Stories
stories.hook: He saved a thousand animal tales by writing down what the old storytellers said.
text: In Ouakam, a village near Dakar in Senegal, a boy named Birago sat close to his grandmother after the evening meal. The plates were cleared, the night was warm, and the stories began. Sometimes a griot came — a storyteller whose job is to remember everything a people knows, and to say it out loud so nobody forgets.

Birago grew up and became a veterinary doctor, a doctor for animals. He travelled all across West Africa, caring for cattle with long curved horns, for goats and sheep and donkeys. And in every village where he stopped, he did one more thing: he listened. He asked the old people for their tales, and he wrote them down in his notebook before they could be forgotten.

Then he made them into a book, 'Les Contes d'Amadou Koumba', named after the griot who taught him most. Inside live Leuk the hare, so clever he can trick anyone, and Bouki the hyena, so greedy he always wants the biggest share and always ends up with nothing. The animals argue and boast and share and forgive — and if you listen closely, they are really telling you about people, and about you.

Birago also wrote a beautiful poem saying that those we love who have died are not truly gone: they are in the rustling tree, in the running water, in the wind on your face. He is remembered because he saved Africa's animal stories on paper, and showed the whole world that they are every bit as wise and as funny as any fable ever told.
textM: Long ago, in Ouakam — a fishing village of white sand and low houses just outside Dakar, in Senegal — there lived a boy named Birago Diop. He was born in 1906, when evenings were lit by oil lamps and the loudest sound at night was the sea. After the evening meal the plates were cleared away, the mats were spread out, and the children pressed close to their grandmother. That was when the best part of the day began. That was when the stories started.

Sometimes a very special visitor came: a griot. A griot is a storyteller and a rememberer. In West Africa, a griot's job is to hold everything a people knows — the names, the songs, the old jokes, the wise sayings — and to say it all out loud so that nobody forgets. The griot Birago loved best was called Amadou Koumba. When Amadou Koumba spoke, he changed his voice for every animal, and even the fire seemed to lean in and listen.

Birago grew up, and he was very good at school. He read every book he could find. As a young man he sailed all the way to France, to a city called Toulouse, to learn something surprising: how to be a doctor for animals. It was cold there, far from the sea he knew, and he missed his mother's cooking. But he studied hard, and one day he came home a real veterinary doctor.

Then began the years of travelling. Birago went out across West Africa — through the land we now call Mali, through Ivory Coast and Mauritania — along roads of red dust, caring for animals in places that had no other doctor. He treated cattle with long curving horns, and goats, and sheep, and donkeys, and horses. He touched their noses, listened to their breathing, and gave medicine to whole herds while the herders stood watching with folded arms, hoping.

And in every village where he stopped, he did one more thing. In the evening, when the work was finished, he sat down beside the oldest people and asked them politely: “Grandmother, grandfather — will you tell me a story?” Then, by lamplight, he wrote down what they said in his notebook. He was in a hurry, because the old storytellers were growing older, and when a storyteller goes without ever being listened to, the tales go too.

In 1947 he turned his notebooks into a book: 'Les Contes d'Amadou Koumba' — 'The Tales of Amadou Koumba' — named after the griot who had taught him most. Inside live Leuk the hare, so clever he can talk his way out of anything, and Bouki the hyena, so greedy that he always demands the biggest share and always ends up with nothing at all. The animals boast and argue and share and forgive. And if you listen closely, you notice that they are really telling you about people. About you.

Birago also wrote a poem called 'Breaths'. In it he says that those we love who have died are not truly gone. They are in the tree that rustles, in the water that runs, in the fire that crackles, in the wind that touches your face. Listen more often to things than to beings, the poem says. Grown-ups all over the world still read it aloud when they are missing somebody.

Later Birago became Senegal's first ambassador to another country, Tunisia — the boy from Ouakam, carrying his country's greetings. But what he is loved for is the listening. He saved hundreds of African animal tales by writing them down, and showed the whole world that they are every bit as wise, as funny and as beautiful as any fable told anywhere. Tonight, somewhere, a child is laughing at Bouki the hyena — because a young doctor once took out his notebook and said, “Please, tell me again.”

stories.name: Joy Adamson
stories.title: Elsa, the Lioness Who Went Free
stories.hook: She loved a lion cub so much that she taught her to live without her.
text: Joy was born far away in Austria, in a land of snow and pine trees. Then she came to Kenya, and she never wanted to leave. She carried her paints everywhere, sitting quietly for hours to paint the faces of Kenya's peoples and the wild flowers that grow in the red soil. Her husband George was a game warden, whose work was looking after wild animals.

One day three lion cubs with no mother came into their care. Two were sent to a zoo far away, but the smallest, softest one stayed. They called her Elsa. Elsa slept on their beds, rode in their car with her chin on the window, and chased Joy's shoelaces across the floor. She purred like a very large cat.

But Joy believed a wild animal belongs in the wild. So she did the hardest, most loving thing. For months she took Elsa out into the bush and taught her, slowly, how to be a real lioness — how to walk softly, how to hunt, how to sleep in the shade of a thorn tree. Elsa was the first lioness raised by people ever to live free again. And one wonderful day she came padding back through the grass, bringing her own cubs to show them. Joy wrote her story in a book called 'Born Free'.

Joy's own life ended sadly in Kenya in 1980, and many people cried for her. But what she began did not stop. Because of Elsa, people all over the world began to see lions differently — not as things to keep, but as families with names and hearts. Joy taught us that real love sometimes means opening your hands and letting something run free.
textM: Joy was born in 1910, far away in Europe, in a house surrounded by snow and dark pine trees. She was a girl who could not sit still: she played the piano, learned to sew, and drew everything she saw. Then, when she was twenty-seven, she sailed to Kenya — and the moment she saw the red earth, the flat-topped thorn trees and the enormous sky, she knew she would never want to leave.

Joy carried her paints everywhere. She would sit perfectly still for hours — sometimes for days — painting the faces of Kenya's peoples in their beads and bright cloth, so that every pattern would be remembered exactly as it was. She painted the wild flowers too, hundreds of them, each petal just so. Many of those pictures still hang in a museum in Nairobi, waiting for you to come and look at them.

Her husband George was a game warden. His work was looking after wild animals, so they lived in tents and camps out in the bush, with lamps at night and the sound of hyenas laughing somewhere far away. Then one day, three lion cubs with no mother came into their care — small spotty things that blinked and squeaked and fitted into two cupped hands. Two were sent to a zoo far away. The smallest and softest one stayed. They called her Elsa.

Elsa grew up believing she was part of the family. She slept on their beds. She rode in the car with her chin on the window and her ears in the wind. She galloped after Joy's shoelaces, splashed about in the river, and rolled onto her back to have her tummy rubbed. She purred — a huge rumbling purr, like a very large cat with a very large engine. And every month she grew heavier, and stronger, and more beautiful.

But Joy believed something that made her heart ache: a wild animal belongs in the wild. So she and George did the hardest, most loving thing anyone had ever tried. Month after month they took Elsa out into the bush and taught her, slowly and patiently, how to be a real lioness. How to walk without a sound. How to find water. How to hunt her own food. How to sleep through the hot hours in the shade of a thorn tree. Sometimes Elsa was hungry and did not understand, and Joy had to turn her face away so she would not give in.

Then came the day they had to leave her out there. They drove away without looking back, and it was the loneliest drive of their lives. But Elsa managed it. She was the first lioness raised by people ever to live truly free again — hunting for herself, sleeping under the stars, belonging to nobody.

And then, one wonderful morning, the long grass moved. Out came Elsa, padding softly, and behind her, tumbling over their own fat paws, came three cubs of her own. She had brought them to be shown, the way any mother would. Joy wrote the whole story in a book called 'Born Free'. It was read in dozens of languages and made into a film, and children all over the world learned Elsa's name.

Joy's own life ended sadly in Kenya in 1980, and very many people cried for her. But what she began did not stop. Because of Elsa, people everywhere began to see lions differently — not as things to be kept, but as families, with names and hearts and cubs to teach. The money from her books still helps to protect wild animals today. And Joy left us one quiet lesson for bedtime: real love sometimes means opening your hands and letting the thing you love run free.

stories.name: Gerald Durrell
stories.title: The Boy With a Net and a Jar
stories.hook: He kept scorpions in matchboxes — and grew up to save animals from disappearing.
text: When Gerald was a small boy, his family packed up and moved to Corfu, a sunny Greek island in a very blue sea. Instead of sitting in an ordinary classroom, he spent five whole years outdoors with a net in one hand and a jam jar in the other, and a kind tutor who let him study animals all day long.

The house filled up with creatures. Tortoises walked slowly across the floor. An owl blinked from the top of a cupboard. Geckos with sticky toes ran up the walls at night. And once — just once — a mother scorpion he had hidden in a matchbox opened her box right at the dinner table, and all her tiny babies went marching over the tablecloth. His family shouted. Gerald thought it was wonderful. Years later he wrote it all down in a very funny book called 'My Family and Other Animals'.

When he grew up, Gerald had a new idea. He built a zoo on the island of Jersey, but not a zoo for showing animals off. His zoo was a safe nursery for the rarest animals in the world — the ones so few that they might vanish altogether. There they could have babies in peace, and then be carried back home to their own forests and islands.

It worked. The pink pigeon of Mauritius, soft and rosy, was down to a handful of birds — and today it flies wild again. The golden lion tamarin, a little monkey with a mane like a tiny lion made of sunshine, was saved the same way. Gerald used his funny stories to pay for serious work. He showed that if you love animals enough to laugh with them, you will fight to keep them.
textM: Gerald was born in India in 1925, the youngest of four children, and everybody called him Gerry. When he was still very small his family moved to England, where the sky was grey and the rain tapped on the windows. Then, when Gerry was ten, his mother made a wonderful decision. The family packed everything up and sailed away to Corfu, a sunny Greek island in a very blue sea.

For a boy who loved animals, it was paradise. Instead of sitting in an ordinary classroom, Gerry spent five whole years outdoors with a net in one hand and a jam jar in the other. He had a dog called Roger who followed him everywhere. Olive trees, hot white stones, the smell of the sea — and under every rock, something alive. He learned to swim long before he learned his times tables, and he came home each evening brown as a nut, with his pockets full of shells.

A kind Greek doctor named Theodore became his teacher and his friend. Theodore seemed to know the name of everything. One day he showed Gerry a single drop of pond water under a microscope, and inside that one drop a whole city of tiny creatures was swimming about. Gerry never forgot it: a whole world hiding in a drop of water no bigger than a tear.

The house filled up with creatures. Tortoises walked slowly across the floor. An owl blinked from the top of a cupboard. Geckos with sticky toes ran up the walls at night. And once — just once — a mother scorpion that Gerry had hidden in a matchbox opened her box right at the dinner table, and all her tiny babies went marching over the tablecloth. His family shouted and jumped up from their chairs. Gerry thought it was wonderful.

Years later he wrote it all down in a very funny book called 'My Family and Other Animals', and people laughed until they cried. But Gerald had a serious plan too. He had seen that some animals were growing rarer and rarer, until only a handful were left anywhere in the whole world.

So he built a zoo on the island of Jersey — but not a zoo for showing animals off. His was a safe nursery for the rarest creatures on Earth. There they could have babies in peace, be counted and cared for, and then be carried home again to their own forests and islands. He had to work out everything himself: what each animal ate, how it liked to sleep, what made it settled enough to raise a family. People told him it would never work.

It worked. The pink pigeon of Mauritius, soft and rosy as the inside of a shell, was down to about ten birds in all the world — and today it flies wild again in its own trees. The golden lion tamarin, a little monkey with a mane like a tiny lion made of sunshine, was saved in the same patient way.

Gerald used his funny stories to pay for very serious work, and the place he started is still saving animals today. He showed us something simple and true: if you love animals enough to laugh with them, you will fight to keep them. Every creature that is still here because of him began with a boy, a net and a jam jar.

stories.name: E. O. Wilson
stories.title: The Ant Man
stories.hook: He couldn't watch the birds up high — so he looked down, and found a whole world.
text: In Alabama, in the warm American south, there was a boy called Edward who loved being outdoors more than anything. When he was seven, an accident while fishing left him seeing well with only one eye. Birds high in the treetops became hard to follow. So Edward did something clever: he looked down instead, close up, at the small busy things right by his feet.

And there they were. Ants. Thousands of them, hurrying along their little roads. He watched them for hours, and he never stopped — people called him 'the ant man' for the rest of his life. He discovered something amazing: ants talk to each other with smells. They lay invisible trails of scent called pheromones, and that is how a line of ants finds its way straight to a crumb on your kitchen floor.

His favourites were the leafcutter ants. They march home in long lines carrying snipped pieces of green leaf above their heads, like tiny flags in a parade. But here is the surprise — they do not eat the leaves at all! They chew them into a soft mulch to grow a special fungus garden deep underground, and they eat the garden. Their nests can be as big as a room, with nurseries for the babies, tidy rubbish rooms, and millions of sisters all working together.

Edward gave the world a word we all use now: biodiversity — all the different living things sharing one Earth. He asked us to keep half the planet wild, so the beetles and frogs and ants would always have a home. And he liked to say that ants and worms and bees are 'the little things that run the world.' Next time you see one ant crossing a path, stop and look. You are watching a farmer going home.
textM: In Alabama, in the warm American south, there was a boy called Edward. He was born in 1929, in a place of pine woods and red dust, where the evenings hummed with insects and the air smelled of rain and warm earth. Edward loved being outdoors more than anything else in the world. He kept jars and boxes and notebooks, and he was always coming home with something small and alive in his pocket.

When he was seven, something happened while he was fishing. A fish flicked, and a sharp fin spine hurt one of his eyes. Afterwards, Edward could see well with only one eye. Birds high up in the treetops became hard to follow, and he had loved watching birds. It could have been the end of his adventures. Instead, he noticed something surprising: close up, his good eye was extraordinarily sharp. He could see the tiny hairs on the leg of a beetle.

So Edward did something clever. He stopped looking up, and he looked down — right down, at the small busy world by his feet. And there they were. Ants. Thousands of them, hurrying along their little roads, carrying seeds and crumbs and each other. He lay on the ground and watched them for hours. He never really stopped. People called him “the ant man” for the rest of his life.

When he was thirteen, Edward went exploring near the docks in Mobile and found a kind of ant nobody in his country had seen before. It had arrived from far away on a ship. A boy with a notebook had made a real discovery, and grown-up scientists listened to him.

Later he discovered something truly amazing: ants talk to each other with smells. He worked out exactly which tiny part of an ant's body makes the message. Then he did a wonderful experiment — he drew an invisible line on a glass plate with a smear of that scent, and a whole crowd of ants marched carefully along the line he had drawn. Scientists call these scent-messages pheromones, and that is how a line of ants finds its way straight to a crumb on your kitchen floor.

His favourites of all were the leafcutter ants. They march home in long lines carrying snipped pieces of green leaf above their heads, like tiny flags in a parade. But here is the surprise — they do not eat the leaves at all! They chew them into a soft mulch to grow a special fungus garden deep underground, and it is the garden they eat. They are farmers, and they were farming millions of years before people were.

Their nests can be as big as a room, with nurseries for the babies, tidy rubbish rooms far from the food, tunnels for fresh air, and millions of sisters all working together. Edward spent his life writing down what he saw, and he wrote so beautifully about ants that his books won some of the biggest prizes in the world. He named hundreds of new kinds of ants, and he was still learning about them when he was ninety.

Edward carried a word around the world until we all knew it: biodiversity — all the different living things sharing one Earth. He asked us to keep half the planet wild, so that the beetles and frogs and ants would always have a home. And he liked to say that ants and worms and bees are “the little things that run the world.” They mix the soil, carry the seeds, and clean up the forest floor, quietly, every day. So next time you see one ant crossing a path, stop and look. You are watching a farmer going home.

stories.name: Imhotep
stories.title: The Boy Who Built With Stone
stories.hook: Long, long ago in Egypt, an ordinary boy grew up to build the very first great house of stone.
text: A very long time ago, longer ago than almost any story you know, a boy was born in Egypt. His family were not kings or queens. They were ordinary people who lived by the wide green river called the Nile, where boats slid past and birds waded in the reeds.

His name was Imhotep, and he was a noticer. He watched how mud dried in the sun. He watched how builders stacked bricks. He asked questions all day long, and he listened very carefully to the answers. Because he was so clever and so kind, the pharaoh asked him to become his closest helper.

Then Imhotep had a big idea. Everyone built with soft mud bricks that crumbled away. What if a building were made of stone, so it could stand for ever? He drew his plan, and workers cut and lifted great blocks into six huge steps rising into the sky. It was the Step Pyramid, and no one had ever seen anything like it.

Imhotep helped people in another way too. When someone felt poorly, he did not sing spells. He looked, he asked gentle questions, and he wrote down everything he learned so others could learn it too. Long after he was gone, Egyptians still called him the wise teacher of healing. A boy with no crown showed the world how to build, and how to care.

stories.name: Cai Lun
stories.title: The Man Who Made Paper
stories.hook: Before him, one book could weigh as much as a small child.
text: Long ago in China, a boy named Cai Lun grew up and went to work in the emperor's palace. There were red pillars, quiet courtyards, and clerks bent over their writing all day long.

But writing was hard work back then. People wrote on strips of bamboo tied together with string. One single book was so heavy that a grown-up had to carry it in both arms. Rich people wrote on smooth silk instead, but silk cost far too much for ordinary families.

Cai Lun watched and wondered. Then he began to try things. He soaked tree bark, old rags, hemp and worn-out fishing nets in water. He pounded them into a soft, sloppy pulp, spread it thin and even on a screen, and left it to dry in the warm sun. When he peeled it off, it was light and smooth and pale.

He had made paper. Suddenly anyone could write, draw, and send letters far away. Every storybook, every picture you colour, every note you fold and give to a friend began with a patient man by a bucket of pulp, asking, 'What if there were a better way?'

stories.name: Zhang Heng
stories.title: The Dragons That Listened to the Earth
stories.hook: He built eight bronze dragons that could tell him when the ground shook far, far away.
text: In old China, there lived a man named Zhang Heng who loved three things: poems, machines, and the night sky. On clear evenings he counted stars from the palace roof, and he mapped two thousand five hundred of them, one careful dot at a time.

Sometimes the ground would shake in a faraway village. In the capital, nobody knew where it had happened, so nobody knew where to send help. Zhang Heng thought about this for a long time, the way you think about a puzzle before you solve it.

So he made something beautiful. A great bronze jar, ringed with eight dragons. Each dragon held a little ball in its mouth, and below each one sat a bronze toad with its mouth wide open. When the earth trembled somewhere far off, one dragon let its ball drop — clang! — into the toad below, pointing the way.

People laughed and said it could not work. Then one day a ball fell, though nobody in the city had felt a thing. Days later a messenger came galloping from far away with news of a quake. The dragons had been right. It was the world's first seismoscope, and it showed that patient watching can turn something invisible into something you can hear.

stories.name: Aryabhata
stories.title: The Young Man Who Knew the Earth Was Spinning
stories.hook: At twenty-three he wrote a book of stars and numbers — in poems, so students could sing them by heart.
text: In India, long ago, a boy named Aryabhata loved numbers the way some children love songs. He studied by lamplight, and at night he stepped outside to watch the stars turning slowly above the warm dark rooftops.

When he was only twenty-three — still a young man — he wrote a great book. He wrote it in verse, like poetry, so that students could learn it by heart and carry it everywhere without any bag. In it he worked with zero and place value: the reason we can write 5, and 50, and 500 using the same small round symbol.

Then he said something surprising. Everyone believed the sky raced around the Earth each night. Aryabhata said no — it is the Earth that turns, quietly, all night long, like a boat drifting past the riverbank. He also explained that the moon has no light of its own; it simply catches the sunlight and shines it back to us.

He even worked out how long a year is, and he got it astonishingly close to right. Almost a thousand years passed before the rest of the world agreed with him. Aryabhata reminds us that being young is never a reason to stop wondering.

stories.name: Fatima al-Fihri
stories.title: The Woman Who Built the First University
stories.hook: She was given money of her own, and she chose to build a school for everybody.
text: Fatima al-Fihri was born in Tunisia, and when she was small her family travelled west to the busy city of Fez, in Morocco. Imagine the narrow streets: donkeys clopping past, the smell of warm bread and mint tea, and voices calling from every doorway.

Fatima and her sister Mariam loved to learn. When they grew up, their father left them money of their own. Fatima could have bought anything she wished. Instead she sat down and thought carefully about what her whole city needed most.

She decided to build a mosque with a school beside it. It took years, and people say she fasted every single day until the last stone was laid. Her sister Mariam built another mosque nearby, so the two sisters gave their city two gifts at once.

Fatima's school was called al-Qarawiyyin. Students came to study numbers, medicine, the stars and languages — and they never stopped coming. It is the oldest university in the world that is still teaching today, more than one thousand one hundred years later. One African woman decided to share what she had, and children are still learning there because of her kindness.

stories.name: Ibn al-Haytham
stories.title: The Boy Who Wanted to See for Himself
stories.hook: Everyone argued about how eyes work. He decided to test it.
text: Long ago, in the busy river city of Basra, a boy named Ibn al-Haytham was born. Boats came and went on the water. Later he travelled to Cairo, where the sun was bright and the market was loud, and he found a quiet room to think in.

Even as a child, he loved questions more than answers. Grown-ups had argued for hundreds of years about one puzzle: how do we see? Some very clever thinkers said our eyes shoot out tiny invisible rays, like little lamps, to touch the world.

Ibn al-Haytham did something new. Instead of only arguing, he tested. He made a room completely dark and let one thin beam of light in through a tiny hole. On the wall, the whole street outside appeared, upside down and glowing. It was the very first camera. So light comes into our eyes, he said. Not out of them.

For years he sat writing his great Book of Optics, page after quiet page. He taught the world a wonderful rule: if you believe something, go and check it. That rule is called the scientific method, and we still use it every single day.

stories.name: Murasaki Shikibu
stories.title: The Girl Who Listened at the Door
stories.hook: She wrote the very first novel in the world, a thousand years ago.
text: A thousand years ago in Japan, a girl was born near the royal court, in a house of paper walls and wooden floors that squeaked. Outside, pine trees dripped after the rain. Her family called her by a nickname we still use today: Murasaki.

Her brother had lessons in difficult Chinese writing. Girls were not supposed to learn it. So Murasaki sat outside the sliding door and listened, and learned it faster than he did. Her father sighed and said it was a pity she had not been born a boy. Murasaki said nothing, and kept on learning.

When she grew up she served the empress. She watched everything: the rustle of silk robes, the moon rising over the garden pond, who was kind, who was lonely, who loved whom. And she began to write it all down, one brushstroke at a time.

Her story was called The Tale of Genji. It was long and tender, full of people who change and feel and make mistakes, just like real people. Many scholars say it is the first novel ever written, anywhere in the world. A girl who listened at the door wrote it.

stories.name: Bi Sheng
stories.title: The Man Who Made Letters That Moved
stories.hook: One wrong word used to ruin a whole page. He fixed that.
text: In China, almost a thousand years ago, there lived a quiet craftsman named Bi Sheng. He was not rich and he was not famous. He worked with his hands, in a workshop that smelled of ink and clay.

In those days, printing a page meant carving every word of it into one big block of wood. It took weeks. And if a carver slipped and cut one wrong letter, the whole block was spoiled. All that work, gone.

Bi Sheng had a beautiful idea. What if each little character were made separately, out of baked clay? He set them side by side in an iron frame, holding them with warm sticky resin. When the page was printed, he warmed the frame again, and every tiny character lifted out, ready to be used again in a brand-new order.

That idea is called movable type, and it came four hundred years before printing began in Europe. Because of a working man with clever hands, books could be made faster, and stories could travel to more children than ever before. Perhaps even this one.

stories.name: Al-Jazari
stories.title: The Engineer Who Built Wonder
stories.hook: His elephant clock chirped like a bird, every single hour.
text: Long ago, in a palace in the land we now call south-eastern Turkey, there lived an engineer named Al-Jazari. His workshop was full of gears and water and rope. He did not build machines to be useful only. He built them to make people smile.

He made a great elephant clock, taller than a grown-up. Every hour a little man on its back struck a cymbal, ting!, and a small bird on top chirped and turned around. He made a boat of mechanical musicians that floated on the palace lake and played music for the guests.

He made a hand-washing machine with a gentle servant figure who poured out water, then held out a towel for you. And when he finished, he did the kindest thing of all: he wrote a big book with careful drawings, so that anyone else could build them too.

Al-Jazari also invented the crankshaft and clever water pumps that are still inside engines today. And his musical machines, which could be set to play different tunes, were the world's first programmable machines — the great-grandparents of every robot. He built them all for joy.

stories.name: Ibn Battuta
stories.title: The Boy Who Kept Walking
stories.hook: He left home for one journey — and came back twenty-nine years later.
text: Long ago, in the white city of Tangier in Morocco, a boy named Ibn Battuta was born. He could hear the sea from his window. Ships came and went, and he wondered where they were going.

When he was twenty-one, he kissed his mother goodbye and set off alone. He meant to travel to Mecca and then come straight home. But at every city he reached, someone told him about the next one — and his feet would not stay still.

He rode camels across hot deserts and sailed the Indian Ocean. He saw Egypt, and the busy Swahili harbours of Mombasa and Kilwa, and Persia, and India, and the Maldives, and China. Altogether he walked and rode and sailed about 120,000 kilometres — further than any traveller of his time.

When he finally came home, the sultan said, 'Tell everything.' So a writer sat beside him and wrote it all down in a book called the Rihla, which means 'The Journey'. Because one curious boy kept going, we still know how those cities looked and sounded and tasted, seven hundred years ago. Goodnight, little traveller.

stories.name: Ahmed Baba
stories.title: The City Where Books Were Worth More Than Gold
stories.hook: He owned 1,600 books — and called it the smallest library in his family.
text: In the sandy heart of Mali stood a city called Timbuktu. It had golden walls of mud, and inside those walls were libraries. Scholars came from far away just to read there. In Timbuktu, people said, a good book was worth more than gold.

In that city a boy named Ahmed Baba grew up in a family of teachers. Books lay open on every table. He learned to read early, and he loved questions — about law, about grammar, about the stories of long-ago kings.

When he grew up he wrote more than forty books of his own. He gathered a library of 1,600 volumes and smiled and said it was the smallest library among his relatives. Once, soldiers came and he was taken far from home for a while. Everywhere he went people honoured him and asked him to teach — but he missed his city, and at last he came home to Timbuktu.

Even today, families in Timbuktu keep those old manuscripts wrapped safely, page by careful page. They remind us that Africa has been writing down its wisdom for a very, very long time. Sleep well, little scholar.

stories.name: Nana Asma'u
stories.title: The Teachers Who Walked From Village to Village
stories.hook: She wore a special hat, so everyone knew a teacher had arrived.
text: In northern Nigeria, in a land of red dust and tall grass, a princess was born and named Asma'u. Her family loved learning, and she was taught to read from the time she was very small.

Asma'u grew up clever and calm. She could read and write in four languages — Arabic, Fulfulde, Hausa and Tamacheq. She wrote more than sixty poems and books, and people would gather just to hear her words read aloud.

But her greatest idea was this: girls and women in far-off villages had no school. So she trained a group of women teachers called the yan-taru, which means 'those who come together'. They walked from village to village, teaching women and girls to read. Each one wore a special hat, so that the moment she arrived, everyone knew: a teacher is here.

Two hundred years later, people in Nigeria still tell her name with pride, and girls still learn because she began it. One woman with a pen and a plan can open a door for thousands. Goodnight, clever one.

stories.name: Maria Sibylla Merian
stories.title: The Girl Who Watched Caterpillars
stories.hook: Everyone said insects came from mud. She kept watching until she saw the truth.
text: In Germany, long ago, a little girl named Maria grew up in a house full of painters. There were brushes everywhere, and jars of colour, and the smell of fresh paper.

When she was thirteen she began keeping silkworms and caterpillars in little boxes in her room. She fed them fresh leaves every morning and drew them every day. In those days, most people believed insects simply appeared out of the mud, like magic.

But Maria kept watching, quietly, patiently. And one day she saw the whole secret with her own eyes: a tiny egg, then a caterpillar, then a still chrysalis, then wings. That change is called metamorphosis. She painted each creature sitting on the very plant it liked to eat — something nobody had thought to do before.

Then, when she was fifty-two, she and her daughter sailed all the way to Suriname in South America to paint the insects of the rainforest. Very few women made such journeys then. Her pictures are still hanging in museums today — still beautiful, and still exactly right. Goodnight, patient watcher.

stories.name: Mary Anning
stories.title: The Girl Who Found Dragons in the Cliffs
stories.hook: She was poor, she was small, and she found creatures nobody knew existed.
text: In a little seaside town called Lyme Regis, in England, a girl named Mary was born. The sea wind smelled of salt. Grey cliffs stood tall above the beach, and the waves knocked pieces of them down every winter.

Mary's family often had very little to eat. So she and her brother walked the beach with baskets, looking for smooth curly stones called fossils to sell to visitors. Mary had the sharpest eyes of anyone. She could spot a bone the size of a button.

When Mary was about twelve, she brushed away the mud and found something enormous — a whole creature, long as a boat, with a pointed nose and huge round eyes. It was an ichthyosaur, a sea animal from long, long ago. Later she found the first plesiosaurs, and a creature with wings. She borrowed books and copied them out by hand until she understood every bone.

In those days, gentlemen scientists bought her fossils and forgot to write her name. But the fossils remembered. Today her name is on museum walls, and children still say the little rhyme about the girl who sells seashells by the seashore. A child on a beach changed what the whole world knows about long ago.

stories.name: Florence Nightingale
stories.title: The Lady with the Lamp
stories.hook: She carried a little lamp at night — and a notebook full of numbers by day.
text: Florence was born in the beautiful city of Florence, in Italy, and that is how she got her name. Her family was English and very rich. They had big gardens, soft carpets and quiet afternoons, and they expected Florence to grow up and live a quiet life too.

But Florence wanted to be a nurse. When she said so, everyone was surprised. Nursing was hard, messy work. Florence said it gently, then said it again, and kept saying it until they let her go. Sometimes being kind and being stubborn are the same thing.

Far away, she found hospitals that were crowded and dirty. So she got to work. She opened the windows to let in fresh air, scrubbed the floors, brought clean water and warm food. At night she walked between the beds holding a small light, checking that everyone was comfortable. They called her the Lady with the Lamp.

Then Florence did something just as powerful. She counted. She wrote down what happened to every person, and drew big coloured diagrams like flower petals to show it. Her pictures proved that clean air and clean water saved more people than anything else. Powerful men looked at her drawings and changed hospitals forever. She opened the very first real school for nurses — and her lamp is still shining.

stories.name: Grace Hopper
stories.title: The Woman Who Taught Machines Our Words
stories.hook: At seven, she opened seven clocks. Later, she opened up computers for everyone.
text: In the United States, a curious girl named Grace wanted to know what was inside things. When she was seven, she took apart an alarm clock to see how it ticked. Then another. Then another — seven clocks in all! Her mother smiled and said she could keep one, but she had to put that one back together.

Grace loved numbers, and she grew up to be a mathematician. Then she joined the navy, and they gave her a machine as big as a room. It clanked and clattered and did sums. Grace was not scared of it at all. She read its bumps and switches like a story.

Everyone said computers only understood numbers. Grace thought that was silly. Why not let people write in words? So she built the first compiler — a clever program that turns writing people understand into instructions machines understand. That idea grew into a language called COBOL, which still helps banks count money today.

One day the big machine stopped. Grace looked inside and found a little moth resting in the wires. She taped it gently into her notebook, and that is why fixing a computer is called debugging. Grace's least favourite sentence in the world was 'we have always done it this way.' She liked 'let us try something new' much better.

stories.name: Hedy Lamarr
stories.title: The Film Star Who Invented Wi-Fi
stories.hook: The world looked at her face. Inside her head, an idea was waiting for us.
text: In Vienna, a city of music in Austria, a girl named Hedy walked through the streets holding her father's hand. He explained everything they passed. How a printing press pushed ink onto paper. How a streetcar hummed along its rails. How an engine breathed. Hedy asked question after question, and never ran out.

She grew up to become one of the most famous film actresses in the whole world. But saying lines in front of a camera felt a bit boring to her. So at home she kept an inventing table, covered in wires and springs and drawings, and between takes she would sit and tinker.

With a friend who wrote music, Hedy had a wonderful idea. What if a radio message did not stay on one channel, but hopped quickly from one to another, like a bird skipping between branches? Then nobody could block it or listen in. They wrote it down and gave it away. For many years, nobody used it.

But good ideas are patient. That idea is called frequency hopping, and today it lives inside Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and GPS — in tablets, in phones, in maps that find the way home. People had told Hedy she was only a pretty face. She laughed and said looking glamorous is easy; you just stand still. Thinking is the fun part. Never let anyone decide for you which part of your mind counts.
